Only 22 of 130 rftypes XMLs declare a <get request=…> frame at all (all mains-powered or BURST: rf_d*, rf_s*, rf_cf, rf_ddc, rf_keymatic, rf_winmatic, rf_sec_sd, rf_ou_led16); the rest resolve to store/internal reads with no frame.
• BidCos-Wired (hs485d) is not skipped by our code and does reach the bus: HS485PhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:83-115 has the same cache-age test and then SendMessage. 7 of 18 hs485types XMLs declare a <get>. Wired devices are mains-powered on RS-485 — bus traffic, no wake-up queue, no 1 % duty cycle.

Separately, the real steady-state cost is not radio but round trips: sentinelCacheTTL is 5 minutes (value_cache.go:39-44), the same as DefaultUnobservedSweepInterval, and the singleflight key is per-parameter (`<channel>:V:<param>`), so N never-answered parameters on one channel produce N identical getParamset calls per tick, indefinitely.

CUxD (BIN-RPC) is out of scope — its paramset handler is not in this tree.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU reached the device for this call, handleGetValueCommand would have queued an HmipTransaction the way its sibling handleAskValueCommand does. The check demonstrably produces the other answer where the cause is present: handleAskValueCommand queues one, and rfd's RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand::GetData calls SendFrame/QueueAfterWakeupFrame. Same on our side: had the sweep used getValue, runLoadValuesParamset would call loader.GetValue rather than loader.GetParamset.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD ON ITS CORE CLAIM, DEMOTED FROM `contradicted` BECAUSE THE STATED firmwareValue IS OVERBROAD. I re-verified every leg.

Our code, verified myself: LoadValue on a VALUES key → runLoad → runLoadValuesParamset → loader.GetParamset(channel,"VALUES") (value_cache.go:250, :333). tryLoad passes direct=false (unobserved_sweep.go:196), so the `!direct && (VirtualDevices || BidCosRF)` sentinel short-circuit at value_cache.go:329-332 does apply to the sweep. Both of the prior agent's corrections to the premise hold.

HmIP leg, re-read verbatim: DeviceUtil#getParameterSet sends BackendCommandType.DEVICE_VALUE_GET on the "backend.command.hmip" bus; BackendCommandHandler dispatches DEVICE_VALUE_GET to handleGetValueCommand, which walks StateDescription.getParameters(), reads channel.getParameterValue(name), skips nulls, and sends RESPONSE_STATUS_DATA. No HmipTransaction, no queueTransaction. The sibling DEVICE_VALUE_ASK is the only path that reaches TransactionTaskFactory#createRequestStatusTransaction. Confirmed. I also confirmed the prior agent's INSTALL_TEST / CURRENT_ILLUMINATION special-cases in LegacyServiceHandler#getValue, and add that plain HmIP getValue is in-memory too (DeviceUtil#getValue ends at channel.getParameterValue).

WHERE THE STATED firmwareValue IS WRONG. "On every interface the sweep can actually reach, the wire call is getParamset(VALUES) and the CCU answers it from its own in-memory model without emitting a frame" is false for BidCos-Wired, which the sweep does reach (only VirtualDevices and BidCos-RF are skipped) and which hmenum lists as a normal interface. On rfd/hs485d, getParamset is NOT one in-memory read: RFChannel::GetParamsetValues → RFParamset::Get → HSSParamset::Get iterates every readable parameter and calls param->GetValue, which lands in the physical-data-interface GetData — the same frame path as getValue. HS485PhysicalDataInterfaceCommand::GetData:83-115 has the cache-age test then SendMessage. 7 of the 15 hs485types XMLs declare a <get request=…>. The prior agent's own body says this; its firmwareValue line contradicts it. Boundary: the wake-up worry is dead (sleeping devices live on BidCos-RF, skipped, and on HmIP, in-memory; wired devices are mains-powered), but "no frame at all" is HmIP/HmIP-Wired only.

Two corrections to the prior counts: 127 rftypes XMLs, not 130, and 15 hs485types, not 18 (the 22 / 7 <get> counts are right). CUxD is genuinely out of scope — its paramset handler is not in any tree here, so its leg is unverified, not confirmed.

One addition on HSSParamset::Get:162-175: it returns false as soon as ONE parameter's GetValue fails, so on rfd/hs485d a single unanswerable parameter fails the whole getParamset — a different failure shape from the per-parameter sentinel our cache expects.

The round-trip cost note is correct as stated: sentinelCacheTTL = 5 min (value_cache.go:39-44) equals DefaultUnobservedSweepInterval (unobserved_sweep_job.go:21) and singleflightKey is `<channel>:V:<param>` (value_cache.go:235-241), so each never-answered parameter is its own getParamset every tick.

all.title: Install mode is reported active whenever getInstallMode returns a positive number
all.ourValue: secs is remaining seconds; enabled := secs > 0; countdown := secs seconds
all.firmwareValue: identical on both interface families — remaining seconds, 0 when off, never negative, no permanent sentinel
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:638-652; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:550-558; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.h:562; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/interface/getinstallmode.tcl; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler#getInstallMode → de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.AccessPointUtil#getInclusionMode
all.finding:
Our call is jsonrpc Interface.getInstallMode. That method is a pass-through: getinstallmode.tcl documents "Restzeit des Anlernmodus in Sekunden" and does nothing but `xmlrpc $interface(URL) getInstallMode`, so the answer is whatever the interface process returns.

BidCos-RF (rfd), verbatim from XmlRpcMethods.cpp:638-641: "Diese Methode gibt die verbleibende Restzeit im Installations-Modus in Sekunden zurück. 0 bedeutet, der Installations-Modus ist nicht aktiv." The implementation (RFManager.cpp:550-558) returns 0 when !install_mode, else (install_mode_expires - time_millis() + 999)/1000 floored at 1 s — so while active it is ≥1, never 0 and never negative. There is no permanent mode to encode: SetInstallMode clamps seconds to INSTALL_MODE_MAX_TIME = 600 (RFManager.h:562), and setInstallMode's own doc says "seconds darf maximal 600 sein. Defaultwert ist 60."

HmIP: LegacyServiceHandler#getInstallMode delegates to AccessPointUtil#getInclusionMode, which returns (inclusionTimestamp - now)/1000 when the timestamp is in the future AND the inclusion mode is not MODE_OFF, and 0 otherwise. Also seconds, also 0-for-off, also no sentinel.

One unit-in-the-last-place difference between the two, harmless for our rule: rfd rounds the remainder up and floors at 1 s, HmIP truncates down — so HmIP can report 0 during the final sub-second of an active install mode where rfd reports 1. `enabled := secs > 0` therefore drops HmIP install mode up to one second early; nothing else follows from it.

Unsupported interface: HmIP throws an RpcRemoteException (AccessPointNotFoundException), and the tcl wrapper turns any XML-RPC fault into a JSON-RPC error, which our loop already routes to the err branch (skip + firstErr). Correct handling.
all.negativeControl: Had the value been a mode enum or carried a permanent sentinel, RFManager::GetInstallMode would not compute install_mode_expires - time_millis(), and the method's own doc comment would not read "Restzeit … in Sekunden. 0 bedeutet, der Installations-Modus ist nicht aktiv." The same file shows the check can produce the other answer: getKeyMismatchDevice returns a string, and setInstallMode's third argument is a real InstallModes enum validated against INSTALL_OFF..INSTALL_PUSH_DEFAULT_CONFIG.
all.challengeNote:
THE TWO INTERFACE FAMILIES THE PRIOR AGENT CHECKED ARE CONFIRMED VERBATIM; DEMOTED FROM `confirmed` BECAUSE OUR CODE POLLS A THIRD INTERFACE THE GROUNDING NEVER TOUCHED.

Re-read and confirmed. rfd doc comment at XmlRpcMethods.cpp:638-641 verbatim: "Diese Methode gibt die verbleibende Restzeit im Installations-Modus in Sekunden zurueck. 0 bedeutet, der Installations-Modus ist nicht aktiv." RFManager::GetInstallMode:550-558 verbatim: `if (!install_mode) return 0; int64_t time_remain = install_mode_expires - time_millis(); time_remain += 999; if (time_remain <= 1000) time_remain = 1000; return time_remain / 1000;` — the prior agent's "+999 then floored at 1 s" transcription is exact (the floor is on the millisecond value at 1000). SetInstallMode clamps `if (seconds > INSTALL_MODE_MAX_TIME) seconds = INSTALL_MODE_MAX_TIME` with the enum at RFManager.h:562 = 600. HMIPServer AccessPointUtil#getInclusionMode verbatim: returns `(int)((inclusionTimestamp - now) / 1000L)` only when `inclusionTimestamp > now && getInclusionMode() != InclusionMode.MODE_OFF`, else 0 — truncating, as claimed, so the one-ULP asymmetry the prior agent flagged is real. The tcl wrapper is a bare pass-through and dispatch.tcl:132-145 does turn a non-zero catch status into jsonrpc_error, so the fault handling claim holds.

WHAT THE GROUNDING MISSES. hmenum.InterfacesSupportingInstallMode (pkg/hmenum/interface.go:190-194) contains BidCosRF, BidCosWired and HmIPRF, and WireInstallModeDPs (internal/central/adapter/install_mode.go:102-107) registers a DP for each. hs485d exposes no getInstallMode at all — its full registered method set is listDevices, searchDevices, getDeviceDescription, getParamsetDescription, getParamsetId, putParamset, getParamset, deleteDevice, getValue, setValue, getLinkPeers, getLinks, addLink, setLinkInfo, getLinkInfo, removeLink, clearConfigCache, activateLinkParamset, init, updateFirmware, reportValueUsage, logLevel, replaceDevice, getLGWStatus, listReplaceableDevices, ping. Nothing in src/hs485d matches /installmode/i. So on any install with an HMW interface, loadInstallMode's BidCos-Wired leg can only ever take the err branch, setting firstErr on every hub poll forever and leaving that DP permanently unset. The rule about interpreting the returned integer is unaffected — the boundary is that a third polled interface returns no integer at all, and the cited firmware is silent on it because the method is absent.

The prior agent's "unsupported interface" paragraph covered only the HmIP AccessPointNotFoundException case, not this one.

all.title: An unknown TIME_BASE silently decodes as one second, and preset encoding breaks ties by list position
all.ourValue: timeBaseSeconds {0:0.1, 1:1, 2:5, 3:10, 4:60, 5:300, 6:600, 7:3600}, with unit=1.0 for any base outside that set
all.firmwareValue: every LINK *_TIME_BASE in the descriptor corpus is TYPE ENUM, MIN BASE_100_MS, MAX BASE_1_H, VALUE_LIST ['BASE_100_MS','BASE_1_S','BASE_5_S','BASE_10_S','BASE_1_M','BASE_5_M','BASE_10_M','BASE_1_H'] — 8 entries, indices 0..7, matching our table exactly. One step wider the same *_BASE family is different: HmIP-SPDR MASTER EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE is ['100MS','S','M','H'], where index 2 means 60 s and index 3 means 3600 s, not our 5 s and 10 s
all.missingInput: whether a running CCU sets the service property Legacy.Parameter.ReplaceEnumValueWithOrdinal (code default false) — i.e. whether the legacy XML-RPC surface exchanges the ordinal at all or the label string. I could not read a shipped properties file for it; that half stays unverified.
all.citation: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/*.json — LINK *_TIME_BASE: TYPE=ENUM, MIN=BASE_100_MS, MAX=BASE_1_H, VALUE_LIST as above (2940 occurrences across 64 files, e.g. HMIP-PS.json, HmIP-BDT.json, HmIP-ASIR-2.json, ELV-SH-BS2.json); outlier HmIP-SPDR.json VCU1289997:1 MASTER EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE VALUE_LIST ['100MS','S','M','H']. HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#addDesriptionOfParameter; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#convertParameterValue; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.typeconversion.converter.StringEnumToInteger. Absence check: grep TIME_BASE over ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/*.xml → 0 hits.
all.finding:
Right-surface note first: LINK *_TIME_BASE is an HmIP-only parameter. It appears in 64 descriptor files, none of them HM-* (BidCos), and the string TIME_BASE does not occur in any of the 130 ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/*.xml. The bundle's firmwareQuestion pointed at rftypes and src/rfd, where the answer is simply absent; the authority for this surface is the HmIP side.

The base table: confirmed, and the ordinal→unit relation is read from the firmware rather than assumed. addDesriptionOfParameter sets VALUE_LIST = StringEnumToInteger#getEnumStrings() for every ENUM parameter, and convertParameterValue maps an inbound Number n to values[n] over that same array (rejecting n >= values.length as "out of range") and an outbound label to its index in it. So "index into VALUE_LIST" is the firmware's own ordinal, not a convention I supplied. Note StringEnumToInteger separately supports a sparse physical mapping (constructor with int[] enumValues, and an offset variant) — but that sparseness lives strictly below the legacy surface; what our SPA writes is always the VALUE_LIST index.

Consequence for the unknown-base fallback: on the surface ClassifyLinkParameter actually serves (LINK paramset, suffix _TIME_BASE), a base outside 0..7 cannot occur — the domain is closed by the 8-entry VALUE_LIST and the CCU rejects an out-of-range ordinal before it reaches a device. The unit=1.0 branch is unreachable there. Where it stops being true is one step wider: the sibling MASTER parameter EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE uses a 4-entry list with a different meaning per index. Our classifier misses it on both counts — it requires the literal suffix _TIME_BASE (EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE ends in D+TIME_BASE, not _TIME_BASE) and only runs on LINK — so the boundary runs exactly at those two conditions. Widen either and the table becomes wrong rather than merely unused.

The tie-break half of the candidate is not a firmware question, and it is not on a device path. The firmware defines the encoding of a (base,factor) pair; it says nothing about how a UI snaps an arbitrary second-count to a preset. And EncodeTimeValue has no production caller in the repo (grep: only its own definition and its internal DecodeTimeValue call). What ships is GetTimePresets → uischema_link.go:167 → hmapi.UISchemaTimePreset → ParameterTimePair.svelte, where onPresetChange writes preset.a / preset.b by list index — never by nearest-seconds. Within each of the three preset lists all 21/10/9 durations are distinct, so no two presets can even collide on an exact value. reachesDevice is true because that integer base is written to the LINK paramset, but the tie-break itself is unreachable.
all.negativeControl: Had a ninth base or a differently-scaled base existed on this surface, at least one LINK *_TIME_BASE VALUE_LIST in the corpus would carry a different length or different labels. The corpus demonstrably produces that other answer: HmIP-SPDR EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE comes back with 4 entries and a different scale, which is how I know the survey distinguishes the two rather than reporting one shape for everything.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD, TIER RAISED FROM 2 TO 1, AND THE BOUNDARY CORRECTED — THE PRIOR AGENT'S COUNTEREXAMPLE WAS THE WEAK ONE.

Right-surface note confirmed independently: `TIME_BASE` does not occur in any of the 127 rftypes or 15 hs485types XMLs. On BidCos the LINK time parameter is a single FLOAT in seconds (rf_s.xml: `SHORT_ON_TIME`, logical float min 0.0 max 108000.0 with special_value NOT_USED=111600.0) and the base/factor split lives inside the firmware conversion, not on the paramset surface. The base/factor pair is HmIP-only.

TIER 1 UPGRADE. The base→unit table need not rest on the descriptor corpus at all: the CCU's own easymode helper carries it as an ordinal-indexed <select>, hmip_helper.tcl:2847-2854, values 0..7 = optionUnit100MS, 1S, 5S, 10S, 1M, 5M, 10M, H — exactly our timeBaseSeconds. hmipHeatingClimateControlTransceiverEffect.tcl:49-56 emits the same list with class='BASE_100_MS' … class='BASE_1_H' on ordinals 0..7, which ties the descriptor VALUE_LIST labels to the ordinals in one Tier 1 file. And KEY_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:58 pins the domain on the LINK surface itself: `{7 range 0 - 7}`.

I ALSO GROUNDED AN INPUT THE PRIOR AGENT ASSERTED WITHOUT CITING. Its "index into VALUE_LIST is the firmware's own ordinal" rests on DeviceUtil#convertParameterValue, whose entire enum branch is gated on a static flag `replaceEnumValueWithOrdinal` that defaults to FALSE in the Java (set from ServiceProperties "Legacy.Parameter.ReplaceEnumValueWithOrdinal", default false, in LocalServer and HMIPServer). If that flag were off, the legacy surface would carry enum STRINGS and our integer table would never apply. The shipped CCU config sets it to true — crRFD.conf:47. That is the missing input; it now reads from the source instead of from the shape of the answer.

BOUNDARY, CORRECTED. The prior agent named EVENT_BLINDTIME_BASE (HmIP-SPDR) as the counterexample. That one is a MASTER parameter and never reaches ClassifyLinkParameter at all, so it is the weak case. The sharp one, which the prior agent missed, sits on exactly our surface: SHORT_SWITCHING_INTERVAL_BASE is a LINK-paramset parameter on HmIP-FAL230-C10 and HmIPW-FAL230-C6 whose VALUE_LIST is the shifted 8-entry table (ordinal 0 = 1 s, ordinal 7 = 1 day), matching hmip_helper.tcl's getTimeUnitComboBoxB. Our table would be wrong for every ordinal there. It escapes only on the literal suffix test at link_param_metadata.go:191-193 (`_BASE` matches, `_TIME_BASE` does not), i.e. the boundary is one substring wide, on the same paramset. Widening that test to `_BASE` — an obvious-looking cleanup — silently misdecodes it. The SPA repeats the same literal test (assets/ui/src/lib/channel/time-pairs.ts:188), so both sides are consistent, and both sides are one edit away from being wrong.

TIE-BREAK HALF. Confirmed, and stronger than stated: EncodeTimeValue has no production caller (grep over the repo returns its definition, its own DecodeTimeValue call, and three tests), and DecodeTimeValue's only caller is EncodeTimeValue — so timeBaseSeconds is unreached by production code entirely, and the unit=1.0 fallback is doubly unreachable. GetTimePresets (uischema_link.go:167) emits base/factor/label with no seconds arithmetic, and ParameterTimePair.svelte:75-79 writes preset.a / preset.b by list index. reachesDevice is therefore false for the decode table and the tie-break; the integer base that does reach the LINK paramset comes from the hand-written preset lists, not from this table.

all.title: The 3-second test-fire duration claims HmIP "Test-Alarm" parity with no cited source
all.site: internal/alarm/outputs/testfire.go:15-17 (used at :107 and :117 for the OnConfig.Duration and the stop watchdog)
all.ourValue: 3 s, justified as parity with an HmIP "Test-Alarm"
all.firmwareValue: the CCU has no Test-Alarm. Its HmIP siren dialog is setAlarmDialogTitle = "Alarm auslösen", and its fixed duration list is 3 s / 10 s / 30 s / 2 min / 10 min plus a free entry (unit S or M, value 0–600). 3 s is the first and shortest entry. The device descriptor's own DURATION_VALUE DEFAULT is 0
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/pages/msg/asir_setAlarm.htm (DurationSelect options 3_S, 10_S, 30_S, 2_M, 10_M, setDuration; DurationValue range hint "(0 - 600)"); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www_source/ise/js/iseAlarmSirenHMIP.js:85-96; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/lang/de/translate.lang.option.js:185 "optionUnit3S" : "3 Sekunden"; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/lang/de/translate.lang.extension.js:685 "setAlarmDialogTitle" : "Alarm auslösen"; Tier 2 ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-ASIR.json VCU9333179:3 DURATION_VALUE {TYPE INTEGER, MIN 0, MAX 16343, DEFAULT 0, OPERATIONS 2} and DURATION_UNIT {TYPE ENUM, VALUE_LIST ['S','M','H'], DEFAULT 'S'}
all.finding:
The named authority does not exist. There is no "Test-Alarm" action, button or string anywhere in the CCU's HmIP siren surface: the only alarm-firing control is iseAlarmSirenHMIP.activateAlarm, whose dialog title translates as "Alarm auslösen" and which writes DURATION_UNIT / DURATION_VALUE / ACOUSTIC_ALARM_SELECTION / OPTICAL_ALARM_SELECTION as a single Interface.putParamset to VALUES. Grepping the German language files for Testalarm / Test-Alarm returns nothing alarm-related. So the comment's parity claim is unsupported as written.

The number itself is nevertheless the CCU's own: 3 s is the first and shortest of the five fixed durations that dialog offers (3_S / 10_S / 30_S / 2_M / 10_M), i.e. what an operator gets by opening the dialog and firing without changing the duration. That is a real firmware-offered value and a defensible source for a short bounded activation — it is simply not "the Test-Alarm duration". The descriptor default is not a source either: HmIP-ASIR DURATION_VALUE declares DEFAULT 0 with DURATION_UNIT DEFAULT 'S', so the device default is 0 s, which cannot be an audible test.

Same file, one Tier 1 mapping worth having on the record because our own EncodeTimerDuration depends on it: the CCU writes DURATION_UNIT as an int with oUnit.S = 0, M = 1, H = 2, D = 3 (iseAlarmSirenHMIP.js:85), while the ASIR descriptor's VALUE_LIST is only ['S','M','H'] — the WebUI carries a fourth code the ASIR channel does not declare.

Recommendation for the comment, if it is rewritten: cite the dialog's duration list, not a Test-Alarm.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU shipped a fixed test duration, iseAlarmSirenHMIP would write a constant instead of the dialog's selection, or a separate test action would exist — and the check does distinguish the two cases: the same file shows the CCU writing constants elsewhere (oUnit's fixed 0/1/2/3 codes) and reading the dialog for the duration. Had 3 s been absent from the CCU's own options, the DurationSelect list would have started at 10_S.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD AND PROMOTED FROM `narrowed` TO `contradicted`. The comment's named authority does not exist; that is a contradiction of the comment, not a narrowing of it.

I re-ran the absence check with a negative control (below): zero hits for testalarm / test-alarm / test_alarm anywhere under www/ or src/webui/. The only HmIP siren firing control is iseAlarmSirenHMIP.activateAlarm, whose dialog title resolves to setAlarmDialogTitle. Verbatim from the language file, escaping and all: "setAlarmDialogTitle" : "Alarm ausl%F6sen" — note the prior agent quoted the decoded form, which is a paraphrase of the file.

The number is nevertheless the CCU's own, and slightly better grounded than the prior agent argued: 3_S is not merely the first option in the list, it is what the dialog actually loads. asir_setalarmdialog.js calls setTimeShortCut() from bindElements() at construction, and setTimeShortCut splits the selected option on "_" and writes value=3, unit=S into the duration fields. An operator who opens the dialog and confirms without touching anything fires a 3-second alarm. That is a real firmware-offered value; it is simply not "the Test-Alarm duration", because there is none.

The descriptor default is confirmed as no source: DURATION_VALUE DEFAULT 0 with DURATION_UNIT DEFAULT 'S' on all three ASIR variants — 0 s, which cannot be an audible test.

The collateral Tier 1 mapping is confirmed verbatim (iseAlarmSirenHMIP.js:86: `oUnit.S = 0; oUnit.M = 1; oUnit.H = 2; oUnit.D = 3;`) and it does ground our own encoder: pkg/hmenum/timer.go:29-35 declares TimerUnitSeconds=0, Minutes=1, Hours=2, which internal/model/custom/mixins.go:219-249 writes as DURATION_UNIT. Two additions the prior agent did not note — the D option is commented out in asir_setAlarm.htm:66-67 and setMaxValue only handles S and M, so the fourth code is unreachable from that dialog; and the "(0 - 600)" hint is only the initial HTML, replaced by 10 when the unit is M.

The recommended rewrite stands, with a correction: cite the dialog's *default* duration, not just its list.

all.title: The MP3 chirp volume default 0.5 is a bare literal on a device write
all.ourValue: 0.5, on a scale the site does not document, written as ParameterLevel
all.firmwareValue: HmIP-MP3P channel 2 (our IPSoundPlayer primary channel) LEVEL: TYPE FLOAT, MIN 0.0, MAX 1.01, DEFAULT 0.0, UNIT "100%", OPERATIONS 7, CONTROL ACOUSTIC_SIGNAL_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER.LEVEL
all.citation: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-MP3P.json VCU1543608:2 VALUES LEVEL {MIN 0.0, MAX 1.01, DEFAULT 0.0, UNIT "100%", TYPE FLOAT, OPERATIONS 7, FLAGS 1, CONTROL ACOUSTIC_SIGNAL_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER.LEVEL}; contrast ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HM-OU-CFM-Pl.json, whose channels 1 and 2 declare only STATE/ON_TIME/INHIBIT/WORKING/INSTALL_TEST/SUBMIT and no LEVEL at all
all.finding:
The scale question is settled and our value is safe on it: the parameter the chirp writes is LEVEL on the sound-player channel, declared FLOAT 0.0 … 1.01 with UNIT "100%" — a 0..1 fraction, so 0.5 is 50 % and neither inaudible nor full volume. The risk the reader named (a 0..100 or 0..255 scale) is ruled out.

What is not settled is the default. The descriptor's own DEFAULT for LEVEL is 0.0 — silence — so no firmware value backs 0.5. It is a product choice, and it is duplicated: chirp.go:73 has `vol := 0.5` and sound.go:348 has `const defaultVolume = 0.5` applied at :386-390 whenever `volume <= 0`. The second one also means our layer cannot express "write LEVEL 0" through PlaySound at all — a caller passing 0 silently gets 50 %. StopSound is the only path that writes LEVEL 0.

Right-surface note: the bundle's firmwareQuestion named the HM-OU-CFM-Pl family alongside HmIP-MP3P. That device is not on this path and could not answer the question anyway — it exposes no LEVEL parameter, only SWITCH.STATE and ON_TIME, and our SoundPlayer profiles (IPSoundPlayer, IPSoundPlayerLed) are registered for DeviceType "hmip-mp3p" only (internal/model/custom/profiles.go:1150-1167).
all.negativeControl: Had LEVEL been a percent or byte scale, MAX would read 100 or 255 rather than 1.01, and the corpus does report large maxima where they exist — DURATION_VALUE on the same device family comes back MAX 16343 and CURRENT_ILLUMINATION MAX 163830 — so the survey is not flattening every maximum to a small number. Had 0.5 been the device's own default, the descriptor's DEFAULT field would read 0.5 instead of 0.0.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD, TIER RAISED FROM 2 TO 1 FOR THE HALF THAT MATTERS.

The scale question no longer rests on the descriptor alone. The CCU's own easymode profile for the ACOUSTIC_SIGNAL_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER channel — the exact channel role our IPSoundPlayer binds — writes LEVEL bounds as `range 0.0 - 1.0` for the DIM_MIN/DIM_MAX pair and `range 0.0 - 1.005` for ON_LEVEL, which is Tier 1 and settles both that the parameter is a 0..1 fraction and that MAX 1.01 in the descriptor exists to carry the 1.005 old-level sentinel rather than to extend the volume range. 0.5 is 50 %, and the 0..100 / 0..255 risk the reader named is ruled out.

The default half is confirmed unchanged and stays a product choice: DEFAULT is 0.0 on the descriptor and there is no CCU-side volume default of 0.5 anywhere. It is duplicated at chirp.go:73 (`vol := 0.5`) and sound.go:348/386-390 (`const defaultVolume = 0.5`, applied when `volume <= 0`). I verified the consequence the prior agent drew: PlaySound cannot express LEVEL 0 — a caller passing 0 gets 50 % — and StopSound is the only path that writes LEVEL 0.

Right-surface note confirmed by reading both files: HM-OU-CFM-Pl exposes no LEVEL on any channel (only SWITCH-style STATE/ON_TIME/INHIBIT/WORKING/INSTALL_TEST/SUBMIT), so it could not have answered the question. Profile registration confirmed at internal/model/custom/profiles.go:1159-1167: IPSoundPlayer is DeviceType "hmip-mp3p" only, primary channel 2. Worth adding as a nearby hazard the prior agent did not flag: the sibling IPSoundPlayerLed profile (profiles.go:1149-1157) takes channel 6, whose LEVEL is CONTROL DIMMER.LEVEL — same parameter name, same 0..1 scale, entirely different meaning (LED brightness, not volume). Nothing on the chirp path resolves there today, but the two are one profile lookup apart.

One more path detail: resolver.go:141-145 also pins Duration: 2 s on every chirp, so PlaySound writes DURATION_UNIT/DURATION_VALUE alongside LEVEL — the chirp is a three-parameter write, not a single LEVEL write.

all.title: The recovery backoff bounds encode claims about CCU reboot timing with no source
all.citation: ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/RFD/etc/init.d/S61rfd:95-110 (rfd: STEPS=20 × sleep 2 = 40 s, marker /var/status/rfd.status == pidof rfd); ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/init.d/S62HMServer:144-156 (HMServer: STEPS=150 × sleep 2 = 300 s, marker /var/status/HMServerStarted); ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/WebUI/etc/init.d/S70ReGaHss:66-78 (ReGaHss: STEPS=20 × sleep 2 = 40 s, marker = pidof ReGaHss); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/ise/checkrega.cgi:1-9; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/error/error-503.html:20 `CHECK_INTERVAL = 3000;`, :64 `request.open("GET", "/ise/checkrega.cgi", false)`, :67 `if ("OK" == request.responseText)`, :73 `window.setTimeout("check();", CHECK_INTERVAL);`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/rfd.cpp:340 (bindAndListen), :375 (mgr->Init), :394 (writeInitDoneFile); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.cpp:246-352 (PlatformInit)
all.firmwareValue: rfd 40 s / HMServer 300 s / ReGaHss 40 s startup budgets, run sequentially (S61 → S62 → S70); readiness poll = /ise/checkrega.cgi every 3000 ms, unbounded, body must equal "OK"
all.ourValue: backoff 2 s → 120 s cap, 8 attempts; tcpProbeTimeout 3 s; defaultCCUReadinessTimeout 120 s / interval 3 s
all.finding: Tier 1 carries no latency figure for "when does XML-RPC answer after a reboot" — no daemon publishes an expected answer time, and neither rfd nor libhsscomm documents a minimum interval or rate limit between init() calls (HSSManager::PlatformInit has no sleep, no throttle, and keys its handler map by callback URL, so repeated init from one URL does not accumulate registrations). So the 2 s / 120 s / 3 s constants rest on nothing the CCU states. What Tier 1 DOES carry, and what the comments should rest on instead: (1) the boot order is S50lighttpd → S61rfd → S62HMServer → S70ReGaHss, each blocking, with per-service budgets of 40 s / 300 s / 40 s — so the firmware's own worst-case allowance from rfd start to ReGaHss being up is ~340 s, well past the 366 s our 8-attempt curve spends (2+4+8+16+32+64+120+120), which only survives because DefaultHeartbeatInterval re-opens an attempt every 60 s after exhaustion. The comment's "a freshly rebooted CCU often answers on the second attempt" has no support for HmIP-RF, whose server is budgeted at up to 300 s. (2) The comment's "hard-down for longer than two minutes typically needs a full ReGa startup" is not a firmware statement at all; ReGaHss restart is a function of a reboot/service restart, not of downtime length. (3) The 3 s TCP probe in client.go is weaker than it looks: rfd calls bindAndListen at rfd.cpp:340 BEFORE mgr->Init() at :375 and before writeInitDoneFile at :394, and only enters the XML-RPC dispatch loop after Init returns — so the kernel completes the handshake into the listen backlog while rfd is still loading its device database. A successful probe does not mean rfd can answer. (4) The readiness gate we already have is Tier-1 exact: error-503.html polls /ise/checkrega.cgi every 3000 ms forever and accepts only the literal body "OK" — the same interval, the same comparison, and the same unbounded loop as internal/central/adapter/ccu_readiness.go (defaultCCUReadinessInterval 3 s, checkRegaReadyBody "OK", negative timeout = wait forever). checkrega.cgi runs `rega_script {Write("OK");}`, so "OK" implies ReGaHss is serving, which by boot order implies rfd and HMServer already started.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware carried a reboot-latency figure or an init() rate limit, it would have appeared either as a documented timeout constant in the S-scripts' wait loops (which is exactly where the 40 s/300 s/40 s budgets were found) or as a sleep/throttle in HSSManager::PlatformInit and CommController — I read both and found budgets but no answer-latency and no rate limit. The check does discriminate: it returned a concrete 3000 ms poll interval and an exact acceptance string for the readiness surface, so it is not simply blind.

all.title: GetModel resolves a device address across all interfaces by first map-iteration match
all.citation: ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/config_templates/InterfacesList.xml:3-17 (BidCos-RF xmlrpc_bin://127.0.0.1:32001, VirtualDevices xmlrpc://127.0.0.1:39292/groups, HmIP-RF xmlrpc://127.0.0.1:32010); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFCentral.cpp:36-37 `type="HM-RCV-50"; serial="BidCoS-RF";`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/hs485d/HS485Central.cpp:37 `serial="BidCoS-Wir";`; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/eq3/ipc.tcl:25-70 (interface list is read from the XML file, no address bookkeeping); HMIPServer de.eq3.ccu.groupdevice.service.internal.GroupDeviceAddressHelper#getVirtualDeviceAddressFromGroup and de.eq3.ccu.groupdevice.hmip.service.internal.HmIPGroupVirtualDevice#getVirtualDeviceAddressFromGroup ("INT" + group id, left-zero-padded to 7 digits, TRUNCATED to the last 7 digits when longer); HMIPServer de.eq3.ccu.virtualdevice.ip.internal.IpVirtualDeviceFactory#getNextFullSerialNumber ("VIP%07d"); HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.VirtualRemoteControl (DEVICE_ID_BASE "HmIP-RCV-"); Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/device_descriptions/HM-RCV-50.json, HMW-RCV-50.json, HmIP-RCV-50.json — exactly one entry per file has PARENT == ""
all.finding: Tier 1 does not decide it, because nothing in the CCU owns a cross-interface address namespace. Each interface in InterfacesList.xml is a separate daemon with its own generator: rfd mints device serials from the BidCos device plus the fixed central "BidCoS-RF" (RFCentral.cpp:37), hs485d mints "BidCoS-Wir" (HS485Central.cpp:37), HMIPServer's legacy port mints SGTIN-hex addresses plus "HmIP-RCV-<n>", and the /groups (VirtualDevices) endpoint mints "INT"+7 digits and "VIP"+7 digits. There is no shared registry and no uniqueness check anywhere across them; the disjointness our tie-break depends on is a prefix convention held by four independent processes, not an invariant the firmware asserts. Two consequences worth stating precisely: (a) a third-party interface registered into InterfacesList.xml (CUxD is exactly that) chooses its own addresses with nothing to stop an overlap; (b) the group-device generator itself truncates ids longer than 7 digits to their last 7, so it is not even collision-free within one interface. The other half of the rule IS grounded, at Tier 2: every device-level description carries an empty PARENT and every channel a non-empty one, so `Parent == ""` genuinely selects device-level rows. Our code should follow the descriptor for that half and stop relying on the tie-break for the other: the one production caller (configuration.go:233) already holds `iface` and can key the lookup exactly, which removes the nondeterminism without needing the firmware to guarantee anything.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware guaranteed one address per CCU, it would have shown up as a shared address registry or a uniqueness check spanning rfd, hs485d and HMIPServer, or as a validation in the interface-list loader. I looked in all four places (ipc.tcl's loader, rfd's and hs485d's central classes, and the HmIP virtual/group device address helpers) and found four independent generators and no check — the same search DID surface concrete generator formats, so it was capable of returning the opposite answer.

all.title: The burst-pacing defaults describe RF behaviour no running daemon has
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/CommController.cpp:96-190 (TxThreadFunction); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFController.cpp:87-112, with the verbatim comment at :93 `//wait for the sender to become ready without violating the RF timing`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFController.h:161 `INHIBIT_TX=(1<<1)`, :166 `SEND_INHIBIT_TIMEOUT=1500`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/CommMessageQueue.h:26-30 (queue sorted by CommMessage::GetPriority()); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosInterface.cpp:38-51, 234-296 (DUTYCYCLE_THRESHOLDMAP, DUTY_CYCLE reported as an interface attribute); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosInterfaceConcentrator.cpp:1047-1072 (the only duty-cycle-based send refusal, and it guards firmware updates only)
all.firmwareValue: one frame in flight; TX blocks on ACK; send-inhibit gate with SEND_INHIBIT_TIMEOUT = 1500 ms; priority-ordered queue; no unconditional inter-command sleep and no per-window send budget
all.ourValue: ThrottleInterCommandDelay = 0; ThrottleBurstThreshold = 5 / ThrottleBurstWindow = 500 ms (both unset by every pool, so the burst path is off)
all.finding: The firmware question is answerable and the answer supports the code as written. rfd's transmit path is strictly serial: CommController::TxThreadFunction pulls one message from the priority-sorted queue, calls CheckBeforeSend, writes it, and — whenever the message declares a response timeout — blocks on the ACK condition before touching the queue again (CommController.cpp:96-190). RFController::CheckBeforeSend then holds a new CMD_SEND until the previous send/receive is acknowledged or SEND_INHIBIT_TIMEOUT (1500 ms) elapses, under the comment 'wait for the sender to become ready without violating the RF timing' (RFController.cpp:93, RFController.h:166). There is no unconditional sleep between messages and no per-window send budget anywhere on that path. So: (1) ThrottleInterCommandDelay = 0 is correct — the firmware imposes no minimum inter-command gap a client must respect; (2) leaving the burst window unconfigured is a documented no-op and not a live RF risk, because the RF-timing protection lives in rfd, not in the client; (3) the comment's own caveats ('Only ThrottleInterCommandDelay is in force today', 'enabling it is a change to RF transmit behaviour') are accurate. One correction to the reasoning rather than the values: the constants are labelled RF-duty-cycle pacing, but duty cycle is a separate mechanism in rfd — it is tracked as a threshold map and published as the DUTY_CYCLE interface attribute (BidcosInterface.cpp:38-51, 234-296), and the only place rfd refuses to send on it is the firmware-update guard (BidcosInterfaceConcentrator.cpp:1072). Frame-timing inhibition and duty-cycle accounting are not the same thing. The numbers 5 and 500 ms themselves have no firmware counterpart at all — the firmware's pacing constants are 'one in flight' and 1500 ms — so they remain a description of the Python reference, exactly as the file says.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware required client-side pacing, it would have appeared as a usleep/nanosleep between TX messages in CommController::TxThreadFunction, or as a rejection when N frames were sent within a window in CheckBeforeSend — those are the two places the transmit path can express it, and both are what I read. The search discriminates: it did return a real blocking gate (send_inhibit, 1500 ms), so an unconditional gap would not have been missed.
all.challengeNote:
The VALUES survive; the GROUNDING is one layer below our surface and one sub-claim does not survive.

1) Quotes verified. RFController.cpp:93 carries verbatim `//wait for the sender to become ready without violating the RF timing`; RFController.h:161 `INHIBIT_TX=(1<<1)` and :166 `SEND_INHIBIT_TIMEOUT=1500`; CommMessageQueue's class doc (CommMessageQueue.h:26-29) states the priority sort and CommMessageQueue.cpp::AddMessage implements it as a descending-priority insert; TxThreadFunction (CommController.cpp:96-190) is serial and blocks on the ACK when GetResponseTimeout() is set. Two citation nits: the concentrator's duty-cycle guard is 1045-1077 (the comparison and its comment sit at 1071-1076), not 1047-1072; and CommMessageQueue.h:26-30 is the doc comment, not the sort.

2) WRONG LAYER. CommController/RFController is rfd's serial link to the RF coprocessor. Our throttle paces XML-RPC calls INTO rfd — several layers above. Serial-line pacing inside rfd does not by itself answer whether a client must pace, because it does not have to backpressure the caller. The on-surface answer is different code and it is stronger: rfd's XML-RPC server has no threads at all (no pthread_create under src/libXmlRpc/src/; XmlRpcDispatch::work is a select() loop at :114/:128), so requests are executed inline one at a time; and XmlRpcMethodSetValue::execute → RFManager::SetValue → RFDevice::SendFrame → BidcosInterfaceConcentrator::SendFrame blocks on pthread_cond_timedwait until the frame's responses are complete or waitTime (WAIT_TIME_DEFAULT = 1500 ms) expires. A client physically cannot burst against rfd: setValue does not return until the RF round trip is over. That is the reason ThrottleInterCommandDelay = 0 is correct, and it should replace the TX-thread citation.

3) OVERREACH, not supported. The finding's claim that leaving the burst window unconfigured is 'not a live RF risk, because the RF-timing protection lives in rfd' is true only for FRAME timing. Nothing in rfd throttles application traffic against the duty-cycle budget: the RF module reports ERROR_DUTY_CYCLE_FULL (RFCommMessage.h:74) and rfd's CMD_ERROR branch (RFController.cpp:276-297) only logs it and clears the inhibit flags. The single duty-cycle-based refusal, DutyCycleForUpdate (BidcosInterfaceConcentrator.cpp:1045-1077), is called from exactly one place — RFDevice.cpp:1490, the firmware-update path. So application sends consume the budget with no protection anywhere, which is precisely what a per-window burst cap would bound. The correct statement is: a burst window is unnecessary for frame timing (rfd blocks the caller), NOT that it protects nothing.

4) SCOPE — the boundary. All of the above is rfd / BidCos-RF. The constants are pool defaults for every InterfaceClient. HmIP does not go through rfd: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler#setValue allocates a per-call requestID with its own response queue and blocks on that queue, so concurrent calls are not serialised the way rfd serialises them, and neither 'one in flight' nor 1500 ms is established there. Nothing was checked for CUxD/BIN-RPC or hs485d. The 5 / 500 ms constants themselves have no firmware counterpart on any surface examined — that half of the rule stands as written.

all.title: SGTIN is required to be exactly 24 hex characters with no cited source
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/cp_add_device.cgi:566 `devAddress = jQuery("#serialHmIPLocal_" + iFace).val().replace(/-/g,"").toUpperCase();`, :571-580 (the seven-key Interface.setInstallModeHMIP payload); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods.conf:336-341 (ARGUMENTS {_session_id_ installMode interface on time address key keymode}); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/interface/setinstallmodehmip.tcl:55-66 (address → whitelistDev(ADDRESS) → xmlrpc setInstallModeWithWhitelist); HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler#setInstallModeWithWhitelist; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.AccessPointUtil#setInclusionMode; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.server.core.internal.InclusionHandling#handleDeviceInclusionRequest; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicemanagement.util.SGTIN#toString; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.util.core.ByteArrayUtils#getHexString; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.protocol.hmip.networkmanagement.DeviceInclusionRequestFrame#parsePayload and #generatePayload
all.firmwareValue: SGTIN on the HmIP wire is exactly 12 bytes, rendered as uppercase hex ("%02X") → 24 characters; the whitelist is matched by exact string equality against that rendering
all.ourValue: exactly 24 characters, separators stripped, uppercased, all [0-9A-F]
all.finding: The 24-character rule is right, and it is now grounded — but not where the comment says it is. Our call is on the same surface as the WebUI's: JSON-RPC Interface.setInstallModeHMIP with the same seven keys, which setinstallmodehmip.tcl turns into an XML-RPC setInstallModeWithWhitelist carrying a struct {ADDRESS, KEY, KEY_MODE}. Along that whole path nothing validates ADDRESS: the WebUI input has no maxlength and no pattern, cp_add_device.cgi only strips dashes and uppercases, the tcl passes the value through verbatim, and AccessPointUtil#setInclusionMode uppercases ADDRESS and validates only the KEY (it requires exactly 16 key bytes). So the CCU ACCEPTS any string — a too-long or non-hex SGTIN opens a whitelist-mode window that simply never matches, i.e. a silent no-op teach-in. Where 24 comes from is the matching side: an inbound device's SGTIN is parsed as exactly 12 bytes (DeviceInclusionRequestFrame#parsePayload reads 12, #generatePayload asserts 12), SGTIN#toString renders the raw bytes through ByteArrayUtils#getHexString which formats each byte as "%02X", and InclusionHandling#handleDeviceInclusionRequest gates inclusion on inclusionWhiteListContains(sgtin.toString()) — exact string equality. 12 bytes × 2 uppercase hex = 24 characters, and uppercase is required on both sides, which is exactly what NormalizeSGTIN produces. Two boundary notes: our rule is stricter than the CCU's acceptance and that is the better behaviour (we fail loudly where the CCU fails silently); and our separator stripping is a superset of the WebUI's — we strip spaces as well as dashes, so we accept a label the WebUI would forward unmatched. The comment should be reworded: the constraint is the SGTIN wire width and the whitelist string match, not a parameter validation in setInstallModeHMIP.
all.negativeControl: Had 24 been wrong, the frame parser would have read a different byte count or SGTIN#toString would have rendered something other than raw hex — both were read directly and both say 12 bytes / "%02X". The check also produced a genuinely unexpected result in the same pass (that the CCU validates the address not at all), so it was not merely echoing the expected answer.
all.challengeNote:
Upheld, and every load-bearing step re-read independently.

SURFACE — same path, verified both ends. internal/client/backends/ccu_extended.go:118-132 posts JSON-RPC `Interface.setInstallModeHMIP` with exactly the keys {interface, on, time, installMode, address, key, keymode}; methods.conf:336-341 declares exactly {_session_id_ installMode interface on time address key keymode}; cp_add_device.cgi:571-580 sends the same seven. setinstallmodehmip.tcl builds whitelistDev(ADDRESS/KEY/KEY_MODE) and calls XML-RPC setInstallModeWithWhitelist. That is our surface, not an adjacent one.

NO VALIDATION ON THE ACCEPT SIDE — confirmed. The WebUI input at cp_add_device.cgi:236/:338 carries neither maxlength nor pattern; :566 only strips dashes and uppercases; the tcl forwards ADDRESS verbatim; and AccessPointUtil#setInclusionMode does `((String)singleWhiteListValue.get("ADDRESS")).toUpperCase()` and then validates only the KEY (`keyBytes.length == 16` for both LOCAL and DEFAULT). A malformed ADDRESS is added to the whitelist as-is and the CCU opens a MODE_LIST window that can never match — a silent no-op teach-in. Our stricter rule is the better behaviour.

WHERE 24 COMES FROM — confirmed on the matching side. DeviceInclusionRequestFrame#parsePayload reads the sgtin as `readBytes(payload, 0, 12)` and advances by 12; #generatePayload calls `validateParameterLength(this.sgtin, 12, "sgtin")`. SGTIN#toString returns the string built in the constructor as `ByteArrayUtils.getHexString(this.rawFormat)`, and #getHexString appends `String.format("%02X", b)` per byte — uppercase, two chars, no separator (the argument is autoboxed to Byte, so Java's Formatter maps a negative byte to its unsigned 8-bit value and no sign extension widens the field). InclusionHandling#handleDeviceInclusionRequest gates inclusion on `MODE_LIST && !accessPoint.inclusionWhiteListContains(sgtin.toString())`, and HMIPAccessPoint#inclusionWhiteListContains is a bare `HashMap.containsKey` against keys stored verbatim by #addToInclusionWhiteList. 12 bytes × 2 uppercase hex = 24, exact match, uppercase required on both sides — exactly what NormalizeSGTIN produces.

TWO BOUNDARY NOTES, both already in the finding and both correct: our rule is stricter than the CCU's acceptance (we fail loudly where the CCU fails silently), and our separator stripping is a superset of the WebUI's (we also strip spaces, which cannot appear in a hex rendering, so it can only turn an unmatchable label into a matchable one). The wording correction the finding asks for is right: the constraint is the SGTIN wire width plus the whitelist string match, not a parameter validation in setInstallModeHMIP.

all.title: "CUxD closes after one request" and "nil is an empty string" are CUxD protocol claims with no reachable source
all.missingInput: CUxD's own implementation — its connection lifetime after a request/response pair, and how it encodes a void return over BIN-RPC. CUxD is closed third-party software and the string appears in no file in ../OpenCCU-Base or ../OpenCCU. Nothing in either tree, and nothing in the descriptor corpus, carries it. Settling it needs either CUxD's source or a wire capture against a CUxD instance.
all.citation: Adjacent surface only (the CCU's own BIN-RPC endpoints, not CUxD): ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/config_templates/InterfacesList.xml:5 `<url>xmlrpc_bin://127.0.0.1:32001</url>`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libXmlRpc/src/XmlRpcServerConnection.cpp:35 `const char XmlRpcServerConnection::BINARY_SIGNATURE[] = "Bin";`, :98-101 (binary framing: signature + 1 type byte + big-endian u32 length), :157 `_keepAlive = true;` in the binary branch, :222 `return _keepAlive;`, :354-364 (generateResponse writes signature + 0x01 + length + body), :408-414 (fault writes 0xFF); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libXmlRpc/src/XmlRpcValue.cpp:389-404 `toStream()` … :403 `return std::string();   // Invalid value`
all.firmwareValue: (CCU's own BIN-RPC server) connection kept alive unconditionally for binary requests; a void/invalid return is framed as Bin + 0x01 + length 0 + NO body
all.ourValue: client dials per call and server reads exactly one request per connection; WriteResponse(nil) emits Bin + 0x01 + length 8 + [type 3 (string)][length 0]
all.finding: Both claims are about CUxD, and CUxD is in neither tree, so as written they are not performable — I am naming that rather than promoting a substitute. What the trees DO settle is the adjacent surface, and it is worth recording because it is the reference implementation of the same protocol: the CCU serves BIN-RPC itself (BidCos-RF is registered as xmlrpc_bin://127.0.0.1:32001 and hs485dLoader writes the same scheme for BidCos-Wired), implemented in libXmlRpc. That implementation does the opposite of both of our claims. (1) Connection lifetime: the binary branch of readHeader sets _keepAlive = true unconditionally — BIN-RPC carries no Connection header, so the server keeps monitoring the socket and loops back to READ_HEADER after writing each response (XmlRpcServerConnection.cpp:157, :215-222). It expects multiple request/response cycles per connection. (2) Void return: generateResponse frames result.toStream(), and XmlRpcValue::toStream returns an empty std::string for an invalid (void) value (XmlRpcValue.cpp:403), so the CCU emits a zero-length body — eight header bytes and nothing else. Our WriteResponse(nil) instead emits an 8-byte payload holding a zero-length string value. Those are different byte sequences for the same meaning. Note the reverse asymmetry this exposes in our decoder: ReadResponse calls readValue on the payload unconditionally, so a zero-length response body fails with a read error rather than decoding as void. That is not reachable today (our BIN-RPC client only ever dials CUxD; BidCos-RF goes over XML-RPC in our stack), but it is the shape a wire capture should be aimed at. Our per-call dial in client.go is safe either way — it works whether or not the peer keeps the connection alive; the exposed half is server.go:134-141, which reads exactly one request and closes, and would silently drop a second pipelined request from a peer that behaves like libXmlRpc.
all.negativeControl: Had CUxD been present in either tree the search would have found it: the same grep pattern over both trees returned nothing for cuxd/CUxD/CUXD while returning concrete hits for xmlrpc_bin, BINARY_SIGNATURE and the BIN-RPC framing. So the negative result is a real absence, not a failed search — and it is why the verdict is not-performable rather than confirmed or contradicted.

all.title: The per-CCU discriminator is the last 10 characters of the serial, justified by a legacy width rather than the serial's format
all.site: internal/routingkey/canonical.go:17-21 (serialSuffixLen=10, CanonicalSerial); fed by internal/client/rega/scripts/get_serial.fn (board_sgtin → board_serial → plat_eq3ccu2 param) and internal/north/discovery/ssdp/device.go:94
all.citation: ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/init.d/S47InitRFHardware:367-369 — verbatim: "# prefer to use a HM_HMIP_SERIAL with the last\n  # 10 chars of the SGTIN because that is the serial\n  # of the RF module registered at eQ3"; :370-383 writes /var/board_serial from HM_HMIP_SERIAL, else HM_HMRF_SERIAL, else (HM_HOST=="oci") `echo -n "$(hostname)" | sed 's/-openccu//g'`, else `echo -n "$(echo "${MAC}" | tr -d : | tail -c 10)"`; :385-387 writes the FULL SGTIN to /var/board_sgtin. ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/package/eq3configd/S50eq3configd:15 `echo "SerialNumber=$(cat /var/board_serial)" >>/var/ids`. ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/ccu/getserial.tcl:24 `return [read_var /var/ids SerialNumber]`; ../OpenCCU-Base/usr/lib/tcl8.2/homematic/homematic.tcl:15-21 same. ../OpenCCU-Base/www/upnp/basic_dev.cgi:16-26,51-52 — get_serial_number() returns board_sgtin (untruncated) else board_serial, and RESOURCE(SERIAL_NUMBER)/UUID carry it whole.
all.firmwareValue: 10 characters — the CCU's own definition of "the serial" is the last 10 chars of the RF module's SGTIN, the identifier registered at eQ-3; /var/board_serial is written at exactly that width (the MAC fallback truncates with `tail -c 10` in code)
all.ourValue: serialSuffixLen = 10, justified in the comment by "the legacy entry_id[-10:] width"
all.finding: The width is right and the justification is wrong. The CCU does not merely tolerate a 10-character slice — 10 characters IS its serial: S47InitRFHardware states that the last 10 chars of the SGTIN are the RF module's eQ-3-registered serial, writes exactly that to /var/board_serial, and everything downstream (/var/ids SerialNumber → CCU.getSerial, and the UPnP description) reports it. Because /var/board_sgtin holds the full SGTIN untruncated and our get_serial.fn reads that file first, CanonicalSerial's last-10 slice reproduces the CCU's own board_serial byte for byte — which is also why the ReGa identity and the SSDP identity coincide (basic_dev.cgi puts the same full SGTIN in the UDN, and device.go:94 slices it the same way). Collision-freedom therefore rests on eQ-3 serial registration, not on an assumption about string tails. The boundary: two of the four branches in S47InitRFHardware are not registered identifiers. For HM_HOST=="oci" (Docker / HA add-on OpenCCU) the serial is the container hostname minus "-openccu" — unbounded length, operator-chosen, and our last-10 slice of it can collide ("prod-ccu-wohnung" and "test-ccu-wohnung" both reduce to "cu-wohnung"). The MAC branch drops the first 2 of 12 hex digits, keeping 40 bits. Neither is a firmware problem; both are cases where our slice is a truncation rather than a serial. Recommended: keep 10, cite S47InitRFHardware:367-369 instead of entry_id[-10:], and note the RF-less-install caveat.
all.negativeControl: Had the width been wrong I would have found a different number in the same three places: the comment would have named a different count, /var/board_serial would have been written at another width, and the MAC fallback would have read `tail -c <n>` with n≠10. All three read 10. Had the CCU treated the serial as a prefix-plus-suffix composite, get_serial_number()/basic_dev.cgi:51 would have sliced it before publishing; it publishes the whole string.
all.challengeNote:
Upheld as narrowed, with two corrections to the prior finding — one of them a measured error.

What I checked and confirms: the S47InitRFHardware comment and all four branches are transcribed exactly; /var/board_sgtin holds the untruncated SGTIN and both of our producers prefer it (get_serial.fn's first system.Exec, basic_dev.cgi's first `file exist` test), so the ReGa identity and the SSDP identity do read the same string before CanonicalSerial slices it. serialFrom() takes the tail after the last "-" in the UDN, which on "upnp-BasicDevice-1_0-<SGTIN>" yields the full SGTIN, so the two paths converge as claimed.

CORRECTION 1 (measured, not argued): the MAC fallback yields **9** characters, not 10. The inner `echo "${MAC}"` emits a trailing newline, so `tail -c 10` returns 9 hex digits plus \n, and the surrounding command substitution then strips the newline. I ran the exact pipeline from :381-382 with MAC=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and got "bccddeeff" (len 9). The prior finding's "drops the first 2 of 12 hex digits, keeping 40 bits" is wrong on both counts: it drops 3, keeping 36 bits.

CORRECTION 2: "reproduces the CCU's own board_serial byte for byte" is asserted, not measured. The firmware never computes last-10-of-SGTIN anywhere; HM_HMIP_SERIAL and HM_HMIP_SGTIN are independent fields (2 and 3) of `detect_radio_module`, a third-party tool that is NOT in either OpenCCU tree — it is fetched as a pinned tarball (detect_radio_module.mk:6, .hash:3). The equality rests entirely on the Tier-1 comment at :367-369 describing that tool's output. That comment is good grounding for the width; it is not a measurement of the equality.

NEW BOUNDARY the prior finding missed: on the oci branch the two identities can diverge, not merely collide. board_serial is `hostname` with "-openccu" removed, and hyphens are legal in hostnames. For hostname "prod-ccu-openccu": ReGa yields "prod-ccu" (CanonicalSerial passes it through, len<=10), while SSDP's serialFrom takes the tail after the LAST hyphen of "upnp-BasicDevice-1_0-prod-ccu" and yields "ccu". Same CCU, two different identities — so the discovery-flags-configured-central property the comment claims fails on exactly the Docker / HA add-on deployment this project ships.

Recommendation stands (keep 10, cite S47InitRFHardware:367-369 rather than entry_id[-10:]), and add: the width is 10 only on the two registered-serial branches; the MAC fallback emits 9 and the oci branch emits an operator-chosen string that our two readers slice differently.

all.title: HmIP VALVE_STATE is excluded as an activity source on the strength of a comment naming enum ordinal 4
all.site: internal/model/custom/climate/climate.go:1805-1834 (comment + kind-gated switch; VALVE_STATE subscribed only under case KindRF)
all.citation: HmIP side (Tier 1): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.ValveState — enum constants declared in the order STATE_NOT_AVAILABLE, RUN_TO_START, WAIT_FOR_ADAPTION, ADAPTION_IN_PROGRESS, ADAPTION_DONE, TOO_TIGHT, ADJUSTMENT_TOO_BIG, ADJUSTMENT_TOO_SMALL, ERROR_POSITION; #getNames(boolean supportsErrorPosition) fills names[i] = values[i].name(), dropping only the last entry when ERROR_POSITION is unsupported. HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.ClimateStateParameterFactory#createValveStateParameter — builds VALVE_STATE as LogicalType.ENUM / PhysicalType.INTEGER, READ|EVENT only, converter StringEnumToInteger(enumStrings), MIN=enumStrings[0], MAX=last. HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.typeconversion.converter.StringEnumToInteger#convertPhysicalToLogical — with no explicit enumValues it returns enumStrings[physicalValue[0] & 0xFF], and #convertLogicalToPhysical emits (byte)(i + offset) with offset 0, so the wire integer IS the list index. Classic RF (Tier 1/2, device type XML): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_cc_rt_dn.xml:2361-2369 — `<parameter id="VALVE_STATE" operations="read,event">` … docu brief="Ventilposition" … `<logical type="integer" min="0" max="99" default="0" unit="%"/>`; identical in rf_cc_rt_dn_bom.xml:2321-2329 and rf_cc_vd.xml:84-93. Tier 2 corroboration: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-eTRV-2.json VCU3609622:1 VALUES VALVE_STATE {TYPE ENUM, VALUE_LIST [STATE_NOT_AVAILABLE, RUN_TO_START, WAIT_FOR_ADAPTION, ADAPTION_IN_PROGRESS, ADAPTION_DONE, TOO_TIGHT, ADJUSTMENT_TOO_BIG, ADJUSTMENT_TOO_SMALL, ERROR_POSITION], MIN/DEFAULT STATE_NOT_AVAILABLE}; same in HmIP-eTRV-E/-B, HmIP-HEATING, and (8-entry, no ERROR_POSITION) HmIP-FALMOT-C12 and HmIPW-FALMOT-C12; HM-CC-RT-DN.json VCU0000050:4 VALUES VALVE_STATE {TYPE INTEGER, MIN 0, MAX 99, UNIT "%"}.
all.firmwareValue: HmIP: VALVE_STATE = ENUM, index 4 = ADAPTION_DONE (index == wire integer, offset 0). Valve openness on HmIP is a different parameter, LEVEL, a FLOAT 0.0..1.01 with DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0). Classic RF: VALVE_STATE = INTEGER 0..99 %, docu "Ventilposition"
all.ourValue: comment: "HmIP VALVE_STATE is an adaption-state ENUM (4 == ADAPTION_DONE), NOT a valve-openness percentage"; "KindRF derives activity from VALVE_STATE (0–100 %)"
all.finding: The claim is right and, unusually for this bundle, the ordinal is grounded rather than assumed: the wire integer is the VALUE_LIST index by construction (StringEnumToInteger with offset 0 and no explicit value table), and ADAPTION_DONE is the fifth declared constant, so 4 is read from the source, not inferred from list position. The kind gate is therefore correct, and the worry the reader raised — that some HmIP model might ship VALVE_STATE as a percentage — is closed: ClimateStateParameterFactory registers VALVE_STATE under exactly two keys ("default" and "ErrorCode") and both go through createValveStateParameter, so there is no percentage variant anywhere in the HmIP surface; the two variants differ only in whether ERROR_POSITION is present (9 vs 8 entries), which matches the two VALUE_LISTs seen in the descriptors. Two corrections to the comment, neither behaviour-changing because classify() only tests >0: (1) the classic RF range is 0..99 %, not 0–100 % — max="99" in all three RF XMLs; (2) HmIP LEVEL is a 0..1 fraction (MAX 1.01), so calling it "valve openness" is right but it is not a percentage either.
all.negativeControl: Had VALVE_STATE been a percentage on HmIP, createValveStateParameter would have been built like createHumidity/createReadOnlyPercentage — LogicalType.INTEGER or FLOAT with a numeric converter and a 0..100 bound — and the descriptors would carry TYPE INTEGER with MIN/MAX 0/100 instead of TYPE ENUM with a VALUE_LIST. Had ADAPTION_DONE sat at a different ordinal, ValveState's declaration order would show it elsewhere and getNames (which copies values() in order) would place it elsewhere in VALUE_LIST; the descriptors independently show it fifth.
all.challengeNote:
Upheld, and the grounding is now stronger than the prior finding made it.

Every quoted symbol was opened and matches verbatim: the nine-constant declaration order, getNames' copy loop, the two-key registration both routing to createValveStateParameter, and StringEnumToInteger's offset-0 index arithmetic. So the ordinal is not smuggled in from array position — a Java enum's declaration order IS values() order by language definition, and the converter indexes that same array.

But the prior finding grounded the ordinal at the RADIO layer, which is one surface below the one our code sits on. Our code reads VALVE_STATE over legacy XML-RPC, and there the mapping is settled independently and better: DeviceUtil#convertParameterValue converts an ENUM logical string to its index in getEnumStrings(), and the SAME class populates the VALUE_LIST it reports in getParamsetDescription from that identical array. The integer we receive is therefore an index into the list we ourselves receive — self-describing, with nothing assumed. The one thing that could have broken this is that the flag driving it defaults to false in code; the shipped CCU config sets it true (crRFD.conf:47, the HmIP-RF daemon template), so the ordinal form is what a real CCU emits.

Worry closed, as the prior finding said: VALVE_STATE is registered under exactly two keys and both go through createValveStateParameter, so no HmIP percentage variant exists. The 9-entry vs 8-entry split matches the two VALUE_LISTs in the descriptors.

Two notes on the comment, neither behaviour-changing since classify() only tests >0: (1) classic RF is 0..99 %, not 0–100 % (max="99" in all three RF XMLs); (2) rf_cc_vd.xml additionally carries `<conversion type="integer_integer_scale" mul="2"/>` on VALVE_STATE, which the prior finding did not mention — HM-CC-VD's physical is doubled to reach the 0..99 logical range.

all.title: Modulating valve write-suppression epsilon 0.005 is a bare literal
all.citation: HmIP side (Tier 1): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory#createLevel and #createReadOnlyLevel — LEVEL is StateParameter(LogicalType.FLOAT, PhysicalType.INTEGER, …, new DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0), default 0.0, min 0.0, max 1.01); HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.typeconversion.converter.DoubleToInteger#getStepGranularity — verbatim: `return 1.0 / this.factor;`, and #convertLogicalToPhysical multiplies by the factor then rounds half away from zero (`d = d >= 0.0 ? (d += 0.5) : (d -= 0.5); int dIntValue = (int)d;`), #convertPhysicalToLogical divides by the factor. Classic RF (Tier 1): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_dim_1t_dr.xml:279 `<logical type="float" default="0.0" min="0.0" max="1.0" unit="100%"/>` and :289 `<conversion type="float_integer_scale" factor="200"/>`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSTypeConversionFloatInteger.cpp:56-68 `double dval=((double&)in+offset)*factor; if(dval>=0)dval+=0.5; else dval-=0.5; ((int&)*out)=(int)dval;` and :70-78 `((double&)*out)=(((double)((int&)in))/factor)-offset;`. Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-FALMOT-C12.json VCU9245535:1..12 VALUES LEVEL {TYPE FLOAT, MIN 0.0, MAX 1.01, UNIT "100%", CONTROL CLIMATECONTROL_FLOOR_TRANSCEIVER.LEVEL} — and no STEP/granularity field; same for HmIPW-FALMOT-C12 and HmIP-eTRV-2 VCU3609622:1.
all.firmwareValue: 1/200 = 0.005 on the 0..1 LEVEL domain, on both families (HmIP factor 200.0 via DoubleToInteger; classic RF `factor="200"` via float_integer_scale)
all.finding: The literal is exactly one wire step, on both device families, and it is a firmware constant rather than a taste judgement. HmIP encodes LEVEL as round(level × 200) into a physical integer and decodes phys/200; the converter even exposes the quantum directly as getStepGranularity() = 1/factor = 0.005. The classic RF stack does the same arithmetic with `factor="200"` and the same round-half-away-then-truncate in HSSTypeConversionFloatInteger. Two logical levels closer than 0.005 can therefore encode to the same physical integer, so the guard suppresses precisely the writes the wire cannot represent; the `>=` boundary lets a change of exactly one step through, which is right. One correction to the bundle's suggested alternative: the runtime descriptor cannot replace the constant — a HomeMatic ParameterDescription for a FLOAT carries TYPE/MIN/MAX/DEFAULT/UNIT/FLAGS/OPERATIONS and no STEP or granularity field at all (verified across all 12 FALMOT channels and the eTRV-2 climate channel), so getParamsetDescription would not yield 0.005. The honest fix is a named constant citing the factor-200 encoding, not a runtime lookup. Separately, worth knowing: no production profile currently constructs valve.Modulating (only tests and the cdpkind switch reference it), so today the rule is latent.
all.negativeControl: Had the epsilon been wrong I would have read a different factor: HmIP would show DoubleToInteger(20.0, …) or (100.0, …) in createLevel and getStepGranularity would return 0.05 or 0.01, and the RF XML would carry `factor="20"`/`"100"`. Both read 200. Had the LEVEL domain been 0..100 rather than 0..1, rf_dim_1t_dr.xml:279 would declare max="100" and the HmIP StateParameter's max would not be 1.01.
all.challengeNote:
Upheld. Every formula was opened and transcribed correctly, including the rounding direction and the truncation-after-rounding on both stacks; getStepGranularity() literally returns 1.0/factor, so 0.005 is the firmware's own name for the quantum rather than a derived value. I additionally swept all 130 RF device XMLs: no LEVEL parameter anywhere uses a factor other than 200, so the classic-RF half is not device-specific. The Tier-2 correction is right too — a HomeMatic FLOAT ParameterDescription carries no STEP field (verified across all 12 FALMOT channels and eTRV-2), so getParamsetDescription cannot supply this at runtime; a named constant citing the factor-200 encoding is the honest fix.

One overstatement in the prior finding, worth fixing before it is quoted as fact: "the guard suppresses precisely the writes the wire cannot represent" is not true. `cur` is snapped to the 1/200 grid (it came back through phys/200), but `target` is arbitrary, and a full-step epsilon around a grid point spans two wire integers. Concretely: cur=0.005 (wire 1), target=0.00999 — |diff|=0.00499 < 0.005 so the write is suppressed, yet round(0.00999*200)=2, a genuine one-step change. The exact predicate is `round(cur*200) != round(target*200)`; 0.005 is a sound approximation of it, not an equivalent. The `>=` boundary letting exactly one step through is right.

Scope, confirmed by grep: valve.NewModulating has no production caller — every construction is under tests/ or internal/**/*_test.go, and the only non-test reference is the type switch in internal/model/custom/cdpkind/kind.go:189 and the dispatcher's type assertion in internal/central/adapter/custom_dp_dispatcher.go:248. The rule is latent today.

all.title: The COLOR-integer hue round-trip is asymmetric: read divides by 200, write multiplies by 199
all.citation: Read (CCU's own control page): ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/controls/rgbw.fn:30-31 — verbatim: `WriteLine( "if (colorVal > 199) {colorVal = 200; saturation = '0%'}");` / `WriteLine( "var convertedValue = parseInt(colorVal / 199 * 360); " );`. Same arithmetic in two further independent CCU paths: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/js/RGBW_Controller.js:52,55 (`var hsvVal = parseInt(this.curValue / 199 * 360);` … `if (this.showWhite && this.curValue == 200) { saturation = "0%"; hsvVal = 0; }`) and ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/webui.js:18210-18215,18254. Write: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/extern/spectrum.js:1383-1386 — `toHMString: function() { var hsv = rgbToHsv(this._r, this._g, this._b); var h = mathRound(hsv.h * 360) … return parseInt(h / 360 * 199); }`, selected by `preferredFormat: "convert360To200"` (spectrum.js:1490-1493; set at rgbw.fn:37, RGBW_Controller.js:65, webui.js:18219). White sentinel on write: spectrum.js:959-964 `convertWhiteValue` returns 200 only when `(preferredFormat == "convert360To200") && (currentHue == 0) && (currentSaturation == 0) && (currentValue == 1)`. Descriptor (Tier 2, firmware-shipped): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_rgbw.xml:279-292 — `<parameter id="COLOR" operations="read,write,event" control="RGBW_COLOR.COLOR">` with `<logical type="integer" min="0" max="255" default="0"/>`, physical integer value_id="LEVEL", no SPECIAL entries and no `<conversion>`. Witness (Tier 3): ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/model/custom/light.py:456 `return color / 200 * 360, _MAX_SATURATION` and :472 `color = 200 if saturation < 0.1 else int(round(max(min(hue, 1), 0) * 199))` — the Python family carries the identical asymmetry, which is where ours came from.
all.firmwareValue: read hue = parseInt(COLOR / 199 * 360); write COLOR = parseInt(hue / 360 * 199); white ⟺ COLOR > 199 (read) / hue==0 && sat==0 && value==1 → 200 (write); descriptor COLOR is integer 0..255 with no SPECIAL
all.ourValue: read hue = trunc(COLOR / 200 * 360); write COLOR = round(hue / 360 * 199); white ⟺ COLOR >= 200 (read) / saturation < 10 → 200 (write)
all.finding: The comment's model is right and the arithmetic is not. Firmware confirms the hue circle is 0..199 with 200 as the white point: the write factor is 199 (spectrum.js toHMString), the read divisor is also 199, and the white test is `colorVal > 199` — matching our `c >= 200` exactly. But our read divides by 200 where all three CCU paths divide by 199, so the pair is asymmetric on our side and symmetric on the CCU's. Concretely: 135 of the 200 in-circle COLOR values decode to a different hue than the CCU's own UI reports — first divergence at COLOR=26 (ours 46°, firmware 47°), maximum 2°, and at the top COLOR=199 ours reads 358° where the firmware reads 360°. A second, smaller difference on the write half: the firmware truncates (`parseInt`) where we round (`math.Round`), so for 180 of the 360 hues we send one COLOR step more than the CCU's picker would (hue=1° → ours 1, firmware 0). Fixing the read divisor to 199 makes our round-trip converge and matches the CCU; matching the write to truncation would additionally make our writes byte-identical to the WebUI's. Note also that the descriptor declares COLOR up to 255 with no SPECIAL — 200..255 are simply undefined, and both we and the firmware fold the whole tail to white, so that half is already right. One caveat on scope: rfd applies no conversion to COLOR (physical is a plain integer), so the integer's meaning is defined only by the operator layer — the WebUI paths above are the authority here, and they are unanimous.
all.negativeControl: Had our read been right, rgbw.fn:31 and RGBW_Controller.js:52 and webui.js:18215 would read `/ 200 * 360`; all three read `/ 199 * 360`. Had the circle been 0..200 with 201 as white, toHMString would multiply by 200 and the white tests would compare against 200 rather than 199. Had the descriptor reserved 200 as a documented sentinel I would have found a SPECIAL block in rf_rgbw.xml; there is none, which is why the sentinel is a WebUI convention and had to be read there.
all.challengeNote:
Upheld as contradicted. I opened every cited file and every quote is exact, including the two truncation-vs-rounding details that carry the finding.

Surface check (the attack this project keeps catching, and it fails here): this is the same parameter, not a look-alike. rgbw.fn resolves its datapoint by `cObj.DPByControl("RGBW_COLOR.COLOR")`, and rf_rgbw.xml:279 declares COLOR with exactly `control="RGBW_COLOR.COLOR"` on the channel our profile maps. The device XML applies no conversion and declares only an opaque integer 0..255, so the CCU's operator layer is the only place the hue span is stated at all — and it is unanimous across three files written at different times, in both directions.

Patch check (which the prior finding did not do): rgbw.fn is patched twice by the distribution. I read both patched copies; neither touches lines 30-31. The /199 read is what ships.

Arithmetic reproduced independently: read divergences 135 of the 200 in-circle values, first at COLOR=26 (ours 46°, firmware 47°), maximum delta 2° (105 values off by 1, 30 by 2), and COLOR=199 → ours 358° vs firmware 360°. Write divergences 180 of 360 hues, ours one step higher (hue=1° → ours 1, firmware 0), because math.Round is half-away-from-zero where parseInt truncates. The prior finding's numbers are exactly right.

The defect is also internal, independent of which authority one picks: our write uses span 199 and our read uses divisor 200, so our own round-trip is unstable — write(270°)=149, read(149)=268°; write(359°)=198, read(198)=356°. Fixing the read divisor to 199 makes it converge AND matches all three CCU paths; matching the write to truncation would make our writes byte-identical to the WebUI's.

Scope, per notes/parity/by_design.md:3400 and :3449: RfDimmer_Color is registered for exactly one model, HM-LC-RGBW-WM (COLOR on VCU3747418:2), so the divergence reaches one device family. That narrows the blast radius but not the verdict.

One caveat I will state rather than paper over: what a given COLOR integer physically renders is decided inside the device, and the CCU applies no conversion. The WebUI is therefore the authority on the CCU's stated interpretation, not on the LED's response curve. There is no descriptor-level statement of the hue span anywhere; the operator layer is the strongest source available, and it is consistent in both directions.

all.title: Two different saturation-means-white cutoffs (10 and 5) coexist for the same user gesture
all.citation: RGBW / COLOR-integer family: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/extern/spectrum.js:959-964 — `convertWhiteValue` emits the 200 sentinel only when `(currentHue == 0) && (currentSaturation == 0) && (currentValue == 1)`; the read half sets saturation to exactly '0%' for COLOR > 199 (../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/controls/rgbw.fn:30, ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/js/RGBW_Controller.js:55). There is no tolerance band anywhere on that path, and the picker itself pins saturation at 100% for every chromatic pick (rgbw.fn:27 `var saturation = '100%';`). Fixed-colour family: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/controls/opticalsignalreceiver.fn:13,63-88 — the CCU's control for OPTICAL_SIGNAL_RECEIVER.COLOR is an 8-entry `<select>` built from `${lblOff}\t${optionColorBLUE}\t…\t${optionColorWHITE}` with the loop index as the option value; there is no hue or saturation axis on that surface at all. What our rule rests on instead (Tier 3 witness): ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/model/custom/light.py:472 `color = 200 if saturation < 0.1 else …` (0..1 fraction) and light.py:823 `if int(color[1]) < 5:` (0..100 scale).
all.firmwareValue: RGBW family: white ⟺ saturation exactly 0 (with value 1); no tolerance band exists. Fixed-colour family: no saturation input at all — the operator picks one of 8 enum slots
all.ourValue: 10.0 (0..100) in setColorIndex; 5 (0..100) in HSToFixedColor
all.finding: The firmware does not adjudicate this, and it cannot: its own colour surfaces have no arbitrary-saturation input to threshold. The RGBW picker fixes saturation at 100% for every chromatic pick and reaches white only through the dedicated palette swatch, which convertWhiteValue recognises by an exact `currentSaturation == 0`; the fixed-colour surface is a plain 8-entry dropdown with no colour geometry whatsoever. Neither 10 nor 5 appears in the CCU, and neither is contradicted by it — the cutoff exists only because HA-style consumers hand us a continuous saturation the CCU never produces. So the measurement the reader asked for is genuinely not decidable from Tier 1, and the pair rests on the Python family alone: light.py:472 uses `< 0.1` on a 0..1 fraction (= 10 on our 0..100 scale) and light.py:823 uses `< 5` on a 0..100 scale. Both of our values faithfully reproduce their respective reference lines; the inconsistency is inherited, not introduced. That leaves it a product decision rather than a compatibility one: one rule with one value would be defensible, and if a single value is chosen the argument for 5 is that it is nearer the firmware's exact-zero and so surrenders less of the chromatic circle — but nothing in the CCU requires either. Recommended: replace the bare `5` with a named constant next to colorWhiteSaturationCutoff so the divergence is at least visible in one place, and record it as a client convention rather than citing the reference at two different scales.
