all.negativeControl: Had the CCU defined a white threshold I would have found a saturation comparison against a non-zero constant on one of the two paths — a `< n` in convertWhiteValue or in the rgbw.fn/RGBW_Controller.js read halves, or a saturation term anywhere in opticalsignalreceiver.fn. convertWhiteValue compares against 0 exactly, the read halves set 0% only from the COLOR>199 sentinel, and opticalsignalreceiver.fn contains no saturation token at all. That is the result a genuinely silent source produces, and it is what I got.

all.title: The hard-coded RF effect vocabulary carries 'Campemit' where every surrounding comment says 'Campfire'

all.title: Two different CPV-to-level scales, both cited only to the Python reference
all.citation: BidCos: ../OpenCCU-Base/firmware/rftypes/rf_ja_conf_644.xml — `<parameter id="LEVEL" …><logical type="float" default="0.0" min="0.0" max="1.0" unit="100%">…<conversion type="float_integer_scale" factor="200"/></parameter>` and `<parameter id="LEVEL_COMBINED" operations="write" control="JALOUSIE.LEVEL_COMBINED"><logical type="string"/>…<conversion type="hexstring_bytearray" has0XPrefix="true" delimiter=","/></parameter>`. The scale itself: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSTypeConversionFloatInteger.cpp:56-66 `double dval=((double&)in+offset)*factor; if(dval>=0)dval+=0.5; else dval-=0.5; ((int&)*out)=(int)dval;` and :69-77 `((double&)*out)=(((double)((int&)in))/factor)-offset;`. LEVEL_COMBINED carries the physical bytes unscaled: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSTypeConversionHexStringToByteArray.cpp:63-95 (LogicalToPhysical) and :153-172 (`fromHexValue`). The CCU's own client applies the ×2: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www_source/ise/js/iseBlindShutter.js:294-305 `var level = parseInt(this.state) * 2, levelHex = level.toString(16) … dpValue = "0X" + levelHex; dpValue += ","; …`. HmIP: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#convertCombinedParameter — case "L" → key "LEVEL", value = Double.parseDouble(pair[1]) / 100.0; case "L2" → key "LEVEL_2", same; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory#createLevel — LogicalType.FLOAT, PhysicalType.INTEGER, DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0), range 0.0..1.01; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.typeconversion.converter.DoubleToInteger#getStepGranularity returns 1.0/factor.
all.firmwareValue: BidCos LEVEL_COMBINED: comma-separated `0xNN` bytes carrying the PHYSICAL value; physical = round_half_away(level*200); decode = raw/200. HmIP COMBINED_PARAMETER: `L=<percent>`; LEVEL = percent/100.0 (logical 0..1), which the HmIP stack then encodes with its OWN factor 200. Both families' LEVEL therefore sit on the same 0.005 physical grid.
all.ourValue: ConvertCPVToHMLevel = raw/100/2 (= raw/200); ConvertCPVToHMIPLevel = raw/100; ConvertHMLevelToCPV = fmt.Sprintf("0x%02x", int(math.Round(value*100*2)))
all.finding: Both divisors are right, and the encoder matches the firmware exactly — but the reason given in the code is wrong, and that is where the rule will drift. (1) Divisors: confirmed. BidCos /200 is the device XML's own `factor="200"` on LEVEL, and LEVEL_COMBINED is a raw byte-array conversion that adds no scale of its own, so its bytes ARE the physical LEVEL. HmIP /100 is literally `Double.parseDouble(pair[1]) / 100.0` in the CCU's HmIP legacy XML-RPC surface. (2) Rounding: our encoder's `math.Round` (half away from zero) is the firmware's own rule verbatim — HSSTypeConversionFloatInteger.cpp:59-61 adds ±0.5 before truncating. The reference's `int(value*100*2)` truncates and is wrong; our documented divergence from it is the correct call. (3) The NARROWING: the candidate's premise — 'the two radio families really use different level grids' — is false. HmIP LEVEL is DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0), the same factor 200, the same 0.005 step. The boundary runs at the STRING GRAMMAR of the two combined-parameter parameters, not at the radio family: LEVEL_COMBINED transports the already-scaled physical byte, COMBINED_PARAMETER transports a percent number that the CCU divides by 100 into the logical value first. Our doc comment at converter.go:119 calls the HmIP one 'a BidCos CPV integer string', which is the same conflation. (4) Two live acceptance-set facts about the encode path (blind.go:346 / :351, which IS wired): `fromHexValue` requires each token to be EXACTLY 4 characters when has0XPrefix is set (HexStringToByteArray.cpp:155-158) — our `0x%02x` always produces 4 for a clamped 0..200, so we are inside the set, but a 3-character token would be rejected outright with nothing written; and the firmware parses HmIP `L=` with Double.parseDouble, so `L=50.5` is legal, while our `fmt.Sprintf("L2=%d,L=%d", int(w*100+0.5))` restricts us to whole percent — half the resolution the device offers, and coarser than the CCU's own HmIP UI, which quantises to 0.5 % (iseHmIPServo.js:99 `roundValue05`).
all.negativeControl: Had the BidCos divisor been wrong, rf_ja_conf_644.xml's LEVEL conversion would have carried a factor other than 200 (the corpus does contain factor=1, 2, 10, 100 parameters, so 200 is not a constant of the format) and iseBlindShutter.js would multiply by something other than 2. Had the HmIP divisor been wrong, DeviceUtil#convertCombinedParameter's "L" case would divide by something other than 100.0 — the same method's "OT", "DV", "TC" and "H" cases divide by nothing at all, and "IMTL"/"SAT" divide by 100.0, so the method demonstrably distinguishes scaled from unscaled keys. Had the two families used different grids as the candidate assumed, createLevel would have used a factor other than 200 — it uses 200.
all.challengeNote: Verdict UPHELD, boundary widened in two places the candidate missed and one supporting citation withdrawn. Re-verified and confirmed: the /200 and /100 divisors, both quoted formulas character-exact (including that the firmware rounds half-away-from-zero, matching our math.Round and diverging from the reference's truncation), the 4-character token rule our `0x%02x` satisfies, and the candidate's central narrowing — HmIP LEVEL is also DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0), so the boundary is the string grammar of the two write parameters, not the radio family. WIDENING 1: the decode half of this rule is unreachable. ConvertCPVToHMLevel and ConvertCPVToHMIPLevel have no production caller anywhere in internal/ or pkg/ (tests only), and the firmware declares BOTH combined parameters write-only — rf_ja_conf_644.xml `operations="write"` and HMIPServer #addSpecialCommaSeparatedParameter setting IOOperations.WRITE — so no CPV is ever read back to decode. Only ConvertHMLevelToCPV is wired, via internal/model/custom/cover/blind.go:346. WIDENING 2, a fact worth keeping: the CCU's own client emits level first, slats second (iseBlindShutter.js:294-305), which is the order blind.go:346 uses; that ordering was read from the source, not assumed. WITHDRAWN: the candidate's claim that whole-percent HmIP writes are 'coarser than the CCU's own HmIP UI, which quantises to 0.5%' cites iseHmIPServo.js:99, which is a servo control, not a blind. The CCU's HmIP blind control never writes COMBINED_PARAMETER at all — iseBlindShutter.js `iseHmIPJalousieShutter.saveValue` and `saveSliderValue` issue `Interface.putParamset` with LEVEL / LEVEL_2 as doubles (state/100), and the slats slider is declared `step: 5`. The resolution point still stands on Tier 1 without that citation: #convertCombinedParameter parses `L=` with Double.parseDouble and #createLevel gives LEVEL a 0.005 physical grid, so our `int(wireL*100+0.5)` at blind.go:351 discards half the resolution the device can represent.

all.title: 'CONCENTRATION on its own is CO2 by HM convention' — a convention stated as the source
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/lang/en/translate.lang.diagram.js:170 `langJSON.en.diagramValueTypeCONCENTRATION = langJSON.en.lblCO2Concentration;` (:169 does the same for CONCENTRATION_CO2); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/lang/en/translate.lang.stringtable.js:1437 `langJSON.en.stringTableConcentration = langJSON.en.lblCO2Concentration;`; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/webui/js/lang/en/translate.lang.label.js:34 `"lblCO2Concentration" : "CO2 concentration"` (de/translate.lang.label.js:34 `"CO2-Konzentration"`); the stringtable entry that consumes it, ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/stringtable_de.txt:447 `CONCENTRATION\t${lblValue} ${stringTableConcentration}`. Declaration side: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory — a single unqualified `ParameterMapKey("CONCENTRATION")` bound to #createConcentration (LogicalType.FLOAT, PhysicalType.INTEGER, DoubleToInteger(100.0, 0.0), min 0.0, max 163830.0), with the particulate parameters registered separately as MASS_CONCENTRATION_PM_1/2_5/10 (#createMassConcentrationParameter) and NUMBER_CONCENTRATION_PM_* (#createNumberConcentrationParameter). No CONCENTRATION parameter exists anywhere in ../OpenCCU-Base/firmware/rftypes/ or src/devicetypes/, so BidCos never carries this name.
all.firmwareValue: CONCENTRATION → "CO2 concentration" / "CO2-Konzentration" in both of the CCU's own label paths (diagram value type and stringtable). Unit: none declared.
all.ourValue: hmenum.ParameterConcentration → interfaces.MatterMeasurementCO2
all.finding: The substance half of the claim is grounded, and not on a convention: the CCU's own WebUI aliases the bare CONCENTRATION value type to the SAME label constant as CONCENTRATION_CO2, in two independent places (the diagram value-type table and the stringtable). It is also structurally unambiguous on the declaring side — the HmIP channel-specification registry has exactly one unqualified CONCENTRATION entry, with no channel-type-qualified variant that could mean a different substance, and every particulate reading is a separately named parameter. BidCos declares no CONCENTRATION at all, so the classifier cannot be reached by a non-HmIP device. The comment's wording should change from 'by HM convention' to the CCU's own labelling, but the classification it produces is right. What is NOT grounded is the unit: the CCU declares none. Units on the HmIP legacy XML-RPC surface come from `<CHANNELTYPE>.<PARAM>.Unit` keys read by DeviceUtil#fillLegacyParameter, and ../OpenCCU-Base/opt/HmIP/legacy-parameter-definition.config contains no `.Unit` key at all; the string "ppm" appears nowhere in the WebUI tree. The only quantitative facts the firmware gives are the wire scale (physical = logical×100) and the logical range 0.0..163830.0. If our Matter path needs to publish a MeasurementUnit for CarbonDioxideConcentrationMeasurement, that value has to come from somewhere other than the CCU — say so rather than assuming ppm.
all.negativeControl: Had CONCENTRATION been a generic or non-CO2 reading, translate.lang.diagram.js:170 would have aliased it to a neutral label (the file does exactly that for the particulates: `diagramValueTypeMASS_CONCENTRATION_PM_2_5` gets its own "Massenkonzentration PM2.5" string rather than the CO2 one), or a second channel-type-qualified CONCENTRATION entry would exist in the HmIP state-parameter registry. Neither is the case: line 170 aliases to lblCO2Concentration, and the registry key is unqualified and unique.
all.missingInput: The measurement unit. The CCU declares no UNIT for CONCENTRATION (no `.Unit` entry in legacy-parameter-definition.config; no "ppm" token anywhere in the WebUI), so any unit we publish is ours, not the device's.
all.challengeNote: Classification UPHELD as confirmed, and it is better grounded than the candidate argued — but the candidate's unit sub-finding is REFUTED. Every label citation opened and matched verbatim, and I re-ran the exhaustiveness checks: exactly one unqualified ParameterMapKey("CONCENTRATION") in the HmIP registry, every particulate reading separately named, and zero CONCENTRATION parameters across all of firmware/rftypes and src/devicetypes, so a BidCos device cannot reach the classifier. Our enum strings at pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:45,98-100 match the firmware names character-for-character, including the _24H_AVERAGE suffix. STRONGER GROUNDING than label aliasing: the parameter's own channel type is CARBON_DIOXIDE_RECEIVER (a ChannelType constant in the CCU's device-description model), and the descriptor carries CONTROL="CARBON_DIOXIDE_RECEIVER.CONCENTRATION" — the CCU names the substance structurally, not just in a translation catalogue. The comment should cite that rather than 'HM convention'. REFUTED: the candidate wrote 'the CCU declares no unit… the string "ppm" appears nowhere in the WebUI tree… that value has to come from somewhere other than the CCU'. `../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/controls/heating_control.fn:208` is `string co2Unit = "ppm";`, and the Tier-2 descriptor captured from a real CCU carries UNIT "ppm" on this exact parameter on two device types. The candidate's mechanism observation is correct in itself (units are filled from `<typeName>.<param>.Unit` properties by HMIPServer DeviceUtil#fillLegacyParameter, and opt/HmIP/legacy-parameter-definition.config contains no `.Unit` key) — but it inferred CCU silence from one file's absence instead of reading the field the device actually declares. If our Matter path needs a MeasurementUnit, read it from the descriptor UNIT at runtime; do not hard-code ppm and do not report it as unavailable. One honest caveat on co2Unit itself: grep shows it is assigned at :208 and never used — heating_control.fn:273 renders `oCO2Concentration.ValueUnit()` instead — so treat it as corroboration of intent, and the descriptor as the authority. BOUNDARY, not firmware-grounded: our classifier keys on the parameter name alone, so a CUxD or Homegear device that invents a CONCENTRATION parameter would be classified as CO2 with no CCU semantics behind it.

all.title: Optimistic-write confirmation compares floats after half-up rounding to two decimals
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSTypeConversionFloatInteger.cpp:56-66 `double dval=((double&)in+offset)*factor; if(dval>=0)dval+=0.5; else dval-=0.5; ((int&)*out)=(int)dval;` and :69-77 `((double&)*out)=(((double)((int&)in))/factor)-offset;` — every FLOAT parameter with a `float_integer_scale` conversion is quantised to 1/factor on write and echoed back from that quantised integer. The factors are per parameter, from ../OpenCCU-Base/firmware/rftypes/: rf_cc_rt_dn.xml `<parameter id="SET_TEMPERATURE"><logical type="float" min="4.5" max="30.5" default="20.0" unit="°C"/>…<conversion type="float_integer_scale" factor="2"/>` (step 0.5 °C) and `<parameter id="ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE">…factor="10.0"` (step 0.1); rf_dim_2t_644_le_v2_4.xml LEVEL `factor="200"` (step 0.005) and ON_TIME / RAMP_TIME `factor="10"` (step 0.1). The HmIP side names the quantity outright: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.typeconversion.converter.DoubleToInteger#getStepGranularity returns 1.0/factor, and #convertLogicalToPhysical applies the same ±0.5 half-away-from-zero rounding. The step is NOT on the wire we read: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSParameter.cpp:205-218 exports ID, OPERATIONS, FLAGS, TAB_ORDER, CONTROL; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSLogicalTypeFloat.cpp:105-119 adds TYPE, MIN, MAX, DEFAULT, SPECIAL; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSLogicalType.cpp:53-61 adds UNIT. No factor, no step, no precision.
all.firmwareValue: Quantisation is per parameter, step = 1/factor: 0.5 °C for SET_TEMPERATURE, 0.1 for ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE / ON_TIME / RAMP_TIME, 0.005 for LEVEL, 1.0 for factor=1 parameters. The echo is the round-tripped quantised value, so it may differ from the written value by up to half a step.
all.ourValue: A fixed two-decimal comparison for every float parameter — effectively a ±0.005 tolerance, regardless of the parameter
all.finding: The firmware does quantise, and it does echo the quantised value, so the comment's worry is real — but the amount it allows is wrong in both directions and wrong most often in the dangerous one. Two decimals is a ±0.005 window. On a SET_TEMPERATURE write (factor 2) the CCU snaps to the nearest 0.5 °C: a written 20.3 comes back as 20.5, and valuesClose compares round(20.3,2)=20.30 against round(20.5,2)=20.50 and reports a mismatch — precisely the 'tracker cleared as CCU-authoritative, user-visible value flips' failure the comment names, on the single most commonly written float in the product. The same holds for every factor-10 parameter (ON_TIME, RAMP_TIME, ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE): step 0.1, tolerance 0.005, twenty times too tight. In the other direction it is too loose for factor-200 LEVEL, whose step is 0.005 — there a real 0.005 refusal is inside the window. So the fixed constant is not a conservative choice; it is unrelated to what the firmware does. The right driver is the parameter's own step granularity — the HmIP stack calls it exactly that — but that value is NOT PERFORMABLE from what we read: getParamsetDescription carries TYPE/MIN/MAX/DEFAULT/SPECIAL/UNIT/OPERATIONS/FLAGS/TAB_ORDER/CONTROL and nothing about the physical scaling, on both the BidCos and HmIP legacy surfaces. Deriving a step from MIN/MAX, or from the unit string, would be exactly the convention-substitution this audit exists to catch. The honest options are to widen the tolerance deliberately and say why, or to carry a per-parameter step table sourced from the device XMLs — not to leave a two-decimal constant with a Python citation behind it.
all.negativeControl: Had a uniform two-decimal quantisation been the firmware's rule, every float parameter would carry `factor="100"`. Across firmware/rftypes the factors are 200, 100, 10, 2 and 1 on different parameters of the same device, and the HmIP converter exposes 1/factor under the name getStepGranularity — a different answer, and a specific one. Had the step been readable at runtime, it would appear in HSSLogicalTypeFloat::GetDescription alongside MIN/MAX/DEFAULT; that function assigns five keys and none of them is it.
all.missingInput: The per-parameter step granularity (1/factor). It exists in the firmware's device XML and in the HmIP converter, but is not exported by getParamsetDescription on either transport, so the daemon cannot measure it from the CCU.
all.challengeNote: Verdict UPHELD as contradicted; the not-performable pillar is now verified more completely than the candidate verified it; the failure narrative needs correcting. Formulas quoted character-exact; all factors opened in the XMLs and matched. STRENGTHENED: the candidate listed three files as proof that the step is not exported, but stopped before HSSParameter::GetDescription's last line, which delegates to an arbitrary key-value block from the device XML. I inventoried every `<field id=…>` across firmware/rftypes/*.xml — one id, `AutoconfRoles`, 12 occurrences. Nothing resembling a step, precision or factor is exported on either surface, so deriving a per-parameter tolerance from getParamsetDescription is genuinely not performable, and deriving it from MIN/MAX or the unit string would be convention-substitution. CORRECTED consequence: the candidate's SET_TEMPERATURE story — 'tracker cleared as CCU-authoritative, user-visible value flips' — overstates the damage on the confirmation path. datapoint.go:1043 assigns `d.value = v` unconditionally before the tracker is consulted, and both branches at :1088-1098 announce v; the mismatch branch only clears the tracker sooner. The reachable defect is on the OTHER caller the candidate did not open: IsStateChange (datapoint.go:1997-2009) and WithValue (:2054-2059) use the same valuesClose to decide whether a write is sent at all. For a factor-200 LEVEL the ±0.005 window swallows real device steps — a confirmed 0.500 and a commanded 0.503 quantise to 100 and 101, a genuine step the device can execute, yet round(x,2) makes them equal and the write is suppressed. That is reachable from any caller finer than whole percent (a Matter LevelControl 0..254 mapping lands on ~0.004 increments). In the other direction the window is twenty times too tight for factor-10 parameters and ten times too tight for SET_TEMPERATURE, which only costs a redundant radio send. CORRECTED fact: 'step 0.1 for ON_TIME / RAMP_TIME' holds only in the lowest exponent range — the XML chains integer_tinyfloat (11-bit mantissa, 5-bit exponent) after the factor-10 scale, and HSSParameter.cpp:385-387 applies conversions in order, so the step grows with magnitude above roughly 204.7 s. Both corrections push the same way: the two-decimal constant is unrelated to what the firmware does, and the honest options remain widening it deliberately with a stated reason, or carrying a per-parameter step table sourced from the device XMLs.

all.title: The CCU user-level ordinals are restated in the model's interface contract
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/pages/index.htm:93 `ul = <% Write( oUser.UserLevel()); %>;` and :96-103 — comment `/** Privilegstufen. **/` followed by `UPL_NONE  = 0; UPL_GUEST = 1; UPL_USER  = 2; UPL_ADMIN = 8;`. The ReGa names behind them, used as gates in ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/system.fn — :116 `if( (oUser.UserLevel() != iulGuest) && (oUser.UserLevel() != iulNone) )`, :176 / :761 / :874 / :891 / :908 / :1165 / :1425 `if( oUser.UserLevel() == iulAdmin )`, :298 `if( oUser.UserLevel() != iulNone )`; the write side at :1125 `user.UserLevel(system.GetVar("level"));`. Client-side gates use the same form: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/ise/htm/header.htm:86 `if (getUPL() != UPL_GUEST)`, ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www_source/webui/js/dialog/installWizard.js:5,8,47,52,122,135 (`== UPL_ADMIN`, `== UPL_USER`). Our own script: internal/client/rega/scripts/get_user_level.fn — `object oUser = dom.GetObject(ID_USERS).Get("##username##"); if (oUser) { Write(oUser.UserLevel()); } else { Write(-1); }`.
all.firmwareValue: UPL_NONE = 0, UPL_GUEST = 1, UPL_USER = 2, UPL_ADMIN = 8. Every firmware gate on UserLevel is an exact-equality (== / !=) test against one of these four; no ordering comparison exists anywhere in the tree. -1 is not a CCU value.
all.ourValue: hub.go:52 — "returns the user's UserLevel (8/2/1/0) or -1 when the user does not exist"; internal/auth/ccuauth/store.go:145-157 — thresholds `level >= 8` admin, `>= 2` operator, `>= 1` viewer, else deny
all.finding: The ordinals and their meanings are confirmed exactly as the comment states them, from the CCU's own definition block, and I found no fifth value anywhere. Two things one step wider are not the CCU's, and they are where the restatement will drift. (1) The -1 sentinel is OURS — it comes from the else-branch of our own get_user_level.fn, not from ReGa; a CCU user object simply does not exist to be asked. The comment reads as though the CCU returns -1, which it does not. That is harmless as long as both halves stay in one file, and misleading the moment someone treats -1 as a documented CCU level. (2) The CCU never ORDERS these values. Every gate in ReGa, in the WebUI header and in the install wizard is `==` or `!=` against a named constant — there is no `>=` on UserLevel in the tree. Our threshold form (roleForLevel, and the MinUserLevel comparison at store.go:120) is a Loom construction layered on top; it happens to agree with the CCU on the four real values, because 0<1<2<8 orders them the way the names do, but for any value outside {0,1,2,8} the CCU has no privilege rank at all while our code silently assigns one (a hypothetical 3 maps to operator; the CCU would match none of its four constants and deny). The comment at roleForLevel calling threshold form 'tolerant of unforeseen CCU levels' has it backwards: threshold form INVENTS a rank for a level the CCU refuses to rank.
all.negativeControl: Had the ordinals been wrong, index.htm:99-103 would assign different numbers to UPL_NONE/GUEST/USER/ADMIN — the block is explicit and is the same file that reads `oUser.UserLevel()` into `ul`, so it cannot be about a different quantity. Had the CCU itself ordered the levels, at least one gate would compare with `>` or `>=`; a search across www/, src/webui/ and the ReGa scripts finds only `==` and `!=` on UserLevel.
all.challengeNote: Verdict UPHELD as narrowed, but only one of the candidate's two boundaries survives; the other is contradicted by Tier 1. CONFIRMED: the four ordinals and their meanings, read verbatim off the CCU's own definition block at index.htm:96-103, with no fifth value anywhere in the tree. SURVIVING BOUNDARY (the candidate's point 1): the -1 sentinel is ours, produced by the else-branch of our own get_user_level.fn, not by ReGa — a CCU user object that does not exist cannot be asked for a level. hub.go:52 reads as though the CCU returns -1, and that should be reworded; the script's own header comment already states it correctly. REFUTED (the candidate's point 2): 'Every firmware gate on UserLevel is an exact-equality test; no ordering comparison exists anywhere in the tree; our threshold form is a Loom construction layered on top; the roleForLevel comment has it backwards.' The CCU's own WebUI defines the threshold form and names it as such — index.htm:165-167 is `function hasUPL(upl) { return (upl <= getUPL()); }` under the comment "Prüft, ob der Benutzer eine bestimmte Privilegstufe besitzt" (checks whether the user holds a given privilege level), which is precisely our `level >= threshold`. And logout.htm:94 `if (oUser.UserLevel() <= 1)` is a live ReGa gate treating {none, guest} as an ordered range. So `>=` is the CCU's own idiom for 'at least this level', and the roleForLevel comment at store.go:143 is not backwards. Two honest qualifications on the refutation: hasUPL has no caller in the readable tree (grep across www/ and src/webui/ returns only its definition), so as a live gate only logout.htm's ordering is exercised; and the candidate's underlying observation is still true — for a hypothetical level outside {0,1,2,8} our thresholds assign a rank while the equality gates in system.fn would match none. That is a real difference in behaviour, just not evidence that the CCU refuses to order. SEPARATE OBSERVATION on provenance: `iulAdmin` / `iulGuest` / `iulNone` are never defined anywhere in the tree (they are ReGa interpreter built-ins; ReGaHss is not in this checkout), so system.fn establishes the SHAPE of the gates but cannot establish which number iulAdmin is. The ordinals rest entirely on index.htm's JS constant block, which is written next to `ul = <%Write(oUser.UserLevel())%>` and consumed by getUPL()-based gates over that same value — sound, but it is a single source, and the candidate presented system.fn as if it corroborated the numbers.

all.title: The unit lookup table claims to carry the exact CCU-shipped unit notation, with no cited source
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSLogicalType.cpp:39-41 (`temp=node.getAttribute("unit"); if(temp)unit=temp;`) and :56 (`(*val)["UNIT"]=unit;`) — UNIT is the <logical> element's `unit` attribute passed through verbatim, no normalisation, no default. Tier 1 corpus: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/*.xml + hs485types/*.xml — the COMPLETE set of `unit=` literals is s(362+9), 100%(159), minutes(7), deg(4), °C(3), F(2), %(2), hPa(1); e.g. rf_ash550.xml:91,102,111. Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/opt/HMServer/groups/groupdefinitions.xml — °C(281), minutes(277), unit=""(30), day(2), month(2), year(2), %(2), K(1), s(1). Tier 1 (encoding): ../OpenCCU-Base/build-tools/bidcos-devicetype-strip.jar!strip-docu.xsl — an identity-copy XSLT with `<xsl:output indent="no"/>` and no encoding attribute, i.e. XSLT-1.0 default UTF-8, so `°` is resolved to U+00B0 and re-serialised as UTF-8 in the shipped runtime XML; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libxmlparser/xmlParser.cpp:205-250 (`fromXMLString`) decodes ONLY < > & ' " and would have passed a surviving numeric reference through untouched. Tier 1 (HmIP): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#fillLegacyParameter — UNIT is taken from a `<ChannelType>.<Parameter>.Unit` entry of the legacy parameter properties and set via ParameterDescription#setUnit; the properties file itself is not in either tree. Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/*.json, UNIT field, 399 device types.
all.firmwareValue: '°C'=U+00B0,U+0043 (6750×) · '% rF'=U+0025,U+0020,U+0072,U+0046 (29×) · '100%' (2200× corpus, 159× rftypes) · 'µg/m³'=U+00B5(MICRO SIGN),g,/,m,U+00B3 (9×) · '1/cm³' (3×) · 'µm' (1×) · plus 'minutes'(1130), 'Lux'(6), 'mm'(10), 'm3'(3), 'mHz'(14), 'deg'(16)/'degree'(12)/'Grad'/'_Grad_', 'cm'(5), 'day'/'month'/'year'/'hour'/'minute'/'d', 'g/m³', 'L', 'L/min', 'bar', 'Ohm', 'x 200Hz', '0.1 %', '0.1 hPa', '0.1 K', 'U./kWh', 'Imp./kWh', 'm3/Imp.', '""', ' ', '${lblReadings}' and a literal '°C' (282×, HM-CC-VG-1 only). No shipped unit carries surrounding whitespace except the one-space unit ' ' on CMM.
all.ourValue: 33 map keys; 'l/m²', 'dBm', 'lx', 'kW', 'kWh', 'mV', 'A', 'm/s', 'km', 'l', 'm³' appear in no source read (Tier 1 or Tier 2)
all.finding: The four exemplars the file itself cites are confirmed byte for byte, including the codepoints: '°C' is U+00B0 (not the mojibake pair, not the literal entity), 'µg/m³' uses MICRO SIGN U+00B5 (not GREEK MU U+03BC), '% rF' has exactly one ASCII space, '100%' has none. The encoding chain is closed: the source XML declares iso-8859-1 and writes `unit="°C"`; the build's XSLT identity copy resolves the reference and emits UTF-8 (default output encoding, and it also strips the XML declaration); rfd reads the attribute verbatim into HSSLogicalType::unit and emits it as UNIT unchanged. Our Go keys are UTF-8 source literals, so they match. What is false one step wider is the file's framing that the table IS the CCU-shipped notation. The boundary runs in both directions. (a) Eleven of 33 keys correspond to no unit any source ships — most sharply 'l/m²' (RAIN_COUNTER ships 'mm'), 'dBm' (RSSI_DEVICE ships '' or no UNIT at all) and 'lx' (CURRENT_ILLUMINATION ships 'Lux'). (b) The single most common non-'s' unit after '°C' is 'minutes' (1130 in the corpus, 277 in groupdefinitions.xml, 7 in rftypes) and it has no key; the PARTY_START_TIME / PARTY_STOP_TIME family that carries it matches no parameter rule either, so those DPs land on the INTEGER type floor. Also missing: 'Lux', 'cm', 'm3', 'mHz', 'deg'/'degree'/'Grad', 'bar', 'Ohm', 'L', 'day'/'month'/'year'. In practice the damage is smaller than the bundle assumes because parameterHint runs first and catches RAIN_COUNTER, ILLUMINATION, RSSI and the concentration family by name — the wrong keys are dead rather than harmful. Separately, the retry at :195-198 cannot do what its comment claims: every map key with an uppercase letter is unreachable through strings.ToLower, so the comment's own example (descriptor ships '% RF' → matches '% rF') is false; the retry can only ever fire for the 14 already-lowercase keys when the input has surrounding whitespace. One unit form the tree cannot settle: the HmIP UNIT strings come from a legacy parameter properties file that is present in neither OpenCCU-Base nor the HMIPServer component, so 'µg/m³', '1/cm³', 'µm' and '% rF' rest on the Tier-2 descriptor corpus, not on a firmware file.
all.negativeControl: Had our keys been wrong in the cited places, the codepoint dump over 399 shipped paramset descriptions would have printed something other than 'U+00B0 U+0043' for degrees (a bare 0xB0 rendered as U+FFFD, the pair U+00C2 U+00B0, or the 7-character literal '°C'), or 'U+03BC' for micro, or '100 %' with a space. It printed the exact byte sequences our keys contain. The check does discriminate: it printed a literal '°C' for HM-CC-VG-1 and 'Lux' where we key 'lx', so a mismatch is visible when one exists.
all.missingInput: The HmIP legacy parameter definition properties file (the source of the `<ChannelType>.<Parameter>.Unit` entries) is in neither reference tree, so the HmIP-only unit literals are grounded on the descriptor corpus rather than on firmware.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD as narrowed, with the bundle's central mechanism CONTRADICTED and three census errors corrected.

What I confirmed independently: HSSLogicalType passes the attribute through verbatim; the shipped XMLs carry exactly eight unit literals; RAIN_COUNTER ships 'mm' (8 declarations), CURRENT_ILLUMINATION ships no UNIT on 13 of 14 and 'Lux' on one, RSSI_DEVICE/RSSI_PEER carry no UNIT or '' on all 362 declarations, PARTY_START_TIME/PARTY_STOP_TIME carry 'minutes'; the eleven dead keys are dead; devices.go:1083 is the only production caller; the ToLower retry cannot reach any key containing an uppercase letter, so the comment's own example ('% RF' → '% rF') is impossible.

CONTRADICTED — the encoding chain. The bundle grounded '°C' = U+00B0 on 'XSLT-1.0 default UTF-8, so the reference is re-serialised as UTF-8 in the shipped runtime XML'. The stripper's bytecode says otherwise: parseArgs defaults outputEncoding to ISO-8859-1, transform() sets it as the transformer's `encoding` output property AND as the OutputStreamWriter charset, and the CMake target passes no -enc-out. The shipped file is Latin-1; '°' is the byte 0xB0, which is not valid UTF-8. The bundle's further claim that the XSLT 'also strips the XML declaration' is wrong too — `<xsl:template match="processing-instruction()"/>` does not match an XML declaration, and the default omit-xml-declaration is "no".

The conclusion survives, by a mechanism the bundle did not state: rfd's own responses declare `encoding="iso-8859-1"` (XmlRpcServerConnection.cpp:366,414) and our decoder transcodes via charset.NewReaderLabel, so 0xB0 becomes U+00B0 in Go and the literal matches. Right answer, unsound grounding — and it would have been the wrong answer for any consumer that read the shipped XML directly.

Three census errors: (a) 's' is 278 rftypes + 84 hs485types, not '362+9'. (b) The counts on the `firmware value` line are the Tier-2 corpus, not firmware; three of the four exemplars the file's comment cites ('% rF', 'µg/m³', '1/cm³', 'µm') appear in NO firmware file. (c) 'the 14 already-lowercase keys' inverts the sets: 19 keys are already lowercase and reachable through the retry; 14 carry an uppercase letter and are unreachable.

One more: the 282× value the bundle reports as 'a literal °C, HM-CC-VG-1 only' is in fact the 8-character string `°C` — a double-escaping artefact of pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HM-CC-VG-1.json, not a unit any firmware ships. It should not appear on a firmware-value line at all.

all.title: Three different CCU address grammars coexist and the pkg one is a port, not a firmware reading
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:419-427 — `char buffer[5]; if (channel >= 0 && channel <= 255) snprintf(buffer, sizeof(buffer), ":%d", channel); else *buffer = 0; return address + buffer;`. ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:429-437 — unknown device: `snprintf(buffer, sizeof(buffer), "@%06X", address)`. ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFCentral.cpp:37 — `serial="BidCoS-RF";`. ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosFrame.h:57 — `FIELD_SYSINFO_SERIAL = STRUCTURED_FRAME_FIELD_STR(12, 10)` (fixed 10-byte serial field). ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:242 and RFChannel.cpp:972-975 — ADDRESS/PARENT are built by BuildStringAddress. Tier 1 (HmIP): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#getChannelAddress (`getDeviceLegacyAddress(deviceID) + ADDRESS_SEPERATOR + channelIndex`, ADDRESS_SEPERATOR = ":"), #getDeviceLegacyAddress (strips the `Legacy.AddressPrefix` service property, default empty), and the literal device id "CENTRAL_DEVICE" used with channel 63 as a link partner in #getLinkInfo/#createCentralLink. Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/device_descriptions/*.json — 2924 addresses, all 10 chars, max channel index 50 (VCU4264293:50); the corpus is anonymised to VCU*/INT* so it cannot speak to the real charset.
all.firmwareValue: channel suffix 0…255 (`\d{1,3}`); BidCos serial exactly 10 bytes; central's own device address "BidCoS-RF" (mixed case + '-'); unknown-device fallback "@%06X" e.g. "@1A2B3C"; HmIP link-partner address "CENTRAL_DEVICE:63" (underscore)
all.ourValue: pkg/hmtypes `^[0-9a-zA-Z-]{5,20}(:\d{1,3})?$` · rpc_recorder `\b([0-9A-Fa-f]{12,14}|[A-Z]{2,4}\d{6,8})(:\d{1,2})?\b` · diagnostics `\b[0-9A-Z]{8,20}(?::\d{1,3})?\b` + ≥1 uppercase letter and ≥2 digits
all.finding: The channel bound is confirmed exactly: rfd caps the suffix at 255, so `\d{1,3}` in pkg/hmtypes and in diagnostics is the correct upper bound (slightly wide, 256–999 accepted, harmless). rpc_recorder's `\d{1,2}` is narrower than the firmware by one digit — channels 100–255 exist per RFManager.cpp:422. The device-part grammars are narrowed in three concrete places, all of which the firmware issues today: (1) "BidCoS-RF" — the central's own device address, mixed case with a dash, accepted by pkg/hmtypes but matched by neither redactor; (2) "@1A2B3C" — the fallback rfd emits for a frame from a device it has no serial for, rejected by all three grammars because '@' is in none of the character classes and the six hex digits are below every length floor; (3) "CENTRAL_DEVICE" / "CENTRAL_DEVICE:63" — the HmIP legacy surface's own link-partner address, rejected by pkg/hmtypes because '_' is not in `[0-9a-zA-Z-]`. Cases (1) and (2) are not privacy-relevant (a fixed literal and a serial-less device), so the redaction gap they expose is cosmetic. The one redaction gap that is real is in diagnostics: `addressLike` demands at least one A–Z, so an HmIP address whose hex happens to contain no A–F digit passes through unredacted. Two corrections to the bundle's damage claim: pkg/hmtypes' IsChannelAddress and IsDeviceAddress have NO production caller in this repo (only their own tests), so they gate nothing today — they are public surface for downstream consumers, and that is where a too-narrow grammar would bite. And rpc_recorder's `\d{1,2}` does not leak the serial for a 3-digit channel: the optional group simply fails to match and the device part is still hashed, leaving only the bare channel digits in the clear.
all.negativeControl: Had our grammars been right at the firmware's own boundaries, RFManager.cpp:419-437 would have shown a channel formatter with no 255 cap and no non-alphanumeric fallback prefix, RFCentral.cpp would not have assigned a serial containing '-', and the HmIP legacy address builder would not have used an identifier containing '_'. Each of those is a printable literal in the source and each one came out against us — the check discriminates. For the channel bound the control fired in our favour: `channel <= 255` is exactly the range `\d{1,3}` covers.
all.missingInput: The CUxD address grammar is not decidable from these trees: CUxD is a closed third-party addon and the string 'CUxD' does not occur anywhere in ../OpenCCU-Base; the only trace in the distribution is a WebUI name prefix check (`oEName.Find("CUxD.CUX")`) in ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/patches/occu/0027-WebUI-Fix-EmptyTableCUxDDevices.patch:8, which fixes no serial length or charset. Likewise the real BidCos serial character set (as opposed to its 10-byte width) is not asserted anywhere in rfd — the serial is read as an opaque 10-byte field — and the pydevccu corpus is anonymised, so it cannot supply it.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD as narrowed. Every Tier-1 citation contains what is claimed, transcribed exactly, and all three of our regexes are quoted correctly. I re-verified the strongest of the bundle's own corrections myself: `IsChannelAddress` and `IsDeviceAddress` have no production caller anywhere in the repo — the only references outside their own definitions are in pkg/hmtypes/address_test.go. So the pkg grammar gates nothing today and is public surface for downstream consumers only. That correction is sound and it is what keeps this entry from being a false alarm.

Two demotions.

(1) SCOPE. 'channels 100–255 exist per RFManager.cpp:422' conflates what the firmware permits with what a device declares. RFManager caps the suffix at 255; that is a bound, not an existence claim. The highest channel index anywhere in the 2924-address Tier-2 corpus is 50 (VCU4264293:50), and the HmIP side (#getChannelAddress) applies no cap of its own. So rpc_recorder's `\d{1,2}` is narrower than the firmware's ceiling but has no measured instance behind it. The honest statement is: firmware permits up to 255, no source read here declares above 50. On the same footing, `\d{1,3}` in pkg/hmtypes and diagnostics is correct against the BidCos bound and simply unbounded-by-firmware against HmIP.

(2) UNVERIFIED, as to frequency. 'an HmIP address whose hex happens to contain no A–F digit passes through unredacted' is a correct arithmetic reading of addressLike (letters >= 1 && digits >= 2, diagnostics.go:354-366) — an all-digit 14-character token matches addressLikeRe and then fails addressLike. But nothing in either tree states that HmIP legacy addresses always contain a hex letter, and I found no source that enumerates the real address space (the corpus is anonymised to VCU*/INT*). So the leak is a real property of our code; its rate is unmeasured. Report it as a code defect, not as a measured exposure.

One correction the bundle got right and I confirmed: rpc_recorder's optional `(:\d{1,2})?` group failing to match a 3-digit channel does not leak the device part — the alternation still matches and hashes the serial, leaving only bare channel digits in the clear.

all.title: The empty-value acceptance list and the initial-load skip rules are curated lists standing in for a descriptor reading
all.site: pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:346-386 (OptionalParameters/IsOptional) and :388-418 (ignoreOnInitialLoadExact/IgnoreOnInitialLoad); consumed at internal/model/generic/datapoint.go:1365 (allowsNoneValue) and :367
all.citation: Tier 1 (bit semantics): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSParameter.h:53-59 — `OP_NONE=0, OP_READ=1, OP_WRITE=2, OP_EVENT=4, OP_DETERMINE=8`, and :83-88 `IsReadable(){return (operations & OP_READ)!=0;}`. Tier 1 (read path): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFChannel.cpp:141-144 — getValue on a non-readable parameter throws `XmlRpcException("Parameter is not readable", -1)`; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSParamset.cpp:162-176 — getParamset SKIPS non-readable parameters (`if(!param->IsReadable())continue;`) and returns false (→ fault) if a readable one cannot be produced, so no empty value is ever emitted; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:221-224 — ReadValue on a bare device address always returns false. Tier 1 (radio vs cache): ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSPhysicalType.cpp:78-88 — `Get()`→`data_interface->GetData()` versus `Determine()`→`data_interface->DetermineValue()`, and getValue never calls Determine (that is the separate determineParameter method, ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:265 → RFManager.cpp:125-132, matching OP_DETERMINE=8); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSPhysicalDataInterfaceInternal.cpp:37-40 — `GetData` = `inst->GetInternalValue(...)`, purely local; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:152-172 — `if(get_request_frame.id.empty()) return inst->GetStoredValue(...)`, then `if(inst->GetAge(value_id)<VALUE_CACHE_TIME) return inst->GetStoredValue(...)`, then `if(channel->GetDevice()->RxNeedsWakeup()){ if(inst->GetStoredValue(...))return true; channel->GetDevice()->QueueAfterWakeupFrame(frame); return false; }`. Tier 1 (HmIP): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler#getValue — all keys are served from the server-side device model via de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#getValue, EXCEPT exactly two, "INSTALL_TEST" and "CURRENT_ILLUMINATION", which call DeviceUtil#askValue (sends BackendCommandType.DEVICE_VALUE_ASK on the hmip backend bus) and block for a RECEIVED_STATUS_DATA notification. Tier 2: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/{rftypes,hs485types}/*.xml `<physical interface=...>` per parameter, and ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/*.json OPERATIONS/SPECIAL fields. Tier 3 witness (provenance only): ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/const.py:1958-1984 `_OPTIONAL_PARAMETERS` and ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/model/data_point.py:1393-1398 — our list is a verbatim port, comments included.
all.firmwareValue: Parameters that CAN cause a device request on a getValue: BidCos — only those whose <physical> uses interface="command" AND declares a <get request=…> child; HmIP — exactly INSTALL_TEST and CURRENT_ILLUMINATION. SPECIAL ids that exist: NOT_USED, OLD_LEVEL, PERMANENT, LOCKED, ACT_LEVEL, NO_MODIFICATION, VENT_OPEN — never OPTIONAL.
all.ourValue: ignoreOnInitialLoadExact = {DUTY_CYCLE, DUTYCYCLE, LOW_BAT, LOWBAT, OPERATING_VOLTAGE} + prefixes ERROR_/RSSI_ + suffix _ERROR, justified as 'wakes battery-powered devices unnecessarily and may exceed duty-cycle limits'
all.finding: Both halves are contradicted, on different grounds. (1) IgnoreOnInitialLoad's rationale is false for every member of its own set. I scanned all 130 rftypes plus 18 hs485types for the <physical interface> of each targeted parameter: DUTYCYCLE(59) internal, RSSI_DEVICE(126) internal, RSSI_PEER(126) internal, LOWBAT 89 internal + 22 command, and every ERROR_* / *_ERROR occurrence (65 across 12 names) command. I then checked whether any of the command-interface ones carries a <get request=…> child, which per RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:152 is the only thing that lets GetData build a frame: NOT ONE of them does — all 87 are 'no-get'. So on BidCos every parameter in our skip list is served from the local store with zero radio traffic, and even a hypothetical get-capable one on a wakeup device would be queued rather than transmitted (`QueueAfterWakeupFrame`, :168-172), so getValue cannot wake a sleeping device on this transport at all. OPERATING_VOLTAGE does not appear in the BidCos XMLs; on the HmIP side it is served from the device model like everything else. (2) The two parameters that DO reach the device on a getValue — INSTALL_TEST and CURRENT_ILLUMINATION on the HmIP legacy surface, via DeviceUtil#askValue — are ABSENT from the skip list. INSTALL_TEST is in our OptionalParameters set instead, i.e. we marked the one genuinely expensive read as merely optional. (3) The 'CCU sends an empty string for LEVEL_2' rationale answers a surface the firmware does not have: getValue on a non-readable parameter faults with code -1, getParamset silently omits non-readable parameters and faults outright if a readable one fails — there is no path that yields an empty string for a FLOAT. What our code actually does with IsOptional is allowsNoneValue (whether an unobserved DP still counts valid), not empty-value decoding, so both the bundle's summary and our own comment describe a mechanism that does not exist. (4) The descriptor CAN replace part of the list but not all of it. OPERATIONS (Tier-1 bits at HSSParameter.h:53-59) already marks DURATION_UNIT(2), EFFECT(2), ON_TIME(2 on 432 of 435 declarations), RAMP_TIME(2), RAMP_TIME_UNIT(2), RAMP_TIME_TO_OFF_UNIT(2) and INSTALL_TEST(2/4/6) as non-readable, so those are derivable. LEVEL_2(5/7), COLOR(5/7), COLOR_TEMPERATURE(7), HUE(7), SATURATION(7), INHIBIT(6/7) and PARTY_TEMPERATURE(3/7) all declare READ, so for those the descriptor does not decide it and the curated list is doing real work. ON_TIME_UNIT is declared by zero of the 399 device types. (5) The SPECIAL.OPTIONAL fallback at datapoint.go:1367-1375 is dead: SPECIAL is a special-VALUE map, and the complete id set across Tier 1 (rftypes: NOT_USED 122, OLD_LEVEL 14, PERMANENT 7, LOCKED 5) and Tier 2 (adds ACT_LEVEL, NO_MODIFICATION, VENT_OPEN) contains no OPTIONAL. reachesDevice is false today only because DataPoint.IgnoreOnInitialLoad() has no production consumer — it is computed at datapoint.go:367, stored, and read nowhere outside tests. Wire it up as written and the HmIP INSTALL_TEST / CURRENT_ILLUMINATION omission becomes an on-air defect.
all.negativeControl: Had the skip list's rationale been right, the per-parameter interface scan would have printed at least one ('LOWBAT'|'DUTYCYCLE'|'RSSI_*'|'ERROR_*', 'command'+get) row — the same script printed 'command' for 87 of them and 'get' for none, and it does emit 'get' rows for other parameters in the same corpus, so the discriminating case exists and simply is not these. Had SPECIAL.OPTIONAL been real, the SPECIAL-key census over 399 device types would have listed OPTIONAL alongside NOT_USED and PERMANENT; it listed seven ids and OPTIONAL was not among them. Had the empty-string claim been right, HSSParamset::Get would have emitted a default or an empty XmlRpcValue on a failed read instead of `return false`.
all.missingInput: VALUE_CACHE_TIME (RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:155, HS485PhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:91) is referenced but defined nowhere in ../OpenCCU-Base, so the width of the CCU's own value cache is not measurable here — only the fact that one exists. Nothing in either tree is needed for the rest of this finding.
all.challengeNote:
CONTRADICTION UPHELD, and I reproduced the decisive scan independently rather than trusting it: parsing every `<parameter>` in all 148 shipped XMLs and walking its `<physical>` descendants, zero skip-list parameters carry a `<get>` child, so RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand::GetData short-circuits to GetStoredValue for all of them and no radio traffic occurs. The wakeup branch confirms the second half — even a get-capable parameter on a sleeping device is queued, never transmitted. RFChannel.cpp:141-144 and HSSParamset.cpp:162-176 confirm there is no path that yields an empty string for a non-readable FLOAT. The SPECIAL census matches the bundle exactly and contains no OPTIONAL, so the fallback at datapoint.go:1367-1375 is dead. All four legs hold.

But TWO of the bundle's own corrections are themselves wrong, and both cut against it.

(a) reachesDevice is TRUE, not false. The bundle's 'false' rests on `DataPoint.IgnoreOnInitialLoad()` having no production consumer — which I confirmed (datapoint.go:367 sets the field, :1919 returns it, nothing else reads either). But that is not the question. Our daemon has three OTHER per-DP boot read paths and none consults any skip list: relevant_init.go:41 (channel 0, hmenum.RelevantInitParameters = CONFIG_PENDING/STICKY_UNREACH/UNREACH), seedReadableEvents (Event/EventGroup/Button categories), and — decisively — the third pass of UnobservedSweep.sweepDevice at internal/central/adapter/unobserved_sweep.go:132-140, which issues a load for EVERY visible readable VALUES DP with no observed value. CURRENT_ILLUMINATION declares OPERATIONS=5 (read|event) on all 14 corpus declarations and is a visible illuminance sensor, so on the HmIP legacy surface that pass triggers DeviceUtil#askValue and reaches the device on air — today, once per device per boot, wherever the ReGa fetch_all_device_data seed left it unobserved. The bundle wrote 'wire it up as written and it becomes an on-air defect'; it already is one, through a seam the bundle never opened. (INSTALL_TEST escapes: internal/store/visibility/rules.go:240 hides it, so the visibility gate skips it in that pass.)

(b) The OPERATIONS derivability claim is contradicted for INSTALL_TEST. The bundle lists 'INSTALL_TEST(2/4/6)' among the parameters OPERATIONS already marks non-readable. The corpus says 2:251, 4:437, **3:124**, 6:17 — 124 declarations carry READ. OPERATIONS therefore does not settle INSTALL_TEST, and the bundle's own conclusion that it is derivable from the descriptor is wrong on its own evidence. (ON_TIME is 2:433/3:2, not '2 on 432 of 435' — immaterial.)

One further scope correction: the bundle frames the skip list as governing 'the initial load'. Our initial VALUES load is a single ReGa fetch_all_device_data call (device_pipeline.go:1917-1920, :622), not per-parameter getValue — so even wired, the list would gate a call the initial load does not make. The paths where it would bite are the two sweeps above.

all.title: A NUMBER sysvar's float-vs-integer kind is guessed from a decimal point in its current value
all.citation: OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/sysvar/getall.tcl:43-48 — `var sv_type = "UNKNOWN"; if (sv.ValueSubType() == istAlarm) { sv_type = "ALARM"; } … if (sv.ValueSubType() == istGeneric) { sv_type = "NUMBER"; }` and :53 `WriteLine("TYPE {" # sv_type # "}")`. OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/system.fn:830-836 — the WebUI's own sysvar editor: `elseif (ist == istGeneric) { sv.ValueType( ivtFloat ); sv.ValueSubType( istGeneric ); … }`; :838-842 the only ivtInteger path is `elseif (ist == istEnum) { sv.ValueType( ivtInteger ); sv.ValueSubType( istEnum ); … }`. OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/sysvar/createfloat.tcl:21 `sv.ValueType( ivtFloat );` (SysVar.createFloat is the only JSON-RPC creator of a NUMBER sysvar). OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/system.fn:464 `boolean bNumber = ( (iVT==ivtFloat) && (iST==istGeneric) );` and :1488-1497 the NUMBER renderer `sSysVarVal = cObjTmp.Value().ToString(2);`. Witness for provenance (Tier 3, not authority): aiohomematic/client/json_rpc.py:2482 `data_type = HubValueType.FLOAT if "." in raw_value else HubValueType.INTEGER`.
all.ourValue: NUMBER → FLOAT when the scanned value string contains '.', else INTEGER.
all.firmwareValue: NUMBER is unconditionally ivtFloat + istGeneric. There is no integer NUMBER sysvar in the CCU's object model, and SysVar.getAll's `type` field is derived from ValueSubType() alone — ValueType() is never emitted, so the payload carries no int/float distinction to recover.
all.finding: Our code re-derives a distinction the CCU does not make. Two Tier-1 facts settle it independently. (1) `getall.tcl` computes `type` exclusively from `ValueSubType()`; `ValueType()` appears nowhere in the getAll/get scripts, so the reader's premise that the payload might already carry ivtFloat/ivtInteger is false — it does not, and cannot be made to without changing the script. (2) Every sysvar-creation path in the firmware pairs istGeneric with ivtFloat (system.fn:832, createfloat.tcl:21, bin/hm_autoconf:338); `ivtInteger` appears in exactly one pairing, with istEnum (LIST). A repo-wide grep for `ValueType( ivt` across OpenCCU-Base returns no ivtInteger+istGeneric anywhere. The WebUI confirms the reading operationally: it classifies a variable as NUMBER only when `(iVT==ivtFloat) && (iST==istGeneric)` (system.fn:464) and renders it with `.ToString(2)` (:1497), i.e. always with decimals. So the correct mapping is NUMBER → FLOAT, always; the INTEGER branch of inferSysvarType is unreachable in the firmware's model and every integer-looking NUMBER value that hits it is a misclassification. Consequences beyond the reader's summary: model/hub/sysvar.go:754 routes a HubValueTypeInteger sysvar through intToWire, so a write of 21.5 to a float sysvar the daemon classified INTEGER is truncated to 21 before it reaches the CCU — a wrong value written into CCU state, not merely a lost bound. The rule is a faithful port of the Python sibling's heuristic (json_rpc.py:2482), which is a witness to where our rule came from, not evidence that it is right.
all.negativeControl: Had our rule been correct, the CCU would have to distinguish the two, and I would have found either (a) `getall.tcl` emitting `sv.ValueType()` next to `ValueSubType()`, or (b) at least one creation path setting `ValueType(ivtInteger)` together with `ValueSubType(istGeneric)`. The check can produce that answer — it did produce the ivtInteger form, at system.fn:840, but paired with istEnum. Both searches returned the opposite of our rule.
all.challengeNote: Upheld on the firmware side; I re-read every citation and all four transcribe exactly. Surface checked and correct: our consumer really is SysVar.getAll (hub_wiring.go:1139 `jc.Call(ctx, "SysVar.getAll", ...)`, type+value taken at :1190), so getall.tcl is the script whose output we parse — not a different sysvar method. The firmware model has no integer NUMBER: every creation path pairs istGeneric with ivtFloat, and the WebUI's own classifier requires (ivtFloat && istGeneric) to call a variable NUMBER. TWO CORRECTIONS to the previous finding. (1) The stated consequence is wrong about our own code: intToWire (internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:826-852) guards the float branch with `v.Float >= math.MinInt32 && v.Float <= math.MaxInt32 && v.Float == math.Trunc(v.Float)`, so a write of 21.5 to a sysvar misclassified INTEGER is REJECTED with `sysvar %q: value %s is not an integer`, not truncated to 21. No wrong value reaches CCU state by this path; the operator's write silently fails instead. The string branch is the same (ParseInt("21.5") fails). (2) A defect the previous finding missed: inferSysvarType runs inside the scan loop, so the declared kind FLIPS between refreshes as the live value crosses an integral boundary — a variable reading 21.0 is INTEGER this scan and FLOAT the next, and toWire reads whichever Meta() the last scan left. BOUNDARY on severity: whether the INTEGER branch fires at all depends on how ReGa stringifies a float Value(), and that is not in Tier 1 — ReGaHss is a closed binary; only its Tcl/HTML consumers are in the tree. system.fn:1497 forcing `.ToString(2)` for display and system.fn:1491 handling `Value() == ""` both indicate the raw rendering is neither fixed-decimal nor guaranteed non-empty (an empty value has no '.', so it classifies as INTEGER), but I cannot measure the rendering from Tier 1. The mapping is contradicted; the firing rate is unverified.

all.title: The sender channel-type alias table is invented by this repo — the comment says the reference has none
all.citation: OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/linkHmIP_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER.tcl:12-51 — the CCU's own sender-type resolution: `if {[catch {set x $dev_descr_sender(TYPE)}] == 0} { … if {[catch {source [file join $env(DOCUMENT_ROOT) config/easymodes/$ACTOR/$x.tcl]}] != 0} { catch {source [file join $env(DOCUMENT_ROOT) config/easymodes/NO_PROFILE.tcl]} } }`. The only rewrites the firmware performs are explicit and named: :14-29 KEY_TRANSCEIVER on HmIP-MOD-RC8 → SWITCH_TRANSCEIVER (CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE 2) or SHUTTER_CONTACT (mode 3), read from the device's MASTER paramset; :32-45 LEVEL_COMMAND_TRANSMITTER_{CO2,HUMIDITY,TEMPERATURE} → COND_SWITCH_TRANSMITTER_{CO2,HUMIDITY,TEMPERATURE}. Profile sets are files under OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/<RECEIVER_TYPE>/<SENDER_TYPE>.tcl; MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl, MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER.tcl and PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl exist as three separate files under 12 receiver directories. Concrete divergence: ACOUSTIC_SIGNAL_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER/MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:44-45 `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_OFFDELAY_TIME_BASE) 0` / `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_OFFDELAY_TIME_FACTOR) 0` vs PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:44-45 `{0 range 0 - 7}` / `{0 range 0 - 7}`; SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER/MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:31 `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_JT_OFFDELAY) 6` vs PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:30 `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_JT_OFFDELAY) {6 5}`, and :26-27 `SHORT_CT_OFFDELAY/SHORT_CT_ON {3 0}` vs `{3 0 2}`.
all.ourValue: MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER ≡ MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER ≡ PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER for profile selection; SHUTTER_CONTACT_TRANSCEIVER ≡ SHUTTER_CONTACT.
all.firmwareValue: Three distinct sender classes with three distinct profile files per receiver, differing in the jump-table and constraint values they write. SHUTTER_CONTACT_TRANSCEIVER is not a channel type the firmware knows at all.
all.finding: The CCU keys link profiles by the verbatim sender TYPE and normalises only where it says so explicitly, per receiver, in a linkHmIP_<RECEIVER>.tcl file. It has no MOTIONDETECTOR↔PRESENCEDETECTOR alias. It ships all three names as separate profile files, and they are not interchangeable: comparing the three files across the 15 receiver directories that carry any of them, MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER and PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER differ in 10 of the 12 receivers where both exist (identical only under ALARM_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER and STATE_RESET_RECEIVER). The differences are in the values ApplyLinkProfile writes: the presence detector's profile 1 leaves SHORT_OFFDELAY_TIME_BASE/FACTOR operator-editable over 0-7 where the motion detector's pins them to a fixed 0, and under SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER the presence variant widens SHORT_JT_OFFDELAY from a fixed 6 to the acceptance set {6,5} and SHORT_CT_OFFDELAY/SHORT_CT_ON from {3,0} to {3,0,2}. Substituting one for the other therefore hands the operator a different jump table and writes it into the receiver's LINK paramset. The third alias, SHUTTER_CONTACT_TRANSCEIVER → SHUTTER_CONTACT, is unfounded but inert: the literal SHUTTER_CONTACT_TRANSCEIVER appears nowhere in OpenCCU-Base and no device in the descriptor corpus declares it, so that entry can never fire. Separately, the archive our code searches (go-openccu-data v0.1.3 data/profiles) carries PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER under 14 receivers but carries neither MOTIONDETECTOR key at all — the extraction dropped profile files the firmware ships. The alias is papering over that gap with the wrong file rather than extending the extraction.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware treated these as one sender class I would have found either a single shared file (or a symlink/`source` indirection) for all three names, or an entry rewriting one to the other in the linkHmIP_* normalisation step. That step demonstrably can express such a rewrite — it does so for KEY_TRANSCEIVER and for the three LEVEL_COMMAND_TRANSMITTER_* types — and it names neither MOTIONDETECTOR nor PRESENCEDETECTOR. The file comparison likewise can return 'identical': it does, for the MOTIONDETECTOR/MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL pair under 7 receivers and for MD/PD under 2. It returned 'different' for MD vs PD under 10.
all.challengeNote: Firmware grounding upheld; impact narrowed on two counts. WRONG SURFACE (inside our own repo): the finding names `link_profiles_adapter.go:133-165 -> PutLinkParamset` as the alias table's write path. It is not. grep shows resolveSenderType/filterProfileDocBySender have exactly one non-test caller, uischema_link.go:126. LinkProfilesAdapter.ApplyLinkProfile passes the RAW sender type to linkprofile.Store.GetProfileByID, and store.go's sender lookup is a plain map index (`profs, ok := bucket[senderChannelType]`) with no sender aliasing — only a RECEIVER alias file (_receiver_type_aliases.json). So ApplyLinkProfile never sees an aliased sender; for a MOTIONDETECTOR_* sender it returns `profile id=%d not found` and writes nothing. The alias does still reach a device write, by a different route the finding did not identify: uischema_link.go:120-146 -> hmapi.UISchemaProfile -> ProfileSelector.svelte apply() (builds a patch of fixed values + range defaults) -> ChannelPanel.svelte:778-795 applyProfilePatch (stages into the LINK working values) -> the operator's channel Save, which is a LINK putParamset. That is the path to cite. COUNT CORRECTION: MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER and PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER both exist under 11 receiver directories plus hmip/ (12 comparisons, not 12 receivers + more); byte-comparing them, 9 differ and 2 are identical (ALARM_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, STATE_RESET_RECEIVER) — not '10 of 12'. THIRD ENTRY CONFIRMED INERT: the literal SHUTTER_CONTACT_TRANSCEIVER appears nowhere in OpenCCU-Base and in no pydevccu device description; its only occurrence anywhere is our own extractor's sender list, so that alias can never fire. Archive state re-measured: PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER is a key under 14 of the 35 receiver archives; neither MOTIONDETECTOR key appears in any. The honest fix is to extend the extraction (fix the misspelled probe name, add the VIRTUAL form), not to substitute a different sender's file.

all.title: The generic '_VIRTUAL_ → _' sender-type normalisation is a convention, not a value read from the archive or the firmware
all.citation: OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/linkHmIP_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER.tcl:12-51 (and the same shape in all 28 linkHmIP_*.tcl files) — the sender key is `$dev_descr_sender(TYPE)` verbatim, sourced as `config/easymodes/$ACTOR/$x.tcl`, with only the explicit KEY_TRANSCEIVER and LEVEL_COMMAND_TRANSMITTER_* rewrites; no `_VIRTUAL_` handling anywhere. The firmware ships MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER.tcl as a file of its own under 12 receiver directories. Divergence from the non-virtual file: OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER/MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:25 `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_CT_OFF) {2 0}` and :27 `set PROFILE_1(SHORT_CT_ON) {3 0}` vs MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER.tcl:25 `{2 0 1}` and :27 `{3 0 2}`.
all.ourValue: Any *_VIRTUAL_* sender type is profile-equivalent to the same name with the _VIRTUAL_ token collapsed to _ (KEY_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER → KEY_TRANSCEIVER).
all.firmwareValue: No such normalisation exists. The virtual and non-virtual forms are separate profile files with different parameter constraints; MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER vs MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER differ under 5 of the 12 receivers that carry both.
all.finding: The firmware's sender-type resolution is a single verbatim filename lookup plus a short, explicitly enumerated rewrite list; there is no token-stripping step in any of the 28 linkHmIP_*.tcl files. The generic strip is contradicted at exactly the one sender type where it can fire. Enumerating the descriptor corpus, only two channel types containing _VIRTUAL_ are senders — MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER and STATE_RESET_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER; the other seven (SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, DIMMER_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, BLIND_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, SHUTTER_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, ACOUSTIC_SIGNAL_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, ALARM_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, WATER_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER) are receivers and never reach this lookup as a sender key. For MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER the firmware carries a dedicated file under 12 receivers, and it differs from the non-virtual file under DIMMER_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, STATE_RESET_RECEIVER, SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, WATER_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER and hmip/ — in SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER by widening the SHORT_CT_OFF and SHORT_CT_ON acceptance sets, which is a difference in what gets written to the receiver's LINK paramset. Worse, the strip is third in resolveSenderType's candidate order, behind the c004 alias: for MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER the chain yields [raw, PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER, MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER, PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER], so if an archive ever carried both the presence set wins over the motion set the firmware would have picked. The comment's own example, KEY_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER, names a channel type that appears in neither OpenCCU-Base nor the descriptor corpus.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware performed this normalisation, either no MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER.tcl would exist (the lookup would fall through to the non-virtual file), or a linkHmIP_*.tcl would carry a string-rewrite step collapsing the token. The rewrite step exists and demonstrably can express such a mapping — it does, three times over, for other names — and never mentions _VIRTUAL_. The file comparison can also return 'equivalent', and does for 7 of the 12 receivers; it returned 'different' for 5, including the constraint values that get written.
all.challengeNote: Firmware grounding upheld and independently re-measured: the sender key really is a single verbatim filename lookup plus an explicitly enumerated rewrite list, with no token-stripping step anywhere; MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER and MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER differ in exactly the 5 places the finding names (DIMMER_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, STATE_RESET_RECEIVER, SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, WATER_SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER, hmip/) out of 12 receivers carrying both — that count is exact. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The sender enumeration is wrong by one: the finding names MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER and STATE_RESET_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER as the two _VIRTUAL_ senders. Grounding DIRECTION at Tier 1 (SENDER=1, RECEIVER=2) and measuring the descriptor corpus, STATE_RESET_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER declares DIRECTION 2 — it is a receiver. Exactly ONE _VIRTUAL_ channel type in the corpus is a sender. (2) That makes the strip DEAD, not a live hazard, and the finding overstates it. For the one sender type it can see, resolveSenderType's candidate chain is [MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER, PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER (c004 alias), MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER (the strip), PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER]. The archive carries only PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER, so candidate 2 always wins and the stripped form is never the resolved key — the strip cannot change any outcome against today's archive and corpus. It is unfounded code that currently decides nothing; the wrong answer it would otherwise reach is already produced by c004's alias. The comment's own example, KEY_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER, I confirm appears in neither OpenCCU-Base nor the descriptor corpus.

all.title: The binary-sensor VALUE_LIST acceptance set is order-sensitive, and the polarity it records is never read
all.citation: Ordering semantics, BidCos (Tier 1): OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSLogicalTypeOption.cpp:48-59 — `temp=option_node.getAttribute("index"); if(temp){ index=strtoul(temp, NULL, 0); if(options.size()<=index)options.resize(index+1); options[index]=id; }else{ index=options.size(); options.push_back(id); }` and :100-107 — `(*val)["MAX"]=int(options.size()-1); XmlRpcValue& values=(*val)["VALUE_LIST"]; for(unsigned int i=0;i<options.size();i++){ values[i]=options[i]; }`. So VALUE_LIST[i] IS the ENUM ordinal i. Ordering, HmIP (Tier 1): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory#createStateWindowOpenClosed declares `String[] enumStrings = new String[]{"CLOSED", "OPEN"}` with `int[] enumValues = new int[]{0, 200}`; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.ClimateStateParameterFactory#createWindowStateParameter declares the same `{"CLOSED", "OPEN"}`; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.ProcessState declares the enum constants in the order STABLE, NOT_STABLE and exposes them via #getNames in values() order. DRY/RAIN: not present in this OpenCCU-Base rftypes subset (rf_wds declares the 3-entry DRY/WET/WATER list instead); grounded at Tier 2 only — pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HM-Sen-RD-O.json, VCU0000206:1 VALUES STATE `{"TYPE":"ENUM","OPERATIONS":5,"DEFAULT":0,"MIN":0,"MAX":1,"VALUE_LIST":["DRY","RAIN"]}`. Reversal exists elsewhere: OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes declares both ('ABSOLUTE','MINIMAL') (318×) and ('MINIMAL','ABSOLUTE') (40×) for the *_TIME_MODE parameters; the descriptor corpus adds ('OFF','ON') vs ('ON','OFF') and ('RIGHT','LEFT') vs ('LEFT','RIGHT').
all.ourValue: Exactly three ordered pairs are binary; the recorded 'true' token is OPEN / RAIN / NOT_STABLE.
all.firmwareValue: The three pairs are declared in exactly our order everywhere and never reversed; VALUE_LIST[0] is the ordinal-0 token. But the CCU has no notion of 'binary sensor', so it does not settle which two-entry ENUMs belong in the set — and at least a dozen other two-entry ENUMs are equally binary.
all.finding: Split verdict, hence 'narrowed'. (1) The order concern is real in general but does not bite these three pairs. HSSLogicalTypeOption is explicit that VALUE_LIST array position equals the ENUM ordinal — including the sparse case, where an explicit index= attribute resizes the vector and leaves empty holes (rf_dim_1l_644.xml:387-388 declares NO_ERROR index=0 and LOAD_FAILURE index=3, yielding a four-entry VALUE_LIST with two empty strings, which our len==2 test correctly skips). Enumerating every two-entry option list in OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes and every two-entry VALUE_LIST in the descriptor corpus: ('CLOSED','OPEN') 26× (STATE, WINDOW_STATE), ('STABLE','NOT_STABLE') 403× (PROCESS), ('DRY','RAIN') 1× (STATE) — and zero occurrences of any of the three reversed. The reversed order is not hypothetical for other pairs (ABSOLUTE/MINIMAL, OFF/ON and RIGHT/LEFT each appear both ways), so the positional key is a latent hazard, just not for the tokens in this table today. (2) The completeness claim is Tier-1-silent: 'means a binary condition' is a north-bound presentation concept the CCU does not model, so no firmware source can decide the acceptance set. Measurably, the set is incomplete — STICKY_SABOTAGE ('WAS_SABOTAGED','SABOTAGE'), STICKY_POWER ('WAS_POWER_FAILURE','POWER_FAILURE'), STICKY_BATTERY ('BATTERY_WAS_DEFECT','BATTERY_DEFECT'), STICKY_ERR_TTM_{OVERVOLT,UNDERVOLT} and the 597 *_STATUS parameters carrying ('NORMAL','UNKNOWN') are all read-only two-valued conditions that fall through to IntegerSensor. (The ERROR*/SENSOR_ERROR* pairs are diverted earlier by isDeviceErrorEvent.) (3) On the dead polarity value: the firmware does agree with what the table records, but not through it. generic.toBool (internal/model/generic/coerce.go:53-73) maps an int to `x != 0`, so polarity is 'ordinal 0 is false' — which HSSLogicalTypeOption and the HmIP enumStrings arrays both make the negative token, for all three pairs. The map's value is a correct-but-unread second statement of that; the boundary is that it would silently stop agreeing if a future pair put the 'true' token at index 0, and nothing would catch it.
all.negativeControl: Had the declared order been arbitrary, at least one of the three pairs would have appeared reversed somewhere in the ~150 device XMLs or the descriptor corpus. The enumeration demonstrably can return a reversal — it returned three of them, for other pairs — and returned none for CLOSED/OPEN, DRY/RAIN or STABLE/NOT_STABLE. For the completeness half no negative control exists, which is the point: the CCU has no binary-sensor concept, so the check cannot distinguish 'our set is complete' from 'our set is arbitrary'.
all.missingInput: For the acceptance set only: the firmware carries no property marking a two-entry ENUM as a binary condition rather than a two-valued enumeration. That input does not exist in any tier; the set is a north-bound policy of ours and should be documented as such rather than cited to a reference.
all.challengeNote: Split verdict upheld, with three corrections and one strengthening. STRENGTHENED: DRY/RAIN is grounded at Tier 1, not Tier 2 — the shipped device XMLs rf_rd.xml and rf_rd_le_v1_3.xml declare the ordered pair on a read+event STATE parameter. So all three pairs now have a Tier-1 ordering source. CONFIRMED: HSSLogicalTypeOption transcribes exactly, including the sparse branch; searching every device XML recursively for all six orderings of the three pairs returns ('DRY','RAIN') 2x and nothing else, and the corpus adds 26 + 403 + 1 with zero reversals — so the positional key is safe for these tokens today while demonstrably unsafe as a general convention. CORRECTION 1 (the incompleteness examples are wrong): STICKY_SABOTAGE ('WAS_SABOTAGED','SABOTAGE'), STICKY_POWER, STICKY_BATTERY and STICKY_ERR_TTM_{OVERVOLT,UNDERVOLT} all carry OPERATIONS 7 in the corpus — the write bit is set, so datapoint_resolver.go:62 routes them to resolveWritable (ENUM read+write -> NewSelect) and they never reach isBinarySensor. They are not fall-through-to-IntegerSensor cases. The surviving, measured example is ('NORMAL','UNKNOWN') on 597 *_STATUS parameters, every one read-only; ('HIGH','LOW') 166 and ('INACTIVE','ACTIVE') 34 are further read-only two-valued lists, though those read as configuration enums rather than conditions. CORRECTION 2: I could not reproduce ('LEFT','RIGHT') anywhere — the corpus has ('RIGHT','LEFT') 9x only. That half of the reversal list is unverified; ABSOLUTE/MINIMAL and OFF/ON both-ways are confirmed. CORRECTION 3 on tier: the acceptance-set half is Tier-1-silent by construction, so this rule is not fully performable from firmware — 'means a binary condition' is our presentation choice, and no CCU source can settle it. The dead-value observation holds exactly: isBinarySensor reads only the key (`if _, ok := binarySensorValueLists[key]; ok`), the map's value is read nowhere in the repo, and the real polarity comes from generic.toBool's `x != 0`, which agrees with ordinal-0-is-false for all three pairs — a second, unenforced statement of the same fact that would silently stop agreeing if a future pair put the true token at index 0.

all.title: Lock mode is decided by the target-channel key prefix '1_' with no cited source
all.site: internal/model/schedule/lock.go:70-83 (DetectLockMode); internal/central/adapter/schedules.go:908-937 (applyLockEncoding, the '1_1'/'2_1' write defaults); key construction at internal/central/adapter/week_profile_filter.go:237-267 (deriveTargetChannels)
all.citation: HmIP TARGET_CHANNELS definition (Tier 1): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.configparameter.CalendarConfigurationParameterFactory#createTargetChannelsParameter builds it as `LogicalType.INTEGER, PhysicalType.INTEGER` with a null type converter and bounds 0..0xFFFFFF — an opaque 24-bit mask with no declared bit-to-channel mapping and no lock/permission semantics; the sibling #createLevelParameter carries `new DoubleToInteger(200.0, 0.0)` with max 1.01, which is where LockActionOpen's 1.01 comes from. Channel roles (Tier 1): HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.ChannelType declares DOOR_LOCK_STATE_TRANSMITTER, DOOR_LOCK_STATE_TRANSCEIVER, DOOR_LOCK_TRANSCEIVER and PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVER as distinct channel types. Channel layouts (Tier 2): pydevccu/device_descriptions/HmIP-DLD.json — ch1 DOOR_LOCK_STATE_TRANSMITTER, ch2-9 ACCESS_RECEIVER, ch10 SWITCH_WEEK_PROFILE; HmIP-DLP.json — ch1 KEY_TRANSCEIVER, ch2 ACCELERATION_TRANSCEIVER, ch3 DOOR_STATE_TRANSCEIVER, ch4-11 PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVER, ch12 DOOR_LOCK_TRANSCEIVER, ch13 AUTO_RELOCK_TRANSCEIVER, ch14 SWITCH_WEEK_PROFILE. Slot fields (Tier 2): pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-DLD.json VCU9724704:10 MASTER — 01_WP_LEVEL {FLOAT, MIN 0.0, MAX 1.01, DEFAULT 0.0}, 01_WP_TARGET_CHANNELS {INTEGER, MIN 0, MAX 16777215}, 01_WP_DURATION_FACTOR {INTEGER, MIN 0, MAX 31, DEFAULT 31}.
all.ourValue: A slot whose target-channel key starts with '1_' is a door-lock action; anything else is a user permission. Write defaults '1_1' and '2_1'.
all.firmwareValue: Not decided by the CCU sources available here. TARGET_CHANNELS is an opaque 24-bit integer; the firmware's own discriminator between a lock actuator and a permission target is the channel TYPE (DOOR_LOCK_*_TRANSCEIVER/TRANSMITTER vs PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVER / ACCESS_RECEIVER), and on HmIP-DLP the lock actuator is device channel 12 while the permission channels are 4-11.
all.finding: Answering the right surface first: the firmware carries no 'actor_sub' key. Our '1_1' is `fmt.Sprintf("%d_%d", actorIdx+1, subIdx+1)` over the ascending-sorted list of our own custom-profile group numbers (week_profile_filter.go:246-248), so the '1_' prefix means 'the first group our registry produced', not device channel 1. No firmware source carries that value, and TARGET_CHANNELS itself is declared as a bare integer with a null converter, so the CCU sources available here decide neither the bit-to-channel mapping nor any lock/permission classification of a slot. What the firmware does decide is the discriminator it actually uses: channel TYPE. On that basis 'lowest channel is the lock' is false at the device level — HmIP-DLP puts DOOR_LOCK_TRANSCEIVER at channel 12 behind eight PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVERs at 4-11 and a KEY_TRANSCEIVER at 1 — so any reading of our rule that resolves '1_' to a channel number is wrong on the second of the only two devices in scope.
