Strike that half of the grounding.

What replaces it, and why the verdict still stands. libXmlRpc is the value library rfd and hs485d link, so boolFromXml/boolFromStream/boolFromText are the CCU's own decoders for exactly the values we decode. All three reject an empty input as a parse failure, and both emitters produce non-empty tokens, so no CCU surface encodes an unknown boolean as "". Independently, the seeding premise holds in our own repo: fetch_all_device_data.fn emits bare JSON true/false for ValueType()==2 and omits any DP without a valid Timestamp(), so a bool never reaches coerceWire as a string on that path. The "" branch is therefore dead on ingest and live only on the REST generic SetValue path, where a client posting "" gets a confirmed false written toward the device that the CCU itself would have rejected. Dropping "" leaves the DP unobserved instead of confidently off.

all.title: Alarm-taxonomy detection rests on value_list[0] being literally IDLE_OFF or IDLE, a property never read from a descriptor
all.ourValue: ENUM + len(valueList) >= 2 + valueList[0] equal-fold IDLE_OFF or IDLE + some later entry containing "ALARM" → alarm_state hint.
all.firmwareValue: SMOKE_DETECTOR_ALARM_STATUS is built as LogicalType.ENUM from the declaration order of the enum {IDLE_OFF, PRIMARY_ALARM, INTRUSION_ALARM, SECONDARY_ALARM}, with DEFAULT = MIN = element[0] and MAX = element[last]. It is the only readable/eventing ENUM in the firmware whose value list contains an *ALARM* member, and its element 0 is IDLE_OFF. The only other firmware enum starting with IDLE* is CodeState {IDLE, KNOWN_CODE_ID_RECEIVED, …}, which carries no ALARM member.
all.citation: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.SmokeDetectorAlarmStatus; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory#createSmokeDetectorAlarmStatusParameter, #createSmokeDetectorEventParameter, #createSmokeDetectorCommandParameter, #createAcousticAlarmSelectionParameter, #createOpticalAlarmSelectionParameter; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.SmokeDetectorEvent, .SmokeDetectorCommand, .CodeState; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/stringtable_de.txt:1880-1883; Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/** (798 descriptor files) VALUE_LIST + OPERATIONS survey; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/{rftypes,hs485types}/*.xml (zero occurrences of "alarm", case-insensitive)
all.finding:
The premise is a firmware fact, not a convention, and I read it from the source rather than from the ordering of an extracted list: the VALUE_LIST is materialised from the Java enum's declaration order (getNames()), and that order is IDLE_OFF, PRIMARY_ALARM, INTRUSION_ALARM, SECONDARY_ALARM. Index 0 is IDLE_OFF.

I then enumerated every ENUM in the firmware that carries an *ALARM* member and checked its element 0 and its operations, so the check is a positive inventory rather than a spot confirmation:
  · SMOKE_DETECTOR_ALARM_STATUS — [IDLE_OFF, PRIMARY_ALARM, INTRUSION_ALARM, SECONDARY_ALARM], READ|EVENT → our rule fires. Correct.
  · SMOKE_DETECTOR_EVENT — [ALARM_OFF, PRIMARY_ALARM, …], WRITE only → element 0 is ALARM_OFF, rule does not fire. Correct (it is a command surface, not a readout).
  · SMOKE_DETECTOR_COMMAND — [RESERVED_ALARM_OFF, INTRUSION_ALARM_OFF, …], WRITE only → does not fire. Correct.
  · ACOUSTIC_ALARM_SELECTION / OPTICAL_ALARM_SELECTION — WRITE only, and their members (SignalAcoustic / SignalOptical) contain no "ALARM" token → do not fire. Correct.
The Tier-2 descriptor corpus adds two more real value lists that the firmware Java does not name and that both fall outside the rule correctly: ARMSTATE [DISARMED, EXTSENS_ARMED, ALLSENS_ARMED, ALARM_BLOCKED] (OPERATIONS 7) and ACOUSTIC_ALARM_TRIGGER [NO_ACOUSTIC_ALARM, TRIGGER_EVENT_1, …] (OPERATIONS 3). Neither starts with IDLE*, neither is an alarm-state readout.

Two boundaries the reader should know, neither of which unseats the rule:
  · The comment above enumShapeHint is wrong about its own scope. Water-leak detection is not an ENUM: WATER_DETECTION_TRANSMITTER.ALARMSTATE is built as a read/event BOOLEAN bit-0 parameter, so the rule never touches it. And I found no HmIP-SAM ENUM with an ALARM member — SAM's CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE is [OFF, ANY_MOTION, FLAT_DECT]. The honest scope of this rule is: HmIP smoke detectors (SMOKE_DETECTOR channel), and nothing else in the current inventory.
  · One false negative exists at the edge: ERROR_ALARM_TEST [NO_ERROR, ALARM_TEST_FAILED] (OPERATIONS 5, i.e. READ|EVENT) is an ALARM-bearing readable ENUM whose idle member is spelled NO_ERROR. It gets no alarm hint. That is a gap in coverage, not a wrong classification — and it is the shape the bundle's damage note predicted, so it is worth deciding deliberately rather than leaving implicit.

The BidCos half is settled negatively: the shipped device-type XMLs contain no occurrence of "alarm" at all, so no BidCos ENUM can reach this rule.
all.negativeControl: Had element 0 not been the idle member, SmokeDetectorAlarmStatus would have declared IDLE_OFF somewhere other than first, or the factory would have passed an explicit ordinal array (as createSmokeDetectorEventParameter does with SmokeDetectorEvent.getValues() = {0,1,2,3,4,5,7,8,…}) that reorders or sparsifies the list relative to the names. It passes only enumStrings, and DEFAULT/MIN are taken as enumStrings[0] — so a differently-ordered list would have produced a different DEFAULT and a visibly different VALUE_LIST in the Tier-2 corpus. The corpus shows IDLE_OFF first in every SMOKE_DETECTOR_ALARM_STATUS instance.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD as confirmed at Tier 1. The attack this bundle is most exposed to is the ordering convention, so I chased the value-list path end to end rather than spot-checking the enum: SmokeDetectorAlarmStatus declares IDLE_OFF first; getNames() copies values() by index; createSmokeDetectorAlarmStatusParameter passes that array straight into StringEnumToInteger and uses enumStrings[0] as both DEFAULT and MIN; StringEnumToInteger keeps the reference and getEnumStrings() returns it with no sort; DeviceUtil hands that array to ParameterDescription#setValueList, which puts it verbatim under "VALUE_LIST". No step on that path reorders anything, so VALUE_LIST[0] == "IDLE_OFF" is READ from the source, not assumed. The FeatureMap-style failure does not apply here.

I also rebuilt the inventory independently instead of trusting the bundle's. Across all of HMIPServer only three enums carry an *ALARM* member that can become a parameter value list — SmokeDetectorAlarmStatus (READ|EVENT), SmokeDetectorEvent (WRITE only, element 0 = ALARM_OFF), SmokeDetectorCommand (WRITE only, element 0 = RESERVED_ALARM_OFF). ChannelType, LinkType and DirectExecutionActionType also contain ALARM tokens but are not parameter value lists (DirectExecutionActionType is an internal frame action type). ACOUSTIC/OPTICAL_ALARM_SELECTION are WRITE-only and their members carry no "ALARM" token. So the rule fires on exactly one parameter and correctly abstains on the rest.

Tier-2 census over 798 descriptor files reproduces the bundle exactly: the only ALARM-bearing ENUM VALUE_LISTs are SMOKE_DETECTOR_ALARM_STATUS (ops 5, HmIP-SWSD/-2), SMOKE_DETECTOR_COMMAND (ops 2), ERROR_ALARM_TEST [NO_ERROR, ALARM_TEST_FAILED] (ops 5, HM-Sec-SD-2/-Generic), ARMSTATE [DISARMED, EXTSENS_ARMED, ALLSENS_ARMED, ALARM_BLOCKED] (ops 7, HM-Sec-Sir-WM) and ACOUSTIC_ALARM_TRIGGER (ops 3, HmIP-SWD). Only the first starts with IDLE_OFF. A separate sweep for IDLE-first lists found exactly three: the two CodeState variants (HmIP-WKP, HmIP-FWI), neither with an ALARM member, and SMOKE_DETECTOR_ALARM_STATUS. Zero false positives available in the fleet.

Boundaries reproduced and worth keeping: the comment above enumShapeHint is wrong about its own scope. HmIP-SWD's ALARMSTATE is TYPE BOOL (ops 5, DEFAULT false), not an ENUM, so water-leak detection never reaches the rule; HmIP-SAM carries no ALARM-bearing ENUM at all (its CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE is OFF/ANY_MOTION/FLAT_DECT). Honest scope: HmIP smoke detectors. The ERROR_ALARM_TEST false negative is real (idle member spelled NO_ERROR) and is a coverage gap, not a misclassification. BidCos is settled negatively: zero case-insensitive "alarm" occurrences in the shipped device-type XMLs.

all.title: Service-message AlType ordinals 0..5 are mapped to operator-visible labels with no cited source
all.ourValue: 0=generic, 1=sticky, 2=config_pending, 3=alarm, 4=update_pending, 5=communication.
all.missingInput: The numeric values of ReGa's at* alarm-type constants. They are defined inside the ReGaHss interpreter, which ships only as a binary; no source in the OpenCCU-Base tree declares them.
all.citation: Searched and found silent: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/system.fn:819 (`sv.AlType(atSystem);` — the only AlType *write* in the whole tree, and it uses the symbol, never a number); ../OpenCCU-Base/bin/hm_autoconf:222 (same symbol); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/pages/tabs/statusviews/serviceMessages.htm (the operator-facing service-message list — renders AlState, AlOccurrenceTime, LastTriggerID, HssType; never AlType); ../OpenCCU-Base/src/ contains no ReGaHss source (src/tclrega/tclrega.cpp is only the Tcl binding). A repo-wide grep for atGeneric/atSticky/atConfigPending/atAlarm/atUpdatePending/atCommunication over ../OpenCCU-Base and ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/patches returns nothing. Witness (Tier 3, not authority): ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/const.py:1711-1719 `class ServiceMessageType(IntEnum): """Enum for CCU service message types (AlType).""" GENERIC = 0 / STICKY = 1 / CONFIG_PENDING = 2 / ALARM = 3 / UPDATE_PENDING = 4 / COMMUNICATION = 5`
all.finding:
Tier 1 does not decide this and cannot be made to. ReGa's object model exposes AlType() on an OT_ALARMDP, but the at* constant table lives in the closed ReGaHss interpreter; the whole shipped source tree names exactly one of them (atSystem) and never as a number. The CCU's own service-message page does not branch on AlType at all — it classifies by the trigger datapoint's HSSID (e.g. the STICKY_UNREACH special case at www/rega/esp/system.fn:366) — so even the operator-facing behaviour gives no ordinal→meaning mapping to read off.

What our rule actually rests on: a verbatim port of aiohomematic's ServiceMessageType IntEnum, i.e. a single Tier-3 witness. Our six values and their order are byte-for-byte that enum. There is no second independent reading — ccu-jack does not model AlType, and the HmIP side's ServiceMessage class is a different surface (HmIP legacy service messages, not ReGa alarm objects) and so cannot corroborate it.

Two consequences worth stating plainly. First, the label reaches the REST surface and the SPA badge as the service message's *type*, so a wrong ordinal is directly operator-visible — but it cannot be settled by reading; it can only be settled by measurement against a live CCU that has service messages of several classes standing, comparing the raw AlType integer against what the CCU's own WebUI shows for the same alarm. Second, our String() has no default arm for an unmapped ordinal beyond 5 — worth checking, since the interpreter may define more at* constants than the six the port knows about, and nothing in the code or the tests would show it.
all.negativeControl: Had the mapping been readable, a grep for the at* symbols would have hit a constant table (as it does for the ReGa value-type symbols ivt*/ist*, which are also symbol-only in the tree — confirming the grep itself is sound and simply that ReGa's constant tables are never in source). Had the WebUI classified by AlType, serviceMessages.htm would have carried a switch on it; it carries a switch on HssType/HSSID instead. Both checks would have produced a visibly different result if the value were groundable, so the silence is a measurement, not a failure to look.

all.title: CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE gate: the mode labels and the parameter/mode pairing are bare literals
all.ourValue: configurableChannelTypes = {KEY_TRANSCEIVER, MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER}. STATE ← {BINARY_BEHAVIOR}; PRESS_LONG / PRESS_LONG_RELEASE / PRESS_LONG_START / PRESS_SHORT ← {KEY_BEHAVIOR, SWITCH_BEHAVIOR}. Any observed mode outside the listed set forces usage=Ignored and the event source to not-allowed.
all.firmwareValue: There is no single VALUE_LIST for CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE — the firmware defines one per device-family variant of the parameter. The input-channel variants are: {INACTIVE, KEY_BEHAVIOR, SWITCH_BEHAVIOR, BINARY_BEHAVIOR} values {0,1,2,3}; {INACTIVE, KEY_BEHAVIOR, SWITCH_BEHAVIOR, BINARY_BEHAVIOR, LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR, CONDITIONAL_BEHAVIOR} values {0,1,2,3,4,7}; {INACTIVE, KEY_BEHAVIOR, SWITCH_BEHAVIOR} values {0,1,2}; {INACTIVE, KEY_BEHAVIOR} values {0,1}; {INACTIVE, LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR} values {0,4}. (Non-input families use entirely different member sets: OFF/ON/ON_LED, NORMAL_MODE/SILENT_MODE, SHUTTER/BLIND, OFF/ANY_MOTION/FLAT_DECT, and so on.) Channel types: KEY_TRANSCEIVER = 10, MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER = 66.
all.citation: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.configparameter.GeneralConfigurationParameterFactory (the CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE enumeration variants and their value arrays); HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.ChannelType (KEY_TRANSCEIVER, MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER); HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.server.core.persistence.AbstractPersistency#updateAndNotifyChannelOperationMode; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/etc/hmipChannelConfigDialogs.tcl:975 (proc getMultiModeInputTransmitter), :1008-1035 (mode option box: options(3) BINARY_BEHAVIOR, options(4) LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR, options(5) CONDITIONAL_BEHAVIOR, each added only when the channel's own VALUE_LIST contains the member), :1162-1207 (showHideKeyParams: cases 1 and 4 show the key rows, case 3 shows the binary rows, cases 0 and 5 hide both, case 2 shows neither), :669-693 (proc getKeyTransceiver — offers only INACTIVE/active); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/hmip/MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER.tcl:18 (dispatch by channel type); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/stringtable_de.txt:1085-1089; Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/** CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE VALUE_LIST census (68× the four-mode list, 2× the three-mode list, no LEVEL_KEY/CONDITIONAL instance); witness ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/const.py:1789-1797 + aiohomematic/model/data_point.py:963-972
all.finding:
Two halves, and they land differently.

CHANNEL TYPES AND MODE SPELLINGS — confirmed. KEY_TRANSCEIVER and MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER are real firmware channel types (ordinals 10 and 66), and BINARY_BEHAVIOR / KEY_BEHAVIOR / SWITCH_BEHAVIOR are the firmware's own spellings, appearing both in the parameter factory's value arrays and in the CCU's operator string table (KEY_TRANSCEIVER|CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE=KEY_BEHAVIOR etc.).

THE ACCEPTANCE SET — narrowed, and this is the live defect. Our table is complete for the four-mode variant {INACTIVE, KEY_BEHAVIOR, SWITCH_BEHAVIOR, BINARY_BEHAVIOR}, which is what the current fleet uses (68 of 90 CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE instances in the descriptor corpus; none observed with the wider list). One step wider the firmware defines two further input modes on the same channel types — LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR (raw value 4) and CONDITIONAL_BEHAVIOR (raw value 7) — and the CCU's own MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER configuration dialog offers both to the operator whenever the channel's VALUE_LIST carries them. A channel set to either reports a mode string our map does not list, and ApplyChannelOperationModeGating then force-marks STATE and all four PRESS_* parameters Ignored and their event sources not-allowed. That is the "looks like a dead device, not a rule bug" failure, and the boundary runs exactly at those two members. Note also that our gate is two-sided while the reference witness it was ported from returns None (no gating) when it cannot decide — so the blast radius here is ours, not inherited.

THE PARAMETER↔MODE MAPPING — not carried by any firmware source I could reach, and I am not going to substitute a convention for it. The HmIP server exposes the full VALUES set for these channel types regardless of mode; CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE is itself both a config and a state parameter and is merely notified on change (updateAndNotifyChannelOperationMode), never used to narrow a paramset. The WebUI gates only MASTER *configuration rows*, not VALUES: showHideKeyParams shows the key-timing rows (DBL_PRESS_TIME / LONG_PRESS_TIME) for modes 1 and 4, the binary rows (EVENT_DELAY_*) for mode 3, and nothing for modes 0, 2 and 5. Read for what it is worth — it is a different surface from ours — that corroborates STATE↔BINARY_BEHAVIOR and press↔KEY_BEHAVIOR, groups LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR with KEY_BEHAVIOR (a second, independent reason to add mode 4 to the press set), and is silent on SWITCH_BEHAVIOR, where the firmware shows neither group. So our SWITCH_BEHAVIOR→PRESS_* pairing has no firmware witness in either direction; it stays unverified rather than confirmed.
all.negativeControl: Had the mode list been a single fixed enum, GeneralConfigurationParameterFactory would have registered CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE once; it registers it more than twenty times under distinct family qualifiers with different string arrays and, in several cases, sparse value arrays ({0,1,3}, {0,1,3,6}, {0,1,2,3,4,7}) — so a check that assumed one list, or that derived a mode's raw value from its index, would have been wrong and the sparse arrays are what shows it. Had LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR/CONDITIONAL_BEHAVIOR been confined to channel types outside our gate, the dialog offering them would have sat in a proc other than getMultiModeInputTransmitter; it sits in that one, dispatched from the file named for the channel type. And had the firmware gated VALUES by mode, updateAndNotifyChannelOperationMode would have rebuilt the channel's parameter set rather than only publishing a status notification.
all.challengeNote:
UPHELD as narrowed at Tier 1, with one supporting claim demoted and one boundary added.

Verified exactly as quoted: the five input-mode arrays and their raw values verbatim; ChannelType ordinals 10 and 66; getMultiModeInputTransmitter at :975 with the mode option box at :1008-1035 adding options(3)/(4)/(5) only when the channel's own VALUE_LIST carries BINARY_/LEVEL_KEY_/CONDITIONAL_BEHAVIOR; showHideKeyParams at :1162-1207 with cases 0 and 5 hiding both row groups, 1 and 4 showing the key rows, 3 showing the binary rows and 2 showing neither; getKeyTransceiver at :669-693 offering only INACTIVE/active; the MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER.tcl:18 dispatch; the stringtable spellings.

I add independent Tier-1 corroboration the bundle did not have: both extra modes ship with operator translations in the CCU's own language files — stringTableKeyTransceiverChannelOperationModeLevelKeyBehavior = "Level" and ...ConditionalBehavior = "Bedingung"/"Condition", de and en, line 1418-1419. The CCU's UI is fully built out to present modes 4 and 7 to an operator, which makes the gap a live one rather than dead firmware code. And our channel.go resolves an observed enum index through VALUE_LIST to the label, so such a channel reaches the gate as the string "LEVEL_KEY_BEHAVIOR" and is forced Ignored across STATE and all four PRESS_* parameters plus their event sources.

I also resolved the Tier-2 census to channel types, which the bundle left open: the 68 four-mode instances are 60x MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER + 8x KEY_TRANSCEIVER, and the 2 three-mode instances are MULTI_MODE_INPUT_TRANSMITTER. So configurableChannelTypes matches the observed fleet exactly, and note that KEY_TRANSCEIVER channels DO declare BINARY_BEHAVIOR in the corpus even though the CCU's KEY_TRANSCEIVER editor offers only active/inactive — the descriptor and the editor disagree, and our code should follow the descriptor. Zero LEVEL_KEY/CONDITIONAL instances anywhere in the corpus, so the defect is firmware-possible but not yet witnessed on a device.

DEMOTED — the bundle's closing claim is false. "The reference witness returns None (no gating) when it cannot decide — so the blast radius here is ours, not inherited" does not survive reading it: aiohomematic/model/data_point.py:963-972 returns None only for a non-configurable channel type, a non-gated parameter, or an unobserved mode; for a listed parameter on a configurable channel with an unlisted mode it returns `cop in KEY_CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE_VISIBILITY[...]`, i.e. False. Identical two-sided behaviour. The blast radius is inherited, not ours.

ADDED BOUNDARY, reported as a gap and not as a finding. The firmware registers the same four-mode array under the qualifiers "generic_input", "generic_input_binary" and "generic_input_switch", and ChannelType declares GENERIC_INPUT_TRANSMITER(33); getChannelType emits ChannelType.name() and legacy-parameter-definition.config carries no GENERIC_INPUT remap, so such a channel would surface as TYPE "GENERIC_INPUT_TRANSMITER" and fall outside configurableChannelTypes entirely. I could not confirm that those qualifiers bind to that channel type — the binding is in resources I cannot read — and no device in the corpus declares it. I am naming it rather than assuming the obvious mapping.

The parameter↔mode half remains not grounded, exactly as the bundle said, and I agree with the reasoning: the WebUI evidence governs MASTER config rows, a different paramset from the VALUES entries we gate, so STATE↔BINARY and press↔KEY are corroborated only by analogy and SWITCH_BEHAVIOR→PRESS_* has no witness in either direction (mode 2 shows neither row group). That half is not-performable on its own; the id stays at narrowed because the mode-set half is settled.

all.title: LOWBAT is accepted only on channel 0, fleet-wide, from a bare literal
all.site: internal/store/visibility/rules.go:413-417 (map), internal/store/visibility/registry.go:242 (IsAcceptedOnlyOnChannel), internal/store/visibility/decider.go:271 (applied inside computeIgnoredValues, which feeds Registry.IsAllowedForChannel at registry.go:137 and therefore gates data-point creation)
all.ourValue: acceptParameterOnlyOnChannel = {"LOWBAT": 0} — a LOWBAT on any channel != 0 is ignored, for every model on every interface
all.firmwareValue: The firmware declares LOWBAT on non-zero channels on 18 BidCos models, and the CCU's own control pages read the non-zero-channel copy by CONTROL name
all.citation: Tier 1, device XMLs the firmware ships: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_sc.xml:175 declares `<parameter id="LOWBAT" operations="read,event" control="NONE">` inside the SHUTTER_CONTACT channel (`<channel index="1" type="SHUTTER_CONTACT">`), i.e. HM-Sec-SC's channel 1, not only the MAINTENANCE channel 0. The same shape appears in rf_rhs.xml (ROTARY_HANDLE_SENSOR, index 1), rf_sci_3.xml, rf_sec_sco.xml, rf_sec_sd_2.xml (SMOKE_DETECTOR, index 1), rf_tis.xml (TILT_SENSOR, index 1), rf_wds_v1_0.xml / rf_wds_v1_1.xml (WATERDETECTIONSENSOR, index 1), rf_wds30_ot2.xml (WEATHER, index 1 count 4 and index 5), rf_em_8.xml (KEY, index 1). Tier 1, the CCU's own operator surface: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/rega/www/esp/controls/alarmsirene.fn:5 `object oLowBat = cObj.DPByControl("DEVICE.LOWBAT");` and ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/rega/www/esp/controls/digitalstate.fn:5 `object oLowBat = cObj.DPByControl("BATTERIE.LOWBAT");` — `cObj` is the channel being rendered. Tier 2, the descriptor: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/*.json carries 38 LOWBAT declarations on channels 1..5 across 18 models; HM-Sec-Sir-WM VCU0000261:4 declares LOWBAT with CONTROL "DEVICE.LOWBAT", FLAGS 1, OPERATIONS 5, TYPE BOOL, and HM-MOD-EM-8Bit VCU0000127:3 with CONTROL "BATTERIE.LOWBAT" — exactly the two CONTROL strings the two WebUI fragments look up. On every such device the channel-0 copy carries FLAGS 9 (service) and no CONTROL. Tier 3 witness for where our rule came from: ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/store/visibility/rules.py:308-311 `ACCEPT_PARAMETER_ONLY_ON_CHANNEL = {Parameter.LOWBAT: 0}` under the comment "Some devices have parameters on multiple channels, but we want to use it only from a certain channel" — a de-duplication preference, never a device fact.
all.finding: The rule as written is contradicted by the firmware. LOWBAT is not a channel-0-only parameter: 18 BidCos models declare it additionally on channels 1..5, with read+event operations and (unlike the channel-0 copy) a visible, non-service flag set. For two of them the CCU's own control pages bind the non-zero-channel copy by CONTROL name — the siren arming control reads DEVICE.LOWBAT off HM-Sec-Sir-WM channel 4, the digital-state control reads BATTERIE.LOWBAT off HM-MOD-EM-8Bit channel 3 — so the firmware's operator surface treats the off-channel copy as the battery display for that channel, while the channel-0 copy is the service-message parameter (FLAGS 9). Our rule suppresses exactly the datapoints the CCU renders. What the rule gets right is narrower than what its map says: across the whole 399-device descriptor corpus there is no device that declares LOWBAT off channel 0 without also declaring it on channel 0, so the feared total loss of a battery warning does not occur today; the damage is the loss of the per-channel copy the CCU itself uses, and a latent trap for any future device that declares LOWBAT only off channel 0. Follow Tier 1 here: the descriptor and the firmware agree, and both say the restriction is a preference, not a fact. If the intent is de-duplication, the honest form is to keep the channel-0 copy as the device-level battery datapoint and stop asserting that the others do not exist; the map comment currently states a device property that the source does not carry. Two secondary claims at the site are also refuted: the decider comment at decider.go:266-267 justifies the branch with "the LOWBAT parameter surfaces on every actor channel (HmIP-PSM, HmIP-BSM, …)", but HmIP-PSM and HmIP-BSM declare no battery parameter at all in the descriptor (no key containing BAT on any of their channels) — HmIP devices use LOW_BAT, a different name this map never matches. The rule has no HmIP effect whatsoever; its entire reach is BidCos.
all.negativeControl: Had our rule been right, the LOWBAT parse over the 130 rftypes + 15 hs485types device XMLs would have returned channel index 0 for every occurrence, the descriptor scan would have shown LOWBAT only at ':0', and no WebUI control fragment would resolve a LOWBAT through a channel-scoped CONTROL string. All three produced the opposite: 38 off-channel-0 declarations, ten device XMLs with a non-MAINTENANCE LOWBAT channel, and two control fragments binding DEVICE.LOWBAT / BATTERIE.LOWBAT. The same scans returned a clean channel-0-only answer for UNREACH on all but one model, which shows the scan can produce the confirming result.
all.challengeNote: The grounding stands, and I upheld it from Tier 1 rather than from the delivered citation — which is defective in the load-bearing place. Confirmed independently: LOWBAT is declared off channel 0 in the firmware's own device XMLs, in VALUES, with read+event, and on HM-Sec-Sir-WM channel 4 and HM-MOD-EM-8Bit channel 3 with the exact CONTROL strings the two WebUI fragments look up. I also ran the surface check the previous agent did not: is DPByControl channel-scoped or device-scoped? It is channel-scoped, and the proof is inside the same device — alarmsirene.fn resolves three controls (ARMING.ARMSTATE, DEVICE.SABOTAGE, DEVICE.LOWBAT) and all three exist only on VCU0000261:4, while channel 0's own ERROR_SABOTAGE carries CONTROL "NONE" and its LOWBAT carries no CONTROL at all. A device-scoped lookup would have made the channel-4 copies redundant; they are not. Citation defects to correct before this is quoted onward: (1) the delivered Tier-1 list cites rf_em_8.xml for the BATTERIE.LOWBAT chain, but rf_em_8.xml:296's channel-1 LOWBAT carries control="CHANNEL_NOT_ACTIVE" — the BATTERIE.LOWBAT declaration is rf_em_8_bit.xml:323, a different file and a different channel type; (2) no Tier-1 file was cited for HM-Sec-Sir-WM at all, so the strongest half of the claim arrived on Tier 2 when Tier 1 carries it (rf_sec_sir_wm.xml:592); (3) "18 BidCos models" is 19 in the descriptor corpus (the 38-declaration count is right); (4) "the channel-0 copy carries FLAGS 9 and no CONTROL" holds for 17 of 19 — HM-WDS30-OT2-SM and -SM-2 carry FLAGS 9 with CONTROL "NONE", semantically the same but not "no CONTROL". One characterisation is also wrong and matters for whoever fixes this: the finding says "the map comment currently states a device property that the source does not carry", but rules.go:412-414 states a policy ("the single channel number on which it should be accepted"). The comment asserting a false device property is decider.go:266-267 — "Without this branch the LOWBAT parameter surfaces on every actor channel (HmIP-PSM, HmIP-BSM, …)". That is refuted fleet-wide at Tier 2: HmIP-PSM, HmIP-BSM and HmIP-PS declare no parameter containing "BAT" on any channel, and across all 399 descriptor models the sets {declares LOWBAT} (194) and {declares LOW_BAT} (68) are disjoint with zero HmIP models in the first. The rule's entire reach is BidCos. Scope of the contradiction: 19 models, 38 datapoints, all BidCos-RF; every one of them also declares LOWBAT on channel 0, so no device loses a battery signal outright. The site claim is sound — paramsets.go:561 calls IsAllowedForChannel on the data-point creation path, so the suppression is real, not cosmetic.

all.title: The connection-probe cadence is an uncited 'upstream value' and its own neighbouring comment says a different number
all.site: internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:56-62 (const connectionCheckerInterval = 15 * time.Second) and ccu_wiring.go:1036 (comment claiming 30 s), consumed by the single ticker at ccu_wiring.go:1054
all.ourValue: 15 s probe cadence, justified as "the established upstream value"; the comment 20 lines above the ticker says 30 s
all.firmwareValue: The CCU applies no time-based staleness to a registered logic-layer client at all: eviction is failure-count-based (10 consecutive failed event deliveries), and only advances when the CCU has an event to push
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:29 `m_pClient->setTimeout(10000);` (per-client socket timeout, 10 000 ms); :70-72 one immediate retry of the `system.multicall` event batch after a transport failure; :77-80 `m_clientSendFailureCount++; if(m_clientSendFailureCount >= 10) { m_clientUnreachable = true; }` with the source's own comment `//10 chosen by dice`; :91 the counter resets to 0 on the first non-fault delivery; :110-113 `isClientUnreachable()`. The eviction itself: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.cpp:110-129 removes the handler only inside the event-push loop, and HSSManager.cpp:39 `removeUnreachableClients = true;` with the config override at HSSManager.cpp:481-484 ("Remove Unreachable Clients"). This is the code path shared by rfd and hs485d — their only outbound callbacks are newDevices / replaceDevice / deleteDevices / readdedDevice / updateDevice (RFManager.cpp:786,793,805,817,1177; HS485Manager.cpp:163,486,494,541,549,561,575) plus event / system.multicall (HSSManager.cpp:368,398). Liveness on our side: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:1198-1206 documents `ping` as "Ping Pong Feature. Calling this method generates a 'pong' event" — a client-initiated method with no interval attached. HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler#ping likewise only sends a pong; no periodic-liveness expectation is declared. Tier 3 witness for the number's provenance, which the comment omits: ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/const.py:195 `connection_checker_interval: int = 1 if _TEST_SPEEDUP else 15`, scheduled at ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/central/scheduler.py:181.
all.finding: The firmware names no cadence, so the value cannot be confirmed or contradicted — but the premise behind the question is wrong, and that is the useful result. There is no window inside which a registered client must show liveness: rfd/hs485d never time out a registration. A handler is dropped only after ten consecutive failed pushes of an event batch (each attempt retried once, each with a 10 s socket timeout), and the counter is only touched while the CCU actually has events to deliver — on a quiet interface a registration survives indefinitely, and one successful delivery resets it. So the constant is free to be chosen on our own grounds (breaker recovery latency vs. RPC load), not against a CCU deadline; the worst-case cost of a probe failing is that our own ping counts toward nothing on the CCU side, because `ping` is a method we call, not a callback the CCU pushes. Our rule therefore rests on the Python reference alone, and that is now citable: aiohomematic const.py:195 sets 15 s. Two things at the site are wrong independently of the firmware. First, the prose: one constant, one ticker (ccu_wiring.go:62 → :1054 → logged at :1129), so the "pings the CCU every 30 s" comment at :1036 is simply false — there is no 30 s probe anywhere in internal/central/adapter (the 30 s constants there are reconnect readiness, channel-flag and master-value eviction, and system-update progress). Second, "the established upstream value" cites nothing; the file:line above is the missing citation.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU applied a time-based keepalive, the grep for the registration/eviction path would have produced a timer or a deadline compared against a last-seen timestamp in HSSManager / HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher, and rfd's `init` handling would have carried an expiry. It produced a pure failure counter with an explicitly arbitrary threshold instead. The check does discriminate: the same reading surfaced a real time value where one exists — the 10 000 ms per-client socket timeout at HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:29. For the 30 s prose the control is direct: had a second 30 s probe existed, the grep for connectionCheckerInterval and for `30 * time.Second` under internal/central/adapter would have shown a second ticker; it showed one ticker and four unrelated constants.

all.title: "Channel 0 is the device-meta channel, suffix always :0" gates the whole bootstrap seed and is asserted, not read
all.site: internal/central/adapter/relevant_init.go:34-36 (ch0Addr := d.Address + ":0") and internal/central/adapter/unobserved_sweep.go:101 (ch0 := d.Channel(d.Address + ":0"), the deliberately visibility-ungated pass)
all.ourValue: The maintenance/meta channel carrying UNREACH, STICKY_UNREACH and CONFIG_PENDING is always index 0, on every interface; both boot paths address only <device>:0
all.firmwareValue: MAINTENANCE is index 0 wherever it exists (130/130 rftypes, 14/14 hs485types with channels, 399/399 descriptor devices, and index 0 by construction for HmIP virtual devices) — but "index 0 carries the init parameters" is not the same statement, and it fails at three edges
all.citation: Tier 1, RF: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/*.xml — all 130 declare `<channel index="0" type="MAINTENANCE" count="1">`, and UNREACH (126 files) / CONFIG_PENDING (126) / STICKY_UNREACH (125) appear on that channel and on no other. Tier 1, wired: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/hs485types/*.xml — 14 of the 15 device XMLs declare MAINTENANCE at index 0 with the same three parameters (13 files); the exception is ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/hs485types/hmw_generic.xml, type id `HMW-Generic`, described in its own docu as the type shown for an unknown BidCos-Wired device, which declares a MASTER paramset and no channels at all — hence no channel 0. Tier 1, HmIP virtual devices: HMIPServer de.eq3.ccu.virtualdevice.service.utils.VirtualDeviceUtils declares MAINTENANCE_CHANNEL_INDEX = 0 and #initVirtualDevice builds that channel at index 0 with type "VIP-MAINTENANCE" and PARAMSETS = {MASTER} only, its paramset description generated by #generateMaintenanceChannelParamsetDescription as a single empty MASTER struct — no VALUES paramset, therefore no UNREACH / CONFIG_PENDING there. Parameter names on the HmIP side: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.StateParameterFactory#getStateParameterList registers "CONFIG_PENDING" and "UNREACH" (and "LOW_BAT", not STICKY_UNREACH). Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/device_descriptions/*.json — 399/399 devices have a MAINTENANCE channel and it is INDEX 0 in every one; ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/*.json — UNREACH and CONFIG_PENDING on channel 0 in 393 of 399, STICKY_UNREACH in 268 (HmIP does not declare it, which our nil-skip already tolerates).
all.finding: The index-0 half of the claim holds fleet-wide at Tier 1 and Tier 2 — including for HmIP virtual devices, where the CCU sets the index in a named constant. Our parameter spelling also matches the firmware exactly (STICKY_UNREACH, one word; the bundle's prose STICKY_UN_REACH is a typo, pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:168 is right). The boundary runs one step wider, at "channel 0 is where the init parameters live", in three places. (1) UNREACH is not exclusive to channel 0: HmIP-DRG-DALI declares UNREACH on channels 1 through 32 in addition to channel 0 — on a DALI gateway that per-channel UNREACH is the reachability of each ballast, and neither the seed nor the sweep's ungated first pass ever loads it, so those 32 datapoints stay unobserved until a push arrives. Device-level availability is unaffected, since channel 0 also carries UNREACH there. (2) A device can have a channel 0 with no VALUES paramset: every HmIP virtual/group device's maintenance channel is MASTER-only by construction, so the seed correctly finds nothing; the comment's "where UNREACH / CONFIG_PENDING live" is not true of them. Six further descriptor devices — the CCU's own pseudo-devices HmIP-CCU3, HmIP-RFUSB, RPI-RF-MOD, HM-RCV-50, HMW-RCV-50, HmIP-RCV-50 — have a channel 0 whose VALUES paramset carries no UNREACH at all. (3) A device can have no channel 0: HMW-Generic, the firmware's fallback type for an unrecognised BidCos-Wired device, declares no channels, so `d.Channel(d.Address+":0")` returns nil and such a device never gets availability tracking. All three degrade quietly through the existing nil-skips rather than failing, so the code is safe; the comment is what overstates. One input this could not settle: CUxD is not present in ../OpenCCU-Base at all (no source, no device XMLs), so the channel layout of CUxD devices is outside every Tier-1 and Tier-2 source available here and remains ungrounded.
all.negativeControl: Had the index been model-dependent, the parse over all 145 firmware device XMLs would have printed a MAINTENANCE channel with index != 0, and the descriptor walk would have shown a MAINTENANCE channel at INDEX != 0 or a device without one; both returned a single-valued distribution. The scan is demonstrably able to produce the disconfirming answer — it did exactly that for the wider claim, listing HmIP-DRG-DALI channels 1..32 with UNREACH, six devices with no channel-0 UNREACH, and HMW-Generic with no channels at all.
all.challengeNote: Every counted figure in the grounding reproduces exactly — 126/126/125, 14 of 15 wired with 13 carrying the parameters, 399/399, 393/393/268, the six pseudo-devices by name, HmIP-DRG-DALI 1..32 — and I extended it in the one place the LOWBAT case proves is load-bearing: after resolving `<subset ref>` into `<paramset_defs>`, the three init parameters still appear on channel 0 and nowhere else in both shipped XML trees. That subset resolution is what a naive scan misses, and it is exactly what turned up the two hidden LOWBAT declarations in c016; here it changes nothing, which is a stronger result than the unresolved scan. I also add a second Tier-1 anchor the grounding lacked: HmIPGroupDispatcher#channelParamsetChanged pins MAINTENANCE to device channel index 0 by literal, i.e. the HmIP server itself makes the assumption our code makes. Two demotions, both inside claim (2). First, wrong surface, correctly cited: `de.eq3.ccu.virtualdevice` is not "HmIP virtual devices" — it is the IP-ping virtual device feature, DEVICE_DESCRIPTION_TYPE "HM-VI-IP", serial prefix "VIP", i.e. our VirtualDevices interface. VirtualDeviceUtils#initVirtualDevice has exactly one caller, IpVirtualDevice, so "every HmIP virtual/group device's maintenance channel is MASTER-only by construction" is established only for VirtualDevices. HmIP group devices are built on a different path — HmIPGroupDeviceHandler assembles HmIPGroupVirtualChannels from HmIPGroupChannelDescriptions and HmIPGroupVirtualDevice never calls initVirtualDevice — so the MASTER-only property is not shown for them and should not be claimed. Second, the unqualified half of the same sentence: IpVirtualDevice declares PARAMSET_MASTER_UNREACH = "UNREACH" and PARAMSET_MASTER_CONFIG_PENDING = "CONFIG_PENDING", so those two names do exist on its channel 0 — in MASTER, not VALUES. "No VALUES paramset, therefore no UNREACH / CONFIG_PENDING there" is right about VALUES and wrong as written. Two smaller corrections: the rftypes population is 127 device XMLs, not 130 (the 130 is the directory entry count, and the grounding's own per-parameter figures come from the 127); and #initVirtualDevice builds the address with a literal 0 rather than with MAINTENANCE_CHANNEL_INDEX, so "the CCU sets the index in a named constant" overstates what that method does, even though the constant exists and is 0. The other two edges hold as stated and I found no fourth: HmIP-DRG-DALI's 32 per-ballast UNREACH datapoints are never reached by the seed or by the sweep's ungated first pass (device-level availability is unaffected — channel 0 carries UNREACH there too), and HMW-Generic genuinely has no channel 0, so d.Channel(d.Address+":0") returns nil and the device gets no availability tracking. Our parameter spelling STICKY_UNREACH (pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:168, RelevantInitParameters at :288-292) matches the firmware verbatim. The not-performable corner is real and I confirmed it: a case-insensitive search of the whole OpenCCU-Base tree returns no file whose name or content mentions CUxD, so CUxD channel layout is outside every Tier-1 and Tier-2 source available here.

all.title: 'HM-Sec-xx' is used as a device-model prefix and looks like a transcribed wildcard
all.site: internal/parameter/metadata.go:225-229 (sensorMetadataByDeviceAndParam entry {HmIP-SRH, HM-Sec-RHS, HM-Sec-xx, ZEL STG RM FDK} × STATE → QuantityEnum), matched by modelMatchesAny at metadata.go:434-443
all.ourValue: 'HM-Sec-xx' is a literal device-model prefix whose STATE is an enum quantity
all.firmwareValue: HM-Sec-xx is a real device type id shipped by the firmware, and its STATE is declared as a three-option logical type
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_rhs.xml:21 `<type name="Generic 3-State Sensor" id="HM-Sec-xx" priority="1">` inside `<supported_types>`, alongside `id="HM-Sec-RHS"` (:9), `id="ZEL STG RM FDK"` (:13) and `id="HM-Sec-RHS-2"` (:17). Its STATE, in the same file at rf_rhs.xml:170-187, is `<parameter id="STATE" operations="read,event" control="RHS.STATE">` with `<logical type="option">` and the options `CLOSED` (default), `TILTED`, `OPEN`, converted by `<conversion type="option_integer">` mapping device values 0/100/200 to parameter values 0/1/2. Tier 2 confirmation that this id is what a client sees as TYPE: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/device_descriptions/HM-Sec-xx.json carries `"TYPE": "HM-Sec-xx"` for VCU0000217, and ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HM-Sec-xx.json declares VCU0000217:1 STATE with TYPE "ENUM", VALUE_LIST ["CLOSED","TILTED","OPEN"], MIN 0, MAX 2, CONTROL "RHS.STATE", OPERATIONS 5.
all.finding: Not a transcribed wildcard. `HM-Sec-xx` is the literal type id the firmware assigns to the generic three-state sensor variant of the rotary-handle-sensor device family — the fallback entry (priority 1, versus priority 2 for the three named variants) matched when the device's type bytes do not identify a specific model. The rule it carries is correct for it: that device's STATE is an option/enum with CLOSED/TILTED/OPEN, so classifying it as QuantityEnum rather than a binary condition matches the firmware. The neighbouring prefixes in the same entry are equally real and all come from the same file: HM-Sec-RHS (which by prefix also covers HM-Sec-RHS-2, likewise declared there) and ZEL STG RM FDK, the Roto-branded variant — note the firmware spells it with spaces exactly as our literal does. HmIP-SRH is the HmIP counterpart and is not in the rftypes tree, as expected. The one thing worth flagging is not the value but the shape: because the match is a case-insensitive prefix walk, `HM-Sec-xx` is not a pattern and will never match anything but this one type — which is the correct behaviour here, but only by accident of the firmware having chosen an id that reads like a placeholder. A comment naming rf_rhs.xml:21 would stop the next reader from 'fixing' it.
all.negativeControl: Had 'HM-Sec-xx' been a placeholder, the enumeration of `<type ... id=...>` across the 130 rftypes XMLs would have contained no such id and the descriptor corpus no such TYPE — the grep would have returned nothing, and the rule would have been dead code. Both returned the literal string, and the descriptor independently returned TYPE "ENUM" with a three-entry VALUE_LIST for its STATE, so the check could distinguish 'the model exists and is an enum' from 'the model does not exist' and from 'the model exists but STATE is boolean' (which is what the same scan reports for the tilt- and shutter-contact families).
all.challengeNote: Upheld, every quoted string checked character by character against the file, and extended with two checks the grounding did not run. First, the input the rule actually consumes: our literal is the model string, and MetadataByDeviceAndParam is reached from generic.DataPoint.Quantity() with model = Spec.DeviceModel, set from ch.Device().Model at device_pipeline.go:2049 — i.e. the descriptor TYPE. So the question is not how the firmware spells the id in `<supported_types>` but how the CCU reports TYPE, and the two agree: the Roto variant reports "ZEL STG RM FDK" with spaces, exactly our literal, and HM-Sec-xx reports "HM-Sec-xx". Had the descriptor normalised it to the underscore form the pydevccu filename uses (ZEL_STG_RM_FDK), that literal would never have matched anything and the entry would be dead — worth stating, because the filename form is the one a reader is most likely to copy. Second, over-match: a case-insensitive prefix walk across all 399 descriptor models matches exactly five (HM-Sec-RHS, HM-Sec-RHS-2, HM-Sec-xx, ZEL STG RM FDK, HmIP-SRH) and none of the five declares a STATE that is not ENUM, so the prefix shape costs nothing here. The nearby ZEL STG RM FFK (VCU0000239) does not match, as intended. HM-Sec-xx is not a wildcard: it is the priority-1 fallback type matched when the device's type bytes identify the family but not a specific variant (the three named variants are priority 2), and the classification the entry carries is the firmware's own. One surface caveat the grounding does not mention: DataPoint.Quantity() short-circuits to BinarySensorQuantityFor whenever the DP's category is BinarySensor, before MetadataByDeviceAndParam is consulted, so this entry only bites on a STATE created as an enum sensor. The ENUM/VALUE_LIST descriptor makes that true for all five models, so the rule works — but it is not what would protect a mis-categorised STATE, and a reader should not cite it as such. The grounding's own suggestion stands: a comment naming rf_rhs.xml:21 is what stops the next reader from "fixing" a literal that reads like a placeholder.

all.title: The error-callback code space is described from an XML-RPC convention, not from the CCU that sends it
all.site: internal/central/rpcserver/handlers.go:42-50 (Error interface doc), handlers.go:57-63 (asFault stamping Code: -1), dispatch at internal/central/rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go:446-463 and internal/central/rpcserver/binrpc_server.go:341,537
all.ourValue: "errorCode is the CCU-side error class (negative integers follow the XML-RPC fault convention)"; asFault returns Code: -1 for anything unclassified
all.firmwareValue: No CCU component emits an error() callback at all; the negative code space that does exist (-1 … -9) belongs to a different surface — the faults the CCU's own XML-RPC server returns to our calls
all.citation: Tier 1, the emitting side does not exist: the complete set of outbound logic-layer calls in ../OpenCCU-Base is newDevices / replaceDevice / deleteDevices / readdedDevice / updateDevice (src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:786,793,805,817,1177 and src/hs485d/HS485Manager.cpp:163,486,494,541,549,561,575), plus event and system.multicall from the shared sender (src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.cpp:368,398, dispatched via HSSManager::XmlRpcCallAsync at :147). There is no `error` among them. The HmIP and BidCos servers declare the same callback set explicitly: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.IBackendApi and HMServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.IBackendApi both list exactly event, listDevices, newDevices, deleteDevices, updateDevice, replaceDevice, readdedDevice, system.multicall and firmwareUpdateStatusChanged — and no error. Tier 1, the surface the negative codes really belong to: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp throws `XmlRpcException` with an explicit code on its own server methods, and across src/ the distinct codes are -1 (generic / "Insufficient parameters." at XmlRpcMethods.cpp:562, "Wrong usage of setInstallMode" at :618,:626, "Parameter is not readable", "UndefinedValues invalid for this Paramset", "wrong mode"), -2 "Unknown instance" (38 sites), -3 "Unknown paramset" (23), -4 "Device expected", -5 "Unknown parameter" / "Value not supported at parameter 4. Supported values are WAKEUP and BURST", -6 "Operation not supported", -7 "the interface is not able to carry an update", -8 "not enough DutyCycle free", -9 "Device is out of range".
all.finding: The claim answers a different surface from the one it is written on, and the surface it is written on has no firmware speaker. Nothing in rfd, hs485d or libhsscomm ever calls an `error` method on a registered client, and both servers' declared backend interfaces omit it — so no CCU-side code space exists for the `errorCode` argument our doc describes, and the daemon's handler at xmlrpc_server.go:446 (and the BIN-RPC twin) is for a callback this firmware does not send. What the firmware does say is about the opposite direction: the faults the CCU's own XML-RPC server returns to the daemon's calls are negative, and they form a real, small, enumerated space, -1 through -9, with -1 as the generic/usage code. That grounds the "negative integers" half of the sentence but attaches it to getValue/putParamset/setInstallMode responses, not to a callback argument. Two consequences for our code. asFault's Code: -1 is at least consistent with the firmware's own generic code, so nothing is wrong with it; but our rule for it rests on that server-side table, not on anything the CCU sends us, and the doc should say which. And the -1 collision the bundle worries about is real but harmless in the direction that matters, because the CCU-originated -1 the comment fears cannot occur — the callback never arrives. What our rule genuinely rests on, then, is the published eQ-3 XML-RPC interface description of error(), which is not in any tree available here; either that document is cited or the doc comment stops asserting a CCU-side class. Adjacent gap found while enumerating the callback set, worth its own ticket: both servers declare firmwareUpdateStatusChanged(interfaceId, address, int) as part of the backend API, and the repository implements no handler for it under internal/central/rpcserver — a declared CCU callback we silently do not accept.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU emitted error(), the enumeration of outbound calls would have shown an `XmlRpcCallAsync("error", …)` beside the five device-lifecycle calls in RFManager.cpp / HS485Manager.cpp, or an `@RpcMethod(value="error")` entry in IBackendApi beside the eight that are there. Neither appeared, while the same two enumerations did return every callback we do implement — and one we do not (firmwareUpdateStatusChanged) — so the check can distinguish 'this callback exists' from 'it does not'. For the code space itself the control is the fault table: had the firmware used a positive or vendor-specific space, the scan of explicit XmlRpcException codes would have returned non-negative values; it returned -1 through -9 only.

all.title: The HmIP-STHO blacklist rests on the port, and its justification comment is corrupted
all.site: /Users/markus/Documents/GitHub/openccu-loom/internal/model/custom/default.go:41 (entry) + registry.go:333-362 (prefix semantics) + profiles.go:1298-1307 (the profile it shadows)
all.citation: Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/rega/www/esp/controls/climate_transceiver.fn:1-80: the CCU's own operator control for a CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER channel resolves exactly three data points, `cObj.DPByControl("CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER.ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE")`, `...HUMIDITY`, `...AIR_PRESSURE`, and renders all three as read-only text — there is no setpoint field and no write path. Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/rega/www/pages/tabs/control/function.fn:130-132: `if (chn.HssType() == "CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER")` emits the label `${chType_CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER_TEMP}`, resolved in ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www/webui/js/lang/en/translate.lang.channelDescription.js:40 as "Temperature sensor". Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www/webui/js/lang/en/translate.lang.deviceDescription.js:257: `"HmIP-STHO": "Homematic IP Temperature and Humidity Sensor - outdoor"`. Tier 2 — ../pydevccu/pydevccu/device_descriptions/HmIP-STHO.json declares VCU4523900:1 TYPE=CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER (STHO-A: VCU8255833:1, identical), and ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-STHO.json gives that channel VALUES = ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE, ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE_STATUS, HUMIDITY, HUMIDITY_STATUS and MASTER = TEMPERATURE_OFFSET only. Tier 3 witness — ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/model/custom/climate.py:990 `DeviceProfileRegistry.blacklist("HmIP-STHO")` (the comment's `climate.py:963` is stale by 27 lines), and registry.py:94-96/203-206 show the same global, lowercase, prefix-match semantics our Registry.Blacklist/IsBlacklisted implement.
all.finding: The exclusion is correct and the firmware says why. HmIP-STHO and HmIP-STHO-A are sensor-only devices: channel 1 is a CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER, which the CCU itself treats as a read-out (three read-only DPs in climate_transceiver.fn, channel label "Temperature sensor", device label "Temperature and Humidity Sensor - outdoor"). It carries no SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE, no CONTROL_MODE, no BOOST_MODE. The sibling HmIP-STH/STHD put a HEATING_CLIMATECONTROL_TRANSCEIVER on channel 1 (ChannelType ordinal 6 vs 51 in HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.ChannelType) whose VALUES include SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE, CONTROL_MODE, BOOST_MODE, ACTIVE_PROFILE. Our causal chain is exactly the one the entry defends: profiles.go:1298 registers profile IPThermostat with DeviceType "hmip-sth", GetConfigs does a prefix match, and "hmip-stho" starts with "hmip-sth" — so without the blacklist both STHO variants materialise an IPThermostat Climate custom DP on a channel that has none of its control parameters, and materialize.go has no required-field gate that would stop it. The prefix semantics are also right rather than merely convenient: "hmip-stho" is the exact set {HmIP-STHO, HmIP-STHO-A} — the CCU's device-description catalogue lists no third model with that prefix. Two caveats, neither a firmware disagreement: (a) our blacklist is global across all categories, not Climate-scoped — that matches the reference implementation, which is also global, and today no non-Climate profile would match "hmip-stho" anyway, so nothing else is being suppressed; (b) the justification comment at default.go:30-40 is textually corrupted ("Emitted by g.", a dangling "While", "When a future") and cites a stale line number, so the reason is unreadable in the repo even though the rule is right. The firmware wording that would fix it: HmIP-STHO channel 1 is CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER (a temperature sensor), not HEATING_CLIMATECONTROL_TRANSCEIVER; it has no SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE, and "hmip-stho" would otherwise prefix-match the "hmip-sth" IPThermostat profile.
all.firmwareValue: HmIP-STHO ch1 = CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER; VALUES = {ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE, ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE_STATUS, HUMIDITY, HUMIDITY_STATUS}; no SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE anywhere on the device
all.ourValue: model prefix "hmip-stho" is blacklisted from every custom-DP category (so no IPThermostat Climate DP)
all.negativeControl: Had the rule been wrong — i.e. had HmIP-STHO been a real thermostat — the same three probes would have returned visibly different answers, and they demonstrably do for its sibling: HmIP-STH's descriptor gives VCU8063453:1 TYPE=HEATING_CLIMATECONTROL_TRANSCEIVER with SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE / CONTROL_MODE / BOOST_MODE / ACTIVE_PROFILE in VALUES, and the CCU dispatches that HssType to a heating control, not to climate_transceiver.fn. I also swept the whole descriptor corpus for CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER channels (ELV-SH-CTH, ELV-SH-TACO, HmIP-SCTH230, HmIP-STHO, HmIP-STHO-A): not one carries a setpoint, so the channel type itself is the discriminator and the probe is not merely echoing the STHO file.
all.challengeNote: Upheld, and the causal chain re-measured independently rather than taken on report. What I checked: (1) climate_transceiver.fn read end to end — three read-only text cells, no write path, no setpoint field; (2) the STHO/STHO-A descriptors and the STH/STHD contrast in the descriptor corpus; (3) that "hmip-sth" is the ONLY registered DeviceType in the whole profiles.go catalogue that prefix-matches "hmip-stho"/"hmip-stho-a" — which independently establishes the previous agent's caveat (a): the global, all-category blacklist suppresses nothing except the IPThermostat match, today; (4) that GetConfigs prefix-matches with longest-DeviceType-wins, so without the entry the IPThermostat profile is selected; (5) that materialize.go has no required-field gate. Two legs of the previous grounding do not survive, neither of them load-bearing. FIRST, the function.fn:130-132 citation is a misquote by omission. The actual code is `if (chn.HssType() == "CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER") { if (chn.Label() == "ELV-SH-TACO") { ... ${chType_CLIMATE_TRANSCEIVER_TEMP} ... } }` — the "Temperature sensor" label is emitted ONLY for the ELV-SH-TACO device, never for HmIP-STHO. Dropping the inner guard turns a device-specific branch into a claimed channel-type-wide label; that leg must not be cited. SECOND, the completeness claim "the CCU's device-description catalogue lists no third model with that prefix" cannot be supported by the source cited for it: translate.lang.deviceDescription.js carries only "HmIP-STHD" and "HmIP-STHO" in the whole HmIP-STH* space — it lists neither HmIP-STHO-A nor HmIP-STH, both of which demonstrably exist. That catalogue is not an exhaustive model registry, so it cannot bound the prefix set. The prefix "hmip-stho" being exactly {STHO, STHO-A} is therefore unverified — it is a scoping assumption, not a firmware fact. It does not change today's outcome (both known members are sensor-only) but a future HmIP-STHO<x> with heating control would be silently suppressed. The comment corruption is confirmed by reading: default.go:30-40 contains "Emitted by g.", a dangling "While", and "When a future" with no predicate, and cites climate.py:963 where the call sits at :990.

all.title: The device-details loader silently rewrites an unrecognised interface token to BidCos-RF on a comment-claimed completeness argument
all.citation: Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www/api/methods/device/listalldetail.tcl:23-28: `var interface = dom.GetObject(device.Interface()); ... Write(" INTERFACE {"# interface.Name() # "}");`, emitted as the JSON field at :219 `append result ",\"interface\":[json_toString $device(INTERFACE)]"`. The value is therefore the ReGa interface object's *name*, not a compiled-in enum. Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/eq3/ipc.tcl:14 and :54-70: those names are read at runtime from `/etc/config/InterfacesList.xml` by a regexp over arbitrary `<name>` elements (`regexp {<name[^>]*>(.+)</name[^>]*>}`), cached in /var/tmp/api_ipc.cache. Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/config_templates/InterfacesList.xml:1-18: the shipped template contains exactly three `<ipc><name>` values — `BidCos-RF`, `VirtualDevices`, `HmIP-RF`. Tier 1 — ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/overlay/base/etc/init.d/S49hs485d:33-65: boot only *deletes* `>HmIP-RF<` or `>BidCos-RF<` blocks from that file; nothing constrains what may be added. Tier 1 — `BidCos-Wired` is the fourth CCU-side spelling: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www/config/cp_maintenance.cgi:931 `homematic("Interface.getLGWStatus", {"interface": "BidCos-Wired"}, ...)` and ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www/config/ic_deviceFirmwareOverview.cgi:99 `set bidcosWiredID "BidCos-Wired"`. Tier 1 — `CUxD` is the fifth: ../OpenCCU/buildroot-external/patches/occu/0027-WebUI-Fix-EmptyTableCUxDDevices.patch:8 matches the ReGa datapoint-name prefix `CUxD.CUX` alongside `HmIP-RF.`.
all.finding: Two separable claims, and the firmware splits them. (1) The five spellings are exact — `BidCos-RF`, `HmIP-RF`, `VirtualDevices` verbatim in the shipped InterfacesList.xml template, `BidCos-Wired` verbatim in two WebUI call sites, `CUxD` verbatim as the ReGa name prefix. Casing and hyphenation match our hmenum constants character for character, so the accept branch is right. (2) The completeness argument the comment rests on is not something the firmware supports. `interface` is `interface.Name()` off a ReGa DOM object whose name came from a plain config file parsed with a permissive regexp; add-ons (CUxD is precisely this case) extend it, and the boot script only ever removes entries. There is no closed enum of interface names anywhere on the CCU side to read. So the boundary runs here: for a stock image plus the CUxD add-on our set is complete and the else-branch is dead; for any further `<ipc>` entry — another add-on interface, a future eQ-3 one — the CCU returns a name we do not know and the loader records that device as BidCos-RF, a wrong protocol/backend classification, with no log line. Note the comment's literal wording ("covers every valid Interface constant") is true but circular: InterfacesSupportingRPCCallback is the union of XMLRPCInterfaces and BINRPCInterfaces (interface.go:149-169) and every one of our five constants appears in one of them, so the predicate cannot reject any value of our own type — it is only load-bearing against strings the CCU chooses. One firmware detail that shrinks the live surface: listalldetail.tcl:176 filters the device list with `if (true == device.ReadyConfig() && dom.GetObject(device.Interface()))`, so every listed device has a resolvable interface object, and ipc.tcl's regexp requires a non-empty `<name>`. The `d.Interface == ""` half of our condition is therefore unreachable from this source; only the unrecognised-token half can fire.
all.firmwareValue: open set: `interface` = ReGa interface object name, sourced from `<name>` elements of /etc/config/InterfacesList.xml at runtime (base image: BidCos-RF, VirtualDevices, HmIP-RF; plus BidCos-Wired and add-on-registered names such as CUxD)
all.ourValue: closed set of 5 (InterfacesSupportingRPCCallback); anything else → hmenum.InterfaceBidCosRF, silently
all.negativeControl: Two directions, both able to come back different. On spelling: had our tokens been wrong ("BidCos_RF", "HmIP", "Virtual Devices"), the InterfacesList.xml template and the two BidCos-Wired call sites would have shown those other literals — they are quoted strings I read, not inferred, and a mismatch would have been visible immediately. On completeness: had the CCU carried a closed enum of interface names, I would have found it as a C/C++ enum in src/rfd or a fixed Tcl list; what I found instead is a file-driven loader with a wildcard regexp and a boot script that only deletes entries — an observably different shape from the one the comment assumes.
all.missingInput: none for the spellings; for completeness the CCU carries no enumeration to read — the acceptance set is whatever /etc/config/InterfacesList.xml holds on a given installation, which is deployment state, not firmware
all.challengeNote: Direction upheld, boundary moved, and three of the cited legs corrected. The accept branch is right for the four spellings I could attest directly: functions.fn:578-587 and danger.fn:22-27 compare the very `Name()` that listalldetail.tcl emits against the literals "BidCos-RF", "HmIP-RF", "VirtualDevices", "BidCos-Wired" — character-for-character our hmenum constants. Three corrections to the previous grounding. (1) SURFACE: ipc.tcl was cited as the source of `interface.Name()`. It is not — ipc.tcl feeds `INTERFACE_LIST`, the JSON-RPC API's own array; the ReGa DOM object is built by ReGaHss. The two are the same namespace, but that join was never shown. It is shown by homematic.cgi:53 plus haslinksorprograms.tcl:13-27 (a ReGa interface object indexed straight into INTERFACE_LIST), and by ReGaHss's own LoadInterfacesFromFile over the same path. Leg replaced, conclusion intact. (2) BidCos-Wired was grounded on a WebUI JS string and a Tcl variable. The real source is hs485dLoader.cpp:229/238, which APPENDS `<ipc><name>BidCos-Wired</name>` to InterfacesList.xml at boot — which is also the strongest available proof of the open-set claim: a shipped CCU program writes new interface names into that file. (3) S49hs485d was characterised as "only deletes". It also replaces the active file wholesale from the template when the two differ (`cmp -s ${CFG_TEMPLATE_DIR}/InterfacesList.xml /etc/config/InterfacesList.xml || cp`, :36-38) before the strip blocks. NEW AND MATERIAL: the previous agent's unrecognised-token case is not hypothetical. "HmIP-Wired" is a fifth interface-object name the CCU's own code expects — functions.fn:583 compares `_oIface.Name()` against it, haslinksorprograms.tcl:19 indexes `$INTERFACE_LIST(HmIP-Wired)`, and ic_ifacecmd.cgi:26/110/343/649, ic_setprofiles.cgi:17, ic_deviceparameters.cgi:615/1183 and cp_add_device.cgi:275-297 all treat it as a first-class interface. Our hmenum has no HmIP-Wired constant by deliberate decision (pkg/hmenum/interface.go:16-20). On any CCU carrying that ipc entry, Device.listAllDetail returns `"interface":"HmIP-Wired"`, isKnownInterface rejects it, and loader.go:156 records every such device as BidCos-RF with no log line — a wrong protocol and backend classification. So the boundary is: our five-token set is complete for a stock OpenCCU image plus the CUxD add-on, and the else-branch is dead there; it is NOT complete against the interface names the CCU's own WebUI enumerates. Weaker than presented: the CUxD spelling is absent from OpenCCU-Base/src and the OpenCCU overlay entirely (grep over both trees returns nothing) — it rests on patch 0027's ReGa datapoint prefix plus the firmware's datapoint-naming shape, two grounded steps, not a direct attestation of `<name>CUxD</name>`. Also unverified: the claim that `d.Interface == ""` is unreachable. listalldetail.tcl:176 `if (true == device.ReadyConfig() && dom.GetObject(device.Interface()))` is verbatim and does guarantee a resolvable interface object, but nothing in the firmware shows such an object cannot carry an empty Name(); the supporting reason given (ipc.tcl's non-empty regexp) is off-surface for the same reason as (1). Finally, the comment's own wording at loader.go:220-222 ("covers every valid Interface constant") is circular as noted — InterfacesSupportingRPCCallback is `unionInterfaces(XMLRPCInterfaces, BINRPCInterfaces)` (pkg/hmenum/interface.go:169) and every one of our five constants is in one of them, so the predicate cannot reject a value of our own type. It is load-bearing only against strings the CCU chooses, and against "HmIP-Wired" it fails.

all.title: The WEEK_PROGRAM_CHANNEL_LOCKS key-to-bit assignment is explicitly unestablished
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www_source/ise/js/iseHmIPWeeklyProgram.js:357 `valCheckBox = Math.pow(2, index);` (expert) and :363 `valCheckBox = tmpVal << 3;` (non-expert, seeded `tmpVal = 1` at :361); :614 `for (var x = 0; x < bVal.length; x += 3) { tmp += bVal[x]; }`; :239-241 `_bit"+index+"0").attr("checked",true); // Auto` else `_bit"+index+"1") // Manu`; :517-555 getRelevantChannels (pushes the device's channel-list index of every `*_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER` / access-control channel); per-family overrides at :52 (HmIP-BSL `[4,5,6,8,9,10,12,13,14]`), :57 (HmIP-WKP `[1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15]`), :336-345+:470-476 (HmIP-FWI Wiegand: list index 0-7 -> bits 3-10, index 8-10 -> bits 0-2), :351 (HmIP-DRG-DALI `Math.pow(2,(val-1))`, channels 1-48 -> bits 0-47). Door-lock surface: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/webui/www_source/ise/js/iseHmIPWeeklyProgram_AccessReceiver.js:302 `Math.pow(2, index)`, :308 `value='256'` (DOOR_LOCK_TRANSCEIVER :12), :311 `value='512'` (AUTO_RELOCK_TRANSCEIVER :13). The value read is our parameter: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/controls/hmip_weekly_program.fn:17 `object objChannelLocks = cObj.DPByControl("WEEK_PROFILE.CHANNEL_LOCKS");` and :64 `opts.channelLocks`.
all.finding: The firmware DOES define an explicit mapping, and it is not the uniform 8x3 grid our table hard-codes. The CCU's own weekly-program editor derives the bit positionally from the channel's index in `relevantChn` — the device's channel list filtered to `*_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER` plus the access-control channel types — and that list is overridden per device family. Two firmware facts do back our table: the inverted semantics (set bit = Manu = schedule off; :239-241) and the stride of 3 (the easy-mode view takes every third bit, :614, and writes 1, 1<<3, 1<<6, ..., :361-364), so 'actor N primary = bit 3(N-1)' is the firmware's own scheme for ordinary multi-actor virtual-receiver actors (HmIP-BSM/PS/FSM, and HmIP-BSL where the firmware's own override [4,5,6,8,9,10,12,13,14] lands on bits 0-8 exactly as our keys 1_1..3_3 do). It breaks where the firmware overrides the list, and our deriveTargetChannels (custom-DP groups sorted by group number, primary-then-secondaries) has no equivalent: (a) HmIP-DLP — our registry gives IPLock a single scheduled group at channel 12 (profiles.go:887-891), so key 1_1 -> bit 0, while the firmware puts DOOR_LOCK_TRANSCEIVER :12 at bit 8 (256) and bit 0 is PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVER :4 (user 1); (b) HmIP-FWI — our IPAccessPermission gives 8 single-member groups at channels 1..8 (profiles.go:1081-1085), keys 1_1..8_1 -> bits 0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21, while the firmware puts those same 8 ACCESS_TRANSCEIVER channels at bits 3..10 and reserves bits 0-2 for the virtual switch receivers; (c) HmIP-DRG-DALI — our 48 single-member groups (profiles.go:961-965) yield keys 9_1..48_1 that ChannelKeyToBitmask rejects outright, and keys 2_1..8_1 -> bits 3..21 while the firmware uses bit = channelNo-1 (bits 1..7), needing 48 bits, not 24. The '24-bit mask measured on live hardware' in the comment is therefore a per-device property, not a scheme-wide one. HmIP-RGBW is a partial case: our keys 1_1..1_3 land on the firmware's bits 0-2 correctly, but the group's 4th member (channel 4, firmware bit 3) has no key `1_4` in the table and is silently dropped.
all.negativeControl: Had our positional grid been the firmware's universal scheme, iseHmIPWeeklyProgram.js would contain one bit formula and no per-family `relevantChn` overrides; instead it carries eight device-specific overrides and two alternative bit formulas (`index+3`/`index-8` for Wiegand, `val-1` for DALI). Had the firmware carried no mapping at all, the dialog would submit a channel list rather than a summed `Math.pow(2, ...)` bitmask into WEEK_PROGRAM_TARGET_CHANNEL_LOCKS. Both alternatives are visibly absent.
all.ourValue: key `<actor>_<sub>` -> bit 3*(actor-1)+(sub-1), uniformly, 24 bits; actor = rank of the custom-DP channel group by group number, sub = primary then secondaries
all.firmwareValue: bit = index of the channel in the device's schedule-relevant channel list (`*_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER` + access-control types, channel order), with explicit per-family overrides; e.g. HmIP-DLP :12 -> 256, :13 -> 512, :4..:11 -> 1..128; HmIP-FWI ACCESS_TRANSCEIVER :1..:8 -> bits 3..10; HmIP-DRG-DALI bit = channelNo-1 over 48 bits
all.challengeNote: UPHELD and strengthened. I re-read every cited line and closed the one gap the prior agent left open: that the WebUI editor is on our surface. It is — legacy-parameter-definition.config maps the ReGa control `WEEK_PROFILE.CHANNEL_LOCKS` the editor reads onto the legacy parameter `WEEK_PROGRAM_CHANNEL_LOCKS` our code parses, and the editor's write (`WPTCLS=<bit>,WPTCL=<mode>`, iseHmIPWeeklyProgram.js:635) is byte-for-byte the string our datapoint.go:663 BuildCombinedParameterValue emits. Same read parameter, same write parameter, same bit space. The `relevantChn` entries are channel NUMBERS, not array positions guessed from order: three independent places in the source say so — the DALI branch computes the bit as `val-1`, the AccessReceiver renders `relevantChn[8]`/`[9]` as the operator-visible channel label, and the non-expert Wiegand list is hard-coded `[1..8,10,11,12]`, exactly HmIP-FWI's ACCESS_TRANSCEIVER and SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER channels. So the bit position was read from the source, not conventionalised. Our path confirmed device by device: HmIP-DLP — IPLock declares ScheduleChannelNo=14 (profiles.go:892), so ScheduleRelevantChannelGroups keeps only that group; primary channel 12 becomes key 1_1 -> bit 0, while the firmware puts :12 at bit 8 and bit 0 at PERMISSION_TRANSCEIVER :4. HmIP-FWI — IPAccessPermission's 8 single-member groups (profiles.go:1085) yield 1_1..8_1 -> bits 0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21 against the firmware's 3..10. HmIP-DRG-DALI — 48 single-member groups (profiles.go:965) yield 9_1..48_1, which ChannelKeyToBitmask rejects outright, and the parameter is a 48-bit STRING our uint32 path cannot hold at all. Agreement where the prior agent said so, verified: BSM :4,:5,:6 -> bits 0,1,2; BSL's own firmware override [4,5,6,8,9,10,12,13,14] lands on bits 0..8 exactly as keys 1_1..3_3. HmIP-RGBW is worse than 'partial': its ProfileConfig (profile_configs.go:256-262) declares PrimaryChannel + SecondaryChannels {1,2,3}, so deriveTargetChannels MINTS key `1_4` for channel 4 — a key absent from channelKeyBitmask, so ChannelKeyToBitmask returns false and SetScheduleEnabled fails with 'unknown channel key "1_4"' for a channel the firmware addresses at bit 3. The table comment's '24-bit mask measured on live hardware' is a per-device fact (Tier 2: 43 devices at MAX 16777215, DALI at 2^48-1), not a scheme-wide one.

all.title: The RSSI normalisation bands and their rejected sentinels rest on the Python sibling alone
