all.ourValue: a motion detector holds MOTION until its own blocking time expires or RESET_MOTION is written; resettable = the channel exposes a writable RESET_MOTION data point
all.firmwareValue: true only for HmIP MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER / MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER (and PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER via RESET_PRESENCE) on a permanent listener; on BidCos-RF no RESET_MOTION exists and the CCU itself un-latches MOTION on a server-side timer
all.finding: The narrow parts are confirmed exactly. RESET_MOTION and RESET_PRESENCE are declared write-only, LogicalType.ACTION; the pairing our resetParameterFor uses (MOTION -> RESET_MOTION, PRESENCE_DETECTION_STATE -> RESET_PRESENCE) is the firmware's own pairing; the WebUI writes the parameter as a plain `setDpState(<id>, true)`. Two boundaries run tighter than the comment. (1) BidCos-RF has no RESET_MOTION anywhere: no file under src/devicetypes/rftypes mentions it, and HM-Sec-MDIR's descriptor carries MOTION alone. On those devices the un-latching is done by the CCU, not the device: rf_sec_mdir.xml declares MOTION read+event with a domino_event of value 0 and delay_id NEXT_TRANSMISSION, and rfd turns that into an autotimer that writes MOTION back to 0 after NEXT_TRANSMISSION seconds. So for the whole BidCos family the comment is wrong in both halves — there is no writable parameter, and the expiry is a CCU timer, not "the device's own blocking time". Supports() correctly returns false for them, so the code is right and the doc comment is not. (2) On HmIP the firmware gates the reset on a MASTER value our port never reads: motiondetector.fn:112 fetches PERMANENT_FULL_RX via Interface.getMasterValue and :117 shows the reset button only when it is != 0, with the reason at :116 verbatim — "If the device is a non-permanent listener then hide the button. Otherwise the state of the control doesn't change after using the button which will cause enquiries at the customer service." Our Supports() qualifies on the presence of a writable RESET_MOTION alone, so on an HmIP-SMI55 configured as a non-permanent listener the daemon writes on every arm and reports the sensor as resettable, while the firmware's own UI declares that write ineffective. That is where the operator-facing "resettable latched detectors" count over-counts. Not settled, and not settleable from these trees: whether a successful write clears MOTION immediately or only ends the blocking interval, and what the latch duration is. MOTION_ACTIVE_TIME is created by HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.configparameter.GeneralConfigurationParameterFactory as a 3-bit integer config parameter with no type converter (min 0, max 7, default 4) — the source carries an ordinal, not a duration, and no mapping to seconds. Deriving a blocking time from it would be substituting a convention; that sub-question is not performable here.
all.negativeControl: Had the rule been right at full width, RESET_MOTION would appear in the BidCos device-type XMLs and the WebUI would render the reset button unconditionally. Grep over all 130 rftypes XMLs returns no hit, and the button is wrapped in an explicit PERMANENT_FULL_RX != 0 guard.
all.challengeNote: The narrowing verdict stands, but one of its sub-conclusions is wrong and I am overturning it. UPHELD, each re-checked: createStop is verbatim write-only ACTION and RESET_MOTION / RESET_PRESENCE are the only two parameters besides STOP that go through it; the MOTION -> RESET_MOTION and PRESENCE_DETECTION_STATE -> RESET_PRESENCE pairing our resetParameterFor uses is the firmware's own; the WebUI writes it as `setDpState(<id>, true)`; BidCos-RF genuinely has no RESET_MOTION — a find-exec grep over all 127 rftypes and 18 hs485types XMLs returns zero files, and rf_sec_mdir.xml declares MOTION read+event with `<domino_event value="0" delay_id="NEXT_TRANSMISSION"/>`, which rfd converts into a CancelAutotimerEvent/ScheduleAutotimerEvent pair, so on that whole family the doc comment is wrong in both halves while Supports() is right; the pydevccu descriptors read exactly as quoted. The PERMANENT_FULL_RX boundary is real and in fact tighter than described: the reset button's own `<td>` ships `class='hidden'` at motiondetector.fn:99 and is revealed only by :118 inside `if (permanentFullRX != 0)`. Two things to correct. FIRST, and this is the substantive one: the prior agent reported the MOTION_ACTIVE_TIME ordinal-to-duration mapping as "not performable here" because the HmIP source carries an ordinal with no seconds mapping. Tier 1 carries it, in the tree the map itself designates as the authority the descriptor cannot be — the WebUI. www/config/easymodes/hmip/MOTIONDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl builds an index-keyed options array, options(0)="15$s" through options(7)="32$m", with $s and $m bound by `upvar #0 unit_sec s` / `upvar #0 unit_min m` and defined as "s" and "min" in EnterFreeValue.tcl:6-7. The same table appears verbatim in PRESENCEDETECTOR_TRANSCEIVER.tcl and MOTIONDETECTOR_VIRTUAL_TRANSCEIVER.tcl. This is not array order standing in for a mapping — each index is written down next to its value. So: 0=15 s, 1=30 s, 2=1 min, 3=2 min, 4=4 min, 5=8 min, 6=16 min, 7=32 min, and the HmIP factory's default of 4 means the shipped latch is 4 minutes. I verified the factory constants against the createInteger signature rather than by argument position: createInteger(name, listNumber, bitIndex, defaultValue, bitLength) with min defaulting to 0 and max to 2^bitLength - 1, so ("MOTION_ACTIVE_TIME", 31, 2, 4, 3) is bitIndex 2, default 4, 3 bits, min 0, max 7, converter null. SECOND, an over-read: "the firmware's own UI declares that write ineffective" is stronger than the source says. The verbatim reason at motiondetector.fn:116 is "Otherwise the state of the control doesn't change after using the button which will cause enquiries at the customer service" — a statement about the observable control state, not about the write being discarded. The honest form of the boundary: our Supports() qualifies on the presence of a writable RESET_MOTION alone, while the CCU's own UI additionally requires PERMANENT_FULL_RX != 0 before offering the button, so on a non-permanent-listener HmIP-SMI55 the daemon writes on every arm and counts the sensor as resettable where the firmware would not offer the action; whether that write eventually lands is not settled by these trees. Still open and still not settleable here: whether a successful RESET_MOTION write clears MOTION immediately or only ends the blocking interval.

all.title: Optimistic-command TTL (60 s) is shorter than the daemon's own duty-cycle retry window (40 s x N)
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:216 `inst->SetStoredValue(value_id, param, ValueStore::FLAG_VOLATILE)` and :235-237 `if(channel->GetDevice()->RxNeedsWakeup()){ channel->GetDevice()->QueueAfterWakeupFrame(frame); continue; }` | ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/ValueStore.cpp:41-53 (SetStoredValue writes the map only; no event emission) | ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:319 `SendAfterWakeupFrames();` (only on an incoming frame from the device) and :1311-1321 QueueAfterWakeupFrame, :1314-1317 `LOG(Logger::LOG_WARNING, "QueueAfterWakeupFrame: Queue size exceeded, dropped oldest frame.")` | ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosFrameWaitTime.h:20-22 `#define WAIT_TIME_DEFAULT 1500` / `WAIT_TIME_SINGLE_BURST 4500` / `WAIT_TIME_TRIPLE_BURST 12500` | HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler — field responseTimeout initialised from ServiceProperties key "Legacy.ResponseTimeout" with default 25, used as q.poll(responseTimeout, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
all.ourValue: 60 s TTL bounds the window in which an inbound callback still counts as the confirmation of a send
all.firmwareValue: unbounded for a wake-on-radio device — the frame is queued until the device next transmits, with no expiry and a depth-10 queue that silently drops the oldest frame; the synchronous budgets are 1500/4500/12500 ms per BidCos frame (up to 2 tries) and 25 s per HmIP legacy call
all.finding: The firmware places no upper bound on the confirmation latency at all for a wake-up device, so 60 s is a policy choice and the comment's framing of it as sufficient is unsupported. Concretely: for a device whose effective rx mode is WAKEUP, rfd's PutData stores the value in its own volatile store (which emits nothing — ValueStore::SetStoredValue only writes the map), queues the frame, and returns true, so putParamset/setValue answer success without transmitting. The queued frame goes out only when the device itself transmits (SendAfterWakeupFrames is called from the incoming-frame path). There is no timeout on that queue; the only bound is depth 10, and overflow drops the oldest frame with a warning — so the confirming VALUES callback can arrive minutes later or never. 46 of the ~130 shipped RF device types declare a wake-up-only rx mode (rx_modes="CONFIG,WAKEUP" x28, "CONFIG,WAKEUP,LAZY_CONFIG" x15), including rf_cc_tc.xml (HM-CC-TC, a thermostat users write setpoints to), rf_sec_mdir.xml, rf_sc.xml and rf_rhs.xml. Separately, the candidate's duty-cycle framing answers a different surface: RetryDutyCycleDelay = 40 s is our own wait, not a CCU-stated latency; the CCU's duty-cycle rejection is fault -8 and carries no delay. What the firmware does bound is only the synchronous case (1.5/4.5/12.5 s per BidCos frame with up to 2 tries; 25 s per HmIP legacy call), and those all fit inside 60 s comfortably — the TTL is adequate for every non-wake-up path and structurally cannot cover the wake-up path at any value.
all.negativeControl: Had 60 s (or any fixed TTL) been firmware-supported, rfd would carry an expiry on the after-wakeup queue or a delivery deadline after which the queued frame is abandoned and an event or fault raised. It carries neither: the only bound in that code path is a queue depth, and overflow is logged as a dropped frame rather than reported to the caller.
all.challengeNote: Upheld under every attack I could mount, including one the prior agent did not run. All citations verified with one line correction and one count correction. Verified verbatim: WAIT_TIME_DEFAULT 1500 / SINGLE_BURST 4500 / TRIPLE_BURST 12500; ValueStore::SetStoredValue writes `stored_values[name]` and returns true with no emission, and under FLAG_VOLATILE does not even set `dirty`; QueueAfterWakeupFrame caps at `size()>10` and pops the oldest with exactly the quoted warning; SendAfterWakeupFrames drains the queue and is reachable only from ProcessIncomingFrame's `if( frame.DeviceWokenup() )` branch — there is no timer path and no per-frame expiry, so a queued write has no upper latency bound at all; HMIPServer's Legacy.ResponseTimeout defaults to 25 s. Line corrections: SetStoredValue in PutData is at :218 (cited :216) and the wake-up branch at :235-236 (cited :235-237); the drop warning is at :1315. Count correction: rftypes holds 127 XMLs, not ~130, and 45 of them name WAKEUP in an rx_modes attribute, of which 42 declare no BURST and no ALWAYS — so 42 wake-up-only device types, not 46, and the sub-counts are 28 ("CONFIG,WAKEUP") plus 14 ("CONFIG,WAKEUP,LAZY_CONFIG"), not 28 plus 15. The four named devices check out exactly: rf_cc_tc.xml, rf_sc.xml and rf_rhs.xml are "CONFIG,WAKEUP"; rf_sec_mdir.xml is "CONFIG,WAKEUP,LAZY_CONFIG". The attack I added: HSSParameter::SetValue — which is the leaf both setValue and putParamset reach — emits an immediate loopback event when the parameter declares `loopback`, and that would have bounded the confirmation latency and rescued the 60 s TTL. It does not, on the device that matters: rf_cc_tc.xml declares a writable SETPOINT at :271 and carries zero `loopback` attributes, so on an HM-CC-TC the only confirming VALUES callback is the device's own frame out of the unbounded queue. Where `loopback` does appear in the thermostat XMLs it is on INHIBIT (rf_cc_rt_dn.xml:2170,2203,2226,2263,2565,2599), a CCU-side pseudo-parameter, not on a setpoint. The prior agent's dismissal of the candidate's framing also holds: RetryDutyCycleDelay = 40 s is our own constant in pkg/hmreliability/defaults.go:52, the CCU's duty-cycle rejection is fault -8 (pkg/hmerr/errors.go:272) and carries no delay, so the original "40 s x N" comparison was never a firmware quantity.

all.title: Circuit-breaker trip policy (5 / 30 s / 2) is a ported constant governing whether writes reach the CCU at all
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libXmlRpc/src/XmlRpcClient.cpp:83 and :104 `_timeout = -1;`, :196 `if(!_disp.work(_timeout))return false;//wait forever until an event arrives`, :623-626 setTimeout (never called from this tree) | ../OpenCCU-Base/src/tclrpc/tclrpc.cpp:354-363 (the only XmlRpcClient user; no setTimeout) | ../OpenCCU-Base/www/api/methods/interface/dispatch.tcl:132-149 (the fault-code catalogue; :146 `-10 { jsonrpc_error 507 "Transmission pending in HmIP Legacy API" }`) | ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosFrameWaitTime.h:20-22 and ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:92-95 (up to 2 tries) | HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.LegacyServiceHandler (responseTimeout from "Legacy.ResponseTimeout", default 25 s) | HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.NotificationUtil#isTransmissionPendingResult and #createTransmissionPendingRpcRemoteException
all.ourValue: 5 consecutive wire failures trip OPEN; 30 s dwell; 2 half-open successes to close
all.firmwareValue: no counterpart exists — the CCU's own XML-RPC client sets no timeout, performs no retry and keeps no failure counter. What it does state: 25 s per HmIP legacy call; 1500/4500/12500 ms per BidCos frame with up to 2 tries; -10 for both TRANSMISSION_PENDING and UNREACH
all.finding: The CCU source does not decide this rule, because the CCU has no equivalent policy. Its own XML-RPC client — the one ReGa uses to reach rfd and HMIPServer through tclrpc — initialises _timeout to -1 and waits forever (the comment at XmlRpcClient.cpp:196 says so verbatim); setTimeout exists but is called from nowhere in this tree; there is no retry and no failure counter, and ReGa maps every fault straight to a JSON-RPC error. So 5 / 30 s / 2 rests on the Python sibling's Connection constructor, as the code says, and Tier 1 neither confirms nor contradicts it. Two firmware-stated numbers do bear on the concern the candidate raises, and both point away from it. First, one HmIP legacy call is capped at 25 s, so five consecutive timeouts is roughly 125 s of silence — far longer than the 30 s dwell, not the "five slow answers" scenario; and because the breaker wraps the retrier (internal/client/interface_client_orchestration.go:732, 741, 796), each of those five is a whole command with its retries already spent, not one attempt. A BidCos frame is capped at 1.5/4.5/12.5 s with up to 2 tries, so five consecutive BidCos failures is on the order of 45 s. Second, the risk that IS firmware-grounded is the classification rather than the threshold: NotificationUtil#isTransmissionPendingResult returns true for BackendNotificationType TRANSMISSION_PENDING *and* UNREACH, and the legacy verbs turn both into fault -10. ReGa treats -10 as its own distinct, expected condition, while our isSemanticFault deliberately keeps -10 counting as a wire failure. Five quick commands to one unreachable HmIP device therefore open the breaker for the entire interface, including the healthy devices on it — an outcome the CCU's own consumer never produces. I found no firmware-stated maintenance window in which rfd stops answering: src/eq3configd has none, and the firmware-update flags at src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:324 and :1007 gate the device's wake-up request, not the XML-RPC server.
all.negativeControl: Had the firmware carried a comparable policy, the CCU's own client would call setTimeout and a threshold or retry constant would sit beside it. `_timeout = -1` with an explicit "wait forever until an event arrives" comment, and no setTimeout caller anywhere in the tree, is the opposite result — which is also what tells me the silence is real rather than a search miss.

all.title: The HmIP-LSC combined HS+CT variant is keyed by model string, deliberately in place of the descriptor property that decides it
all.ourValue: strings.EqualFold(cfg.Channel.Device().Model, "HmIP-LSC") — exact, case-insensitive equality against the descriptor TYPE (Model is set from dd.Type, internal/central/adapter/device_pipeline.go:437,577)
all.firmwareValue: [string first "HmIP-LSC" $dev_descr(TYPE)] != -1 — case-sensitive SUBSTRING match on the descriptor TYPE, applied as an override after the mode has already been resolved
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/hmip/UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER.tcl:21-31 (identical at src/webui/www/config/easymodes/hmip/UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER.tcl:21-31); ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/etc/hmipUniversalLightReceiverConfigDialogs.tcl:25-27; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/linkHmIP_UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER.tcl:59-62; ../OpenCCU-Base/www/config/easymodes/etc/hmipChannelConfigDialogs.tcl:102-104. Tier 2: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-RGBW.json (VCU5629873:0 MASTER, DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE, TYPE ENUM, OPERATIONS 3, FLAGS 1, DEFAULT "RGBW", VALUE_LIST ["RGBW","RGB","2_TUNABLE_WHITE","4_PWM"]) — and it is the ONLY file in the whole paramset_descriptions corpus containing that parameter.
all.negativeControl: Had our rule been wrong I would have found the CCU dispatching the combined LSC behaviour off a descriptor property rather than the type string — concretely, an easymode branch reading `[info exists dev_ps(DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE)]` and selecting mode 5 on the false arm, or a UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_MAX_CAPABILITIES value dedicated to LSC. Both branches exist in the file and both go somewhere else: the false arm goes to DALI (mode 4), and hmipUniversalLightReceiverConfigDialogs.tcl:442 records that LSC's UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_MAX_CAPABILITIES is 0 and therefore unusable as a discriminator. The check discriminates: the same grep that found the type-string override would have found a descriptor-driven one had the firmware used it.
all.challengeNote:
THE KEYING HALF IS CONFIRMED, THE CAPABILITY HALF IS NOT — and the previous agent's boundary, its recommendation and its supporting argument are each wrong.

1) Confirmed by my own read. UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER.tcl:21-31 is quoted exactly. DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE absence selects devMode 4 (DALI); the TYPE test at :29 overrides to 5 afterwards. So the descriptor property does not decide LSC. Tier 2 agrees: DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE appears in exactly one file of the whole pydevccu paramset corpus (HmIP-RGBW.json). Keying an LSC by device TYPE is what the CCU does — and on the surface our client actually talks to, the sibling discriminator is the same shape: DeviceUtil#isDeviceRGBWController is `device.getDeviceType().getDeviceDescription().getType().equals("RGBW")`, an exact string equality on the device type, not a DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE presence test.

2) WRONG SURFACE for the half that reaches the device. All four cited tcl sites are MASTER config-dialog renderers. getUniversalLightReceiverLSS (hmipUniversalLightReceiverConfigDialogs.tcl:431) emits POWERUP_JUMPTARGET, EVENT_DELAY_*, EVENT_RANDOMTIME_*, ON_MIN_LEVEL, HARDWARE_COLOR_TEMPERATURE_WARM_WHITE/COLD_WHITE — MASTER parameters only. Nothing on that path says whether HUE/SATURATION and COLOR_TEMPERATURE may be commanded together in VALUES, which is the only thing colorTempCombined controls.

3) Where the cited firmware DOES classify LSC capability, it contradicts the label. hmipUniversalLightReceiverConfigDialogs.tcl:442-445 verbatim: `# UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_MAX_CAPABILITIES is always 0 with the HmIP-LSC which is the same as the UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_MAX_CAPABILITIES = 3 of the HmIP-DRG-DALI` / `# Therefore we have to set devMode to 3` / `set devMode 3` / `set dali 1`. In the CCU's own enum (UniversalLightMaxCapabilities) 0 = SWITCH and 3 = DIMMER_RGB; DIMMER_RGBW is 4. So the firmware places the LSC in the DALI family at DIMMER_RGB level — not in a distinct simultaneous-hs+CT class.

4) THE RECOMMENDATION IS CONTRADICTED. The previous agent generalised `string first` (substring) into a firmware convention and recommended strings.Contains. Across ../OpenCCU-Base/**/*.tcl the LSC is tested 130 times: 6 use `string first`, 124 use `string equal $x(PARENT_TYPE) "HmIP-LSC"` or `== "HmIP-LSC"` (e.g. linkHmIP_UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER.tcl:60, and every file under www/config/easymodes/UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER_LSC/). The named boundary (a future "HmIP-LSC-2" taking mode 5) holds at 6 sites and fails at 124. Our EqualFold is the shape the firmware overwhelmingly uses.

5) THE SUPPORTING ARGUMENT IS FALSE AGAINST OUR OWN REGISTRY. "our RGBWLight profile serves LSC and DRDI3 too (rgbw.go:62)" cites a doc comment, not the registry. internal/model/custom/profiles.go registers IPRGBW for exactly two device types: "hmip-lsc" (:1110) and "hmip-rgbw" (:1220). hmip-drdi3 goes to IPDimmer (:949); hmip-drg-dali goes to IPDRGDALI (:959). Inside the constructor's real acceptance set {HmIP-RGBW, HmIP-LSC}, the descriptor-absence rule and the model-string rule are indistinguishable — HmIP-RGBW is the only member carrying DEVICE_OPERATION_MODE. The claimed defect and the claimed refutation are both about a difference that cannot arise.

6) Tier 2 cannot settle it either. HmIP-LSC:1, HmIP-RGBW:1-4 and HmIP-DRG-DALI:1-48 all declare HUE, SATURATION, COLOR_TEMPERATURE, LEVEL, EFFECT, ACTIVITY_STATE in VALUES. The descriptor does not distinguish a combined light from a mode-switched one.

What our code should follow: for identification, the firmware (Tier 1) — exact TYPE equality, which is what we already do. For the capability, neither tier settles it; the value rests on the Python reference (Tier 3 witness, light.py CustomDpIpRGBWColorTempLight), which the code comment names honestly. That is a witness, not authority, and the comment should say so rather than implying a firmware rationale.

all.title: The retryable XML-RPC fault set and the message-substring override decide how often the daemon re-hits a device
all.ourValue: retryable = {-1, -8, -9, -10}; permanent = everything else; five substrings override a retryable code to permanent: "not found", "does not exist", "unknown method", "unknown parameter", "invalid address"
all.firmwareValue: Emitted by the firmware: -1 (default code, XmlRpcException.h:29 — carries BOTH transient and permanent conditions), -2, -3, -4, -5, -6, -7, -8, -9 in rfd/hs485d; -1, -2, -3, -5, -10, -321 on the HmIP legacy surface. -8 and -9 are thrown from exactly one function each, both inside RFDevice::UpdateFirmware(). -10 does not exist anywhere in the C++ sources.
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libXmlRpc/src/XmlRpcException.h:29 (`XmlRpcException(const std::string& message, int code=-1)`); src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:323,328 (setValue → `throw XmlRpcException("Failure")`); src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:1483 (-7), :1492 ("not enough DutyCycle free",-8), :1547 ("Device is out of range",-9); src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:74 et al. ("Unknown instance",-2); src/rfd/RFChannel.cpp:61 ("Unknown paramset",-3), :202 ("Missing parameter "+name, default -1), :208 ("Dependency parameter not found.", default -1), :218,:222 ("Command parameter not found[.]", default -1); src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:120,196 ("Cannot find device instance for given address parameter", default -1); src/libXmlRpc/src/XmlRpcServerConnection.cpp:242 and :337 (`methodName + ": unknown method name"`, faultCode -1); src/hs485d/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:52 et al. ("Failure", default -1), :592 ("Device expected",-4). HmIP side: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.NotificationUtil#getRpcRemoteException, #createTransmissionPendingRpcRemoteException, #getUnknownParamsetRpcRemoteException, #getUnknownParameterValueRpcRemoteException, #getDeviceExpectedException, #createDeleteDeviceRpcRemoteException; de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.communication.rpc.internal.rpc.AnnotationAwareRpcHandler#execute; de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.communication.rpc.internal.format.xml.XmlRpcSerializer#serializeResponse.
all.finding:
The retryable SET is right where the firmware speaks; the OVERRIDE list is half-grounded and misses the cases that matter most.

What the firmware confirms.
-1 must be retryable. Two independent Tier-1 reasons. (a) rfd's setValue throws a bare `XmlRpcException("Failure")` (XmlRpcMethods.cpp:323,328) which takes the default code -1 (XmlRpcException.h:29) — this is the ONLY signal the classic RF path emits for a device that did not answer, and 43 rfd throws plus 22 hs485d throws share it. (b) On the HmIP side, NotificationUtil#getRpcRemoteException maps AP_BUSY, RESPONSE_NAK, TIMEOUT and UNKNOWN to faultCode -1 with faultString "Generic error (<TYPE>)" — AP_BUSY and TIMEOUT are transient by construction. Our comment's reasoning is correct and is now grounded.
-10 exists and is transient. NotificationUtil#createTransmissionPendingRpcRemoteException returns faultCode -10, faultString "Transmission is pending." It appears nowhere in rfd/hs485d — it is an HmIP-RF-only code. Retryable is right.
The permanent codes are all real: -2 ("Unknown instance" rfd, "Invalid device"/"Invalid access point, device or channel" HmIP), -3 ("Unknown paramset" / "Unknown Paramset: <name>"), -4 ("Device expected", rfd/hs485d only), -5, -6 ("Operation not supported"), -7 ("the interface is not able to carry an update"). Defaulting unknown codes to permanent is also right: the HmIP handler emits **-321** for any internal exception that is not an RpcRemoteException (AnnotationAwareRpcHandler#execute), a genuinely permanent condition our catalogue does not name.

Where our rule is narrower than the firmware.
1. -8 and -9 are reachable only through firmware update. "not enough DutyCycle free" (-8) is thrown once, at RFDevice.cpp:1492, and "Device is out of range" (-9) once, at :1547 — both inside RFDevice::UpdateFirmware(), the latter only when the FIRST update frame goes unacked after three tries. Neither is reachable from setValue or putParamset on any interface, and neither exists on the HmIP side at all. Classifying them retryable is harmless but dead outside installFirmware; the fixed 40 s duty-cycle backoff the comment describes will not fire on a normal write, because a duty-cycle rejection during setValue arrives as -1 "Failure" like everything else.
2. Three of the five markers match no firmware fault string on a retryable code. "does not exist" and "invalid address" appear in no fault string in rfd, hs485d, libXmlRpc or the HmIP legacy surface (both appear only in log lines — src/rfd/RFParamset.cpp:84 is a LOG_WARNING). "unknown parameter" matches only code -5 strings ("Unknown parameter"/"Unknown Parameter" in rfd, "Unknown Parameter for value key: <k>" on the HmIP side), which IsRetryable already rejects — so the marker never changes an outcome.
3. Two markers ARE grounded, and precisely: "unknown method" catches libXmlRpc's `methodName + ": unknown method name"`, emitted with faultCode -1 (XmlRpcServerConnection.cpp:242, and :337 inside system.multicall). "not found" catches rfd's `"Dependency parameter not found."` (RFChannel.cpp:208) and `"Command parameter not found[.]"` (:218, :222), all three thrown with the default code -1 and all three permanent (a parameter-definition mismatch on a combined write). These two markers do real work.
4. The list misses permanent -1 messages the firmware does emit. On the same code path: `"Missing parameter " + <name>` (RFChannel.cpp:202), `"Cannot find device instance for given address parameter"` (RFManager.cpp:120,196), plus "Parameter is not readable", "UndefinedValues invalid for this Paramset", "wrong mode", "Insufficient parameters.", "Peering failed. Possibly AES key mismatch." — each -1, each permanent, each currently retried for the ~7 s the comment budgets. Adding "missing parameter" and "cannot find device instance" would be exact-source additions rather than guesses.

The localization worry in the bundle is unfounded. Every fault string on both surfaces is a compiled-in English literal — C++ string literals in rfd/hs485d/libXmlRpc, Java literals in the HmIP legacy surface (NotificationUtil). There is no resource-bundle or catalogue lookup anywhere on the fault path, and none of these strings appear in www/webui/js/lang/*. An English-only marker list is not defeated by the operator's language.

(a) On the retryable set: had -1 been permanent-only in the firmware, NotificationUtil#getRpcRemoteException would have mapped AP_BUSY/TIMEOUT to a distinct transient code — it maps them to -1, so the check discriminates. Symmetrically, had -8/-9 been live on the write path, I would have found them thrown from RFManager::SetValue or PutParamsetValues; the exhaustive throw inventory over src/rfd finds exactly one site each, both in UpdateFirmware. (b) On the marker list: the way to see the list is wrong is a firmware fault string that is transient AND matches a marker, or permanent-on--1 and misses. The first search returned nothing (the transient -1 strings are "Failure" and "Generic error (…)", matching no marker — had the list contained "failure", "timeout" or "generic error", every real duty-cycle and unreach retry would be suppressed). The second returned seven hits, listed above. Both halves of the control fired.

UPHELD IN SUBSTANCE — I re-read every quote and they transcribe correctly — but the boundary is drawn in the wrong place and three citations are misattributed.

WHAT I CHECKED AND CONFIRMED MYSELF.
- XmlRpcException.h:29 default code is -1, verbatim as quoted. rfd setValue throws a bare `XmlRpcException("Failure")` at exactly 323 and 328.
- -8 and -9: grep across src/rfd and src/hs485d returns one site each (RFDevice.cpp:1492, :1547), both after `bool RFDevice::UpdateFirmware()` at :1470 and before the next function. "not enough DutyCycle free" is the ONLY duty-cycle throw in rfd. -10 and -321 appear in no C++ file.
- I enumerated every default-code (implicit -1) XmlRpcException message in rfd + hs485d + libXmlRpc. The complete set is: Failure / Failure. Wrong parameter. / Failure: link successfully added, but SetLinkInfo failed / Cannot find device instance for given address parameter / Command parameter not found[.] / Dependency parameter not found. / Missing parameter <n> / Bootloader in device <s> didn't start / Unable to load updatefile / Unable to set datarate to 100k / Firmware update aborted / Peering failed. Possibly AES key mismatch. / Parameter callerId must be of type string / type error[: expected a struct|an array] / range error: array index too large. Cross-checked against our five markers: the only hits are the three "...not found" parameter-definition throws and libXmlRpc's "unknown method name" — all permanent. NO TRANSIENT -1 MESSAGE MATCHES A MARKER on these surfaces. "does not exist" and "invalid address" match nothing anywhere I searched.

CORRECTION 1 — the -8 gap has a mechanism the previous agent missed. Saying "neither exists on the HmIP side at all" understates it. BackendNotificationType declares DUTY_CYCLE(14), UNREACH(12), STACK_BUSY(13) and ROUTING_BUSY(31) as first-class notification types, and NotificationUtil#getRpcRemoteException(JsonObject) maps NONE of them: they fall through its `default:` arm, keeping faultCode -1 with faultString "Generic error (DUTY_CYCLE)" / "(UNREACH)". So an HmIP duty-cycle rejection is a -1 by construction, not merely by omission — and retry.go:450's DutyCycleDelay branch is unreachable on BOTH surfaces, not just outside installFirmware. Same for DeviceOutOfRange/-9.

CORRECTION 2 — the permanent-message gap list is incomplete in the same direction. That `default:` arm also flattens MISSING_NON_OPTIONAL_PARAMETER(25), INVALID_DEVICE_TYPE(18) and SUBSYSTEM_GET_CONFIG_NOT_SUPPORTED(16) to -1. All three are permanent and NONE is reachable by any string marker, because the message is "Generic error (<ENUM_NAME>)" — SCREAMING_SNAKE, so "not found" (with a space) can never match. A marker list cannot close this gap at all; only a code-plus-notification-type distinction could, and the legacy surface does not expose the type.

CORRECTION 3 — misattributed citations. (a) "Device expected",-4 is at src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:908 and :959 and src/hs485d/HS485Manager.cpp:593 — NOT src/hs485d/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:592, which is a doc comment for the ping/pong method. (b) NotificationUtil#getDeviceExpectedException was listed as evidence for -4; it emits **-5** ("A device address was expected but a chanel address was given"). Both are permanent so behaviour is unaffected, but our XMLRPCFaultAddressExpected(-4) comment describes the rfd condition only. (c) -6 "Operation not supported" is at RFParamset.cpp:262, which the previous agent asserted without a line.

CORRECTION 4 — the localization claim is overstated. XmlRpcSerializer#serializeResponse writes faultString = `response.getErrorCause().getMessage()`, i.e. Throwable.getMessage(), which for RpcRemoteException is its FIRST constructor argument — an English literal for every NotificationUtil construction (the `internalException.toString()` second argument never reaches the wire). But on the -321 path AnnotationAwareRpcHandler#execute passes `e.getTargetException()` straight through, so an arbitrary internal Throwable's message becomes the wire faultString and can be JVM- or library-localized. -321 is already permanent under our default, so there is no behavioural risk — but "every fault string on both surfaces is a compiled-in English literal" is not true as stated.

CORRECTION 5 — a scope boundary that was not named. pkg/hmerr.IsRetryable is shared by all backends, including CuxdBackend (BIN-RPC) and HomegearBackend. Neither emits faults from this firmware tree. Nothing here grounds the classification, or the marker list, for CUxD or Homegear; that is unverified.

UNSOURCED IN OUR OWN COMMENTS (flagged, not part of the rule): errors.go:283 attributes "Unbekannter Parameter oder Wert" to "the catalogue" for -5; that string appears nowhere in ../OpenCCU-Base. Likewise the symbolic names "INSUFFICIENT_DUTYCYCLE" and "DEVICE_OUT_OF_RANGE" in the -8/-9 comments are not firmware identifiers — the firmware strings are "not enough DutyCycle free" and "Device is out of range", and the HmIP enum name is DUTY_CYCLE.

What our code should follow: the firmware (Tier 1) on both surfaces. The retryable set {-1,-8,-9,-10} and default-permanent are correct as written and should stay. The marker list should keep "not found" and "unknown method" (each grounded on an exact -1 fault string), may drop "does not exist", "invalid address" and "unknown parameter" as dead, and cannot be extended to cover the HmIP "Generic error (X)" family at all.

all.firmwareValue: none — the CCU declares no window and no poll cadence for the per-device communication test
all.missingInput: The test's own completion/timeout semantics live in ReGaHss, which ships as a closed binary; DevStartComTest / ChnStartComTest / dom.TestRunningIDs() / TestCompletedTime() / LastTestCompletedTime() are ReGaHss built-ins with no source in this tree.
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/www/rega/esp/channels.fn:16,21 (o.DevStartComTest() / o.ChnStartComTest()); www/rega/esp/system.fn:20-31 (TestRunning), :472-545 (TestReadyIDs / TestRunningIDs / TestCompletedTime / LastTestCompletedTime); www/rega/pages/tabs/admin/views/newdevicechannelsloader.htm:85-108 (ExistComTestDP, testrunning, testtime). Wire side, Tier 2: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/rftypes/rf_dim_1l_644_le_v2_4.xml:171 (frame TOGGLE_INSTALL_TEST) and :375-379 (parameter INSTALL_TEST, operations="write", ui_flags="internal", set request=TOGGLE_INSTALL_TEST); rf_wds_v1_1.xml:176 (parameter INSTALL_TEST, operations="event"). Frame-level timing, Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/BidcosFrameWaitTime.h:19-21; queueing for sleeping devices: src/rfd/RFDevice.h:438 (after_wakeup_queue), :381 (CheckWakeup).
all.finding:
The comment is accurate about our own code and unfounded as a statement about the CCU — those are two different claims and only the first is checkable.

In-repo half, verified: CcuBackend.TestDevice substitutes exactly 30 and 2 when the caller passes non-positive values (ccu_extended.go:157-162), and the adapter passes 0/0. The comment describes the code correctly. Nothing in the adapter pins it, so the numbers can drift out from under the comment, but today they agree.

Firmware half, silent: the CCU carries no timeout for this test. The test is driven entirely through ReGaHss built-ins — DevStartComTest / ChnStartComTest to start (channels.fn:16,21), dom.TestRunningIDs() membership and a TestCompletedTime() timestamp advance to observe (system.fn:472-545, newdevicechannelsloader.htm:85-108) — and ReGaHss is a closed binary. Our two ReGa scripts do exactly what the CCU's own pages do: start, then poll for the timestamp to move past the start. The WebUI's own polling carries no deadline either; iseRefresher.js takes its interval as a constructor argument and is never instantiated anywhere in the tree, and writeTestField is called at newdevicechannelsloader.htm:175 but defined nowhere — the WebUI's client-side com-test timing is not present in these sources.

What the firmware DOES bound is one level lower and does not support 30 s as sufficient. Per-frame ACK waiting in rfd is WAIT_TIME_DEFAULT 1500 ms, WAIT_TIME_SINGLE_BURST 4500 ms, WAIT_TIME_TRIPLE_BURST 12500 ms (BidcosFrameWaitTime.h:19-21). For a device in WAKEUP mode there is no bound at all: the frame is parked in RFDevice's after_wakeup_queue (RFDevice.h:438) and flushed by CheckWakeup() (:381) whenever the device next transmits on its own schedule. On the wire the test is a per-device-type parameter — INSTALL_TEST, written for actuators via the TOGGLE_INSTALL_TEST frame, event-only for battery sensors — and the device XMLs declare no time bound.

So the honest reading of our 30 s: it is a client-side patience budget that covers a burst-capable mains device (12.5 s worst case plus ReGa round-trips) and cannot cover a sleeping device, which may legitimately take minutes. The comment's damage note ("too short a window reports a healthy battery device as unreachable") is therefore right, and no firmware value would let us pick a number that avoids it — a WAKEUP device's answer time is unbounded by construction.
all.negativeControl: Had a firmware-declared window existed, it would have surfaced as a numeric timeout beside the com-test bookkeeping — a constant in the ReGa test functions in www/rega/esp/system.fn or channels.fn, a PeriodicalExecuter interval in the WebUI page that renders the test column, or a per-test timer in rfd beside INSTALL_TEST. I searched all three: the ReGa functions carry no numbers at all, the only WebUI poller (iseRefresher.js) is never constructed, and rfd's only timing constants on that path are the generic frame wait times, which are not test-specific. The search was capable of returning a number — it returned the frame wait times from a neighbouring path, which is the control firing — and returned none for the test itself.

all.title: The check_connection default constant and its own documentation disagree
all.ourValue: defaultCheckConnectionSlot = 30 s (constant, jobs.go:202); doc comment above it argues 120 s; divergence table at :146 says 30 s. Separately, an undocumented second probe runs at 15 s per interface.
all.firmwareValue: none — the CCU imposes no time-based upper bound on callback-probe cadence. Its only de-registration rule is 10 consecutive failed event deliveries, each bounded by a 10 000 ms client timeout and retried once.
all.missingInput: The bundle asked for the registration-keepalive timeout that would be the upper bound for both justifications. It does not exist: the CCU's rule is a failure counter evaluated on the next event, not a clock, so no firmware number can adjudicate 30 s against 120 s.
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:29 (m_pClient->setTimeout(10000)), :39-98 (Handle — invoked only with queued event messages, no timer), :70-74 (one retry on transport failure), :79-82 (m_clientSendFailureCount >= 10 → m_clientUnreachable, with the source comment `//10 chosen by dice`); src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.cpp:110-129 (unreachable handlers erased inside ReportEvent, then SaveXmlRpcHandlers), :448-463 (SaveXmlRpcHandlers skips unreachable), :39 and :482 (removeUnreachableClients, config key "Remove Unreachable Clients", default "true"), :539-542 (HSSManager::Ping → ReportEvent("CENTRAL","PONG",callerId)); src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:1197-1218 (XmlRpcMethodPing) and src/hs485d/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:592-614 (identical).
all.finding:
The firmware cannot settle this, and the reason it cannot is itself the useful result.

The CCU never expires a callback registration on time. HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher::Handle (HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:39-98) is driven purely by queued event messages — there is no ticker, no periodic poke, nothing that fires on a quiet interface. A delivery failure increments m_clientSendFailureCount, and only at 10 consecutive failures does m_clientUnreachable flip (:79-82, `//10 chosen by dice`). The removal is then performed inside HSSManager::ReportEvent (HSSManager.cpp:110-129), i.e. only when a next event exists to deliver, and it is gated on removeUnreachableClients, whose default is "true" (:39, :482). ping is equally passive: HSSManager::Ping (:539-542) does nothing but emit a PONG event, and rfd's and hs485d's XmlRpcMethodPing forward straight to it.

So the deadline our poll cadence must beat is not a firmware timeout. It is event-count-driven and, on a silent interface, never arrives at all. Neither the 30 s in the constant nor the 120 s in the doc comment is constrained from above by anything in the CCU. Both justifications are detection-latency choices, and the doc comment's implied premise — that some CCU-side window has to be caught "within two ticks" — has no firmware referent.

What I can settle is the in-repo confusion, and it is worse than the bundle states. The doc comment at jobs.go:196-201 is visibly corrupted: its first sentence, "DefaultCheckConnectionSlot mirrors\n// cadence.", has lost its object. Its body argues 120 s; the constant on the next line is 30 s; the divergence table at :146 says 30 s and agrees with the constant. The table is right and the doc comment is stale.

And there is a third number neither the comment nor the table mentions. internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:62 declares connectionCheckerInterval = 15 s, and :1054 runs a standalone per-interface ticker at that cadence calling CheckConnectionAvailability(ctx, false) followed by IsCallbackAlive() — the same three signals the 30 s job evaluates. The 30 s job (jobs.go:493, body at :540-575) differs only in passing handlePingPong=true, so it is the one that emits a correlated ping token. The effective per-interface liveness cadence is therefore 15 s, not 30 s and not 120 s; the doc comment describes a single-probe architecture the daemon does not have. Whichever number a reader tunes, they are tuning the slower of two probes.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU enforced a keepalive deadline, it would appear as a timestamp or timer beside the handler bookkeeping — a last-contact field in the xmlrpc_handlers map, a periodic sweep in HSSManager, or a timeout branch in the dispatcher's Handle loop. All three places were read in full. The dispatcher holds only m_clientSendFailureCount and m_clientUnreachable (HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.h:32-33), HSSManager's only removal path is inside ReportEvent, and the one time value on the path is the 10 s per-call client timeout. The search would have returned a duration had one existed — it returned a counter, which is the control discriminating rather than confirming.

all.title: callbackFreshness = 180 s rests on a comment-claimed scheduler tick
all.ourValue: callbackFreshness = 180 s, justified in the comment as "15s scheduler tick × 12"
all.firmwareValue: none — the CCU emits nothing spontaneously on a quiet interface. PONG is reactive to our own ping; there is no firmware keepalive to size a window against.
all.missingInput: A firmware-side spontaneous-delivery interval. It does not exist, so no firmware value bounds 180 s. For CUxD the question is doubly unanswerable here: CUxD is a third-party add-on and is not in the OCCU sources at all.
all.citation: Tier 1: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.cpp:539-542 (HSSManager::Ping is one statement — ReportEvent("CENTRAL","PONG",callerId)); src/libhsscomm/HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:39-98 (Handle runs only over queued event messages; no timer, no periodic emission), :29 (10 000 ms client timeout), :79-82 (10-failure de-registration); src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.h:161 (documented contract: event(CENTRAL_SERIAL, "pong", callerId)); src/rfd/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:1197-1218 and src/hs485d/XmlRpcMethods.cpp:592-614 (both ping methods forward to Manager::Ping and return true).
all.finding:
The firmware answers the bundle's question with a flat no, and that changes what the constant means rather than what it should be.

There is no CCU-side keepalive. HSSManager::Ping (HSSManager.cpp:539-542) is a single ReportEvent emitting PONG — purely a reply to our own call, identically routed in rfd (XmlRpcMethods.cpp:1197-1218) and hs485d (:592-614). The event dispatcher has no timer: Handle (HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:39-98) is entered only with queued event messages. On an interface where no device reports, the CCU sends nothing, ever. Our own ping is therefore not merely one contributor to the freshness timestamp — it is the only one. That makes 180 s purely a multiple of our probe cadence, and nothing in the firmware can raise or lower it.

The comment's arithmetic survives; its label does not. There IS a 15 s cadence, and 15 × 12 = 180 checks out — but it is not a scheduler tick. It is connectionCheckerInterval (internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:62), driven by a standalone time.Ticker at :1054, and the code immediately above that ticker (:1042-1046) explains that it deliberately is NOT scheduler-driven, because reg.StartAll runs before WireCentrals and scheduler.Add would reject the late registration. I found no 15 s value in internal/scheduler at all; the package has no such constant. So the premise is true and the attribution is wrong, which is exactly the shape of claim that survives review and gets cited later.

One substantive gap the comment does not cover, and the firmware sharpens it. That 15 s probe calls CheckConnectionAvailability(ctx, false) — handlePingPong false, so no correlation token is recorded (interface_client.go:981-985). The CCU answers with a PONG regardless, because Ping is unconditional, so the timestamp does get refreshed on the 15 s cadence; the 30 s check_connection job (jobs.go:540-575) is the only one that also correlates. The window is thus 12 uncorrelated probes or 6 correlated ones, not the single-probe picture the comment paints.

And a consequence worth recording: because the CCU de-registers a handler after 10 consecutive failed deliveries (HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher.cpp:79-82) rather than on a clock, by the time a 180 s silence has elapsed on a genuinely broken registration the CCU may already have dropped us and will send nothing further. The window is not racing a firmware timeout; it is the only thing that will ever notice.

For CUxD over BIN-RPC the same 180 s applies via Capabilities.PingPong, and Tier 1 is silent by construction — CUxD is a third-party add-on with no source in the OCCU tree. That leg is unverified, not confirmed.
all.negativeControl: Had a firmware keepalive existed, it would appear as a periodic emitter — a timer or Actor scheduling in HSSXmlRpcEventDispatcher, a heartbeat branch in HSSManager::ReportEvent, or a ping-initiating call in rfd's main loop rather than only the server-side ping method. I read Handle end to end and grepped rfd, hs485d and libhsscomm for pong/keepalive/timeout on the callback path: the only hits are the reactive Ping methods and the 10 s client timeout. The check was able to return a periodic emitter — it returned a reactive one, which is the discriminating outcome. Separately, the '15 s scheduler tick' premise was tested against internal/scheduler, which carries no 15 s constant, while ccu_wiring.go:62 does — so the check distinguished a true cadence from a false attribution rather than confirming both.

all.finding: Site B (500 ms) is contradicted on the surface its own comment names. The comment claims 500 ms is the typical CCU-callback round-trip; the CCU's BidCos layer will not conclude a frame's response window in under 1000 ms (explicit clamp, BidcosFrame.cpp:158-160) and budgets 1500/4500/12500 ms by frame class. The 500 ms is also on the wrong surface relative to its origin: in the Python family 0.5 s is the command-throttle burst-detection window per interface, and we already port that faithfully as ThrottleConfig.BurstWindow (internal/client/reliability/throttle.go:56-58). The optimistic-package copy is a second, wrongly-justified home for the same number, and it is dead: `/usr/bin/grep -rn 'OptimisticBurstWindow|DefaultBurstWindow'` over the repo returns only the constant, the never-read field generic.DataPointFields.OptimisticBurstWindow (datapoint.go:120-128), and burst_window_test.go. Site A (30 s) is narrowed rather than wrong. The firmware nowhere states a command-acknowledgement window; it states component ceilings, and 30 s covers every one of them on the awake path (worst BidCos frame wait 12.5 s; HmIP legacy setValue self-limits at the shipped 20 s and then faults, e.g. -10 "Transmission is pending."). Note the composition, since we arm the rollback timer BEFORE the wire call (datapoint.go:1773 then :1790): a worst-case HmIP CCU-side block consumes 20 s of the 30 s, leaving ~10 s for the event to arrive through a dispatcher that itself allows 10 s + one retry. The boundary where it becomes false: for a device whose effective rx mode is WAKEUP without BURST, PutData queues the frame and returns success without any wire transaction, and the firmware imposes no bound on the wait for the next wake-up — HM-CC-TC SETPOINT is a real writable parameter in that class. There the 30 s timer fires and rolls back a write that will succeed. Rollback is local only (datapoint.go:1657-1690 mutates cached value and notifies callbacks; no wire write), hence reachesDevice=false.
all.negativeControl: Had our 500 ms been right, BidcosFrameWaitTime.h would have carried a sub-second frame wait and CheckReceiveComplete would have had no 1000 ms floor — both are explicit literals I read in a file that could equally have said 300 or 500, so the check discriminates. Had our 30 s been too short on the awake path, Legacy.ResponseTimeout in the shipped crRFD.conf would have read above 30 (it reads 20) or the concentrator's abort ceiling would have exceeded 30000 ms. Had the wakeup path been bounded, RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand::PutData would have called SendFrame rather than QueueAfterWakeupFrame for RxNeedsWakeup devices, and RFDevice would have carried a timer on the wakeup queue — it carries only a depth cap of 10.
all.challengeNote: DEMOTED from contradicted to narrowed. The contradiction leg misreads its own citation. BidcosFrame::CheckReceiveComplete returns true at 'if(GetResponse(0))return true;' (BidcosFrame.cpp:154) BEFORE the 1000 ms clamp at :158-160 is ever evaluated. The clamp therefore bounds how long the CCU keeps waiting when NO response has arrived — a give-up floor — and WAIT_TIME_DEFAULT/SINGLE_BURST/TRIPLE_BURST are the budgets SendFrame hands the wait loop, not observed latencies. A device that ACKs in 80 ms completes the frame in 80 ms. So the firmware says nothing about "typical CCU-callback round-trip latency", which is exactly and only what our comment claims. That leg is tier1-silent, not contradicted: the missing input is an observed/typical latency, which this tree does not carry anywhere I could find. Two further legs of the original finding are not firmware groundings at all and should not have been folded under a tier-1 verdict: (a) the deadness of the constant is a repo fact — I re-ran it, '/usr/bin/grep -rn "OptimisticBurstWindow|DefaultBurstWindow"' returns only tracker.go:44, burst_window_test.go, the field declaration at generic/datapoint.go:120-128, and the compiled binary; '/usr/bin/grep -rn "\.OptimisticBurstWindow"' over internal/ and pkg/ returns nothing, and 'OptimisticTimeout:' is never set anywhere, so 30 s is unconditionally the production value; (b) the "wrong home" argument rests wholly on aiohomematic, a Tier-3 witness — correctly labelled there, and I confirm the docstring reads as a command-rate window, but a witness cannot carry a tier-1 verdict. UPHELD, with the checks: the 30 s narrowing survives. I opened every cited line. The awake-path ceilings are as quoted (12.5 s worst BidCos frame wait; two attempts then a 5 s fail-counter hold; the wait loop aborts above 30 s). The HmIP self-block is real and synchronous — setValue blocks on the response queue for the shipped 20 s and then throws — and our composition does arm the rollback timer at datapoint.go:1773 before the wire call at :1790, so the CCU-side block is spent inside our own 30 s. UPHELD, and I verified it independently: the WAKEUP boundary. PutData queues the frame and 'continue's (RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:235-238), the function then returns true at :263, and the only state change is ValueStore::SetStoredValue (ValueStore.cpp:41), which stores and marks dirty and emits no client event — so nothing confirms the write until the device wakes and SendAfterWakeupFrames (RFDevice.cpp:1327) runs, which the firmware never bounds. Our 30 s timer fires and rolls back a write that will succeed. ONE SCOPE CORRECTION the original missed: RFDevice::RxNeedsWakeup (RFDevice.cpp:1859-1872) consults a temporary rx mode and rx_mode_default before falling through to the descriptor, so a Tier-2 declaration of rx_modes="CONFIG,WAKEUP" does not by itself decide the runtime path — it does for rf_cc_tc (no BURST bit, so the fall-through applies), but the general claim "declared WAKEUP ⇒ queue path" is Tier-1 conditional, not descriptor-decidable.

all.title: Value-cache TTLs cite the reference's MAX_CACHE_AGE and then use three different numbers
all.site: internal/model/device/value_cache.go:19-45 (valuesCacheTTL=0, masterCacheTTL=30m, sentinelCacheTTL=5m; TTL selection at ttlFor(), :98-107; freshness at cacheEntry.fresh(), :63-69, where ttl<=0 means never expires)
all.ourValue: valuesCacheTTL = 0 (never expires); masterCacheTTL = 30 min; sentinelCacheTTL = 5 min. Comment attributes them to "the Python reference implementation's const.py:308 (MAX_CACHE_AGE = 10s)".
all.firmwareValue: CCU-side VALUES read cache: VALUE_CACHE_TIME = 2000 ms, unconditional, in both rfd and hs485d. CCU-side MASTER cache: no TTL at all (completeness-based). No MASTER-change callback exists on either interface family.
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.h:23 'VALUE_CACHE_TIME=2000 //!< Maximales Alter des Wertes in ms fuer das Bedienen einer Abfrage aus dem Cache ohne Kommunikation', enforced at src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:155 'if(inst->GetAge(value_id)<VALUE_CACHE_TIME){ return inst->GetStoredValue(value_id, param); }'; identical constant and use in the wired daemon at src/hs485d/HS485PhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.h:22 and .cpp:91. A VALUES parameter with no get request frame is ALWAYS served from the CCU's own store: src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand.cpp:152-154 'if(get_request_frame.id.empty()){ return inst->GetStoredValue(value_id, param); }'. There is no force-fresh escape: getValue's 3-arg mode only changes the return shape (src/libhsscomm/HSSParameter.cpp:252-268). MASTER: RFConfigData's two candidate validity constants are both commented out (src/rfd/RFConfigData.cpp:19-20 '//const uint32_t RFConfigData::VALID_TIME=60000;' / '=10000;'), and re-reads are gated on completeness, not age — src/rfd/RFLogicalInstance.cpp:34-44 'if(!cd.MustBeRead(list))return &cd;' with src/rfd/RFConfigData.cpp:514-529 testing for missing chunks; MASTER reads come through src/rfd/RFPhysicalDataInterfaceConfig.cpp:65-75. Contrast: the wired daemon does age its config cache — src/hs485d/HS485EEpromCache.cpp:25 'const unsigned int HS485EEPromCache::VALID_TIME=300000;'. No MASTER-change event: src/rfd/RFChannel.cpp:73-89 PutParamsetValues makes no client callback, its only side-effect being GetDevice()->CheckConfigPendingEvent() when the commit fails, which emits a VALUES event (src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:1040 'SendInternalValueEvent("CONFIG_PENDING", val);'). The updateDevice callback exists but is emitted only for link changes (src/rfd/RFChannel.cpp:756,868 with UPDATE_HINT_LINKS) and OTAU rebuild behind a flag defaulting false (src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:1619-1620, src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:219-220); the only hints are UPDATE_HINT_ALL=0 / UPDATE_HINT_LINKS=1 (src/libhsscomm/HSSManager.h:47). HmIP is the same shape: CONFIG_PENDING travels as a VALUES parameter event — HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.LegacyNotificationHandler sets device.parameter.name to CONFIG_PENDING. Witness (Tier 3): ../aiohomematic/const.py:308 'MAX_CACHE_AGE: Final = 10' is real and is on our VALUES surface — it suppresses a re-read in ../aiohomematic/model/data_point.py:1153.
all.finding: Both firmware questions are answered. (1) The CCU does impose a minimum re-read interval on VALUES: 2000 ms, unconditional, in rfd and hs485d alike, and for a parameter without a get request frame it never touches the radio at all. (2) There is no MASTER-change event to subscribe to instead of polling — on BidCos putParamset(MASTER) raises nothing, updateDevice carries only ALL/LINKS hints and is not emitted for config writes, and CONFIG_PENDING is a maintenance-channel VALUES flag meaning "a config write is outstanding", not "MASTER changed". HmIP mirrors that. So masterCacheTTL is genuinely the only mechanism available; Tier 1 does not decide its length. What Tier 1 does refute is the premise the block is written under. The cited const.py:308 exists and reads 10 s, and it sits on our VALUES surface — but we set that tier to 0, i.e. never expire, which is the one value neither the firmware nor the reference uses. And the "CCU-radio-cost policy, every miss is a wire call on a shared radio" framing is false for MASTER on BidCos: the CCU's own config cache has no TTL and re-reads only when chunks are missing, so a MASTER re-read after our 30 minutes normally costs zero radio and simply reads back the CCU's own copy (which the WebUI updates in place on an operator change, so visibility still works). The boundary for valuesCacheTTL=0 runs exactly where the comment puts it — "correct only while push delivery is healthy" — and the firmware gives no signal that would report a lost callback registration, so nothing in the system can move that boundary back. Composed with a never-expiring daemon cache, the CCU's own 2 s freshness guarantee is unreachable: we never ask again. reachesDevice=false: a stale served value misleads readers but is never written back on this path.
all.negativeControl: Had the CCU imposed no re-read interval, RFPhysicalDataInterfaceCommand::GetData would have gone straight to GetFrameDescription/SendFrame with no age test — instead it carries a named constant with an explanatory comment, and the same constant appears independently in hs485d, so the check could have come back empty and did not. Had a MASTER-change notification existed, ReportUpdate would have had a call site in PutParamsetValues or a third UPDATE_HINT_* constant would exist; there are exactly two hints and two emitters, both unrelated to config writes. Had the CCU aged its MASTER cache, RFConfigData::VALID_TIME would be live rather than commented out and MustBeRead would test a timestamp — hs485d shows what that looks like when it is true (VALID_TIME=300000), which is the discriminating counter-example.
all.challengeNote: Verdict kept at narrowed, but two legs demoted and one scope limit added that the original stated as unqualified fact. UPHELD, all cited lines opened: the 2000 ms constant, the no-get-frame short-circuit, the 3-arg mode shape-only change, the two commented-out MASTER validity constants, the completeness gate, the wired 300000 ms contrast, and the absence of any MASTER-change callback on BidCos. I also closed the wrong-surface question the original left implicit — I traced XmlRpcMethodGetValue through HSSParameter::GetValue to physical_type->Get, so VALUE_CACHE_TIME really does govern the getValue our code calls. I independently enumerated every UPDATE_HINT call site in src/rfd and src/libhsscomm: exactly three, none on a config write. DEMOTION 1 — SCOPE. "The CCU imposes a minimum re-read interval on VALUES: 2000 ms" is true for BidCos-RF and BidCos-Wired and for nothing else. HmIP getValue does not pass through rfd at all; the general branch returns DeviceUtil.getValue from HMIPServer's own state with no age constant, and CUxD (BIN-RPC) is not in this tree. Our valuesCacheTTL applies to every interface uniformly, so the tier-1 grounding covers at most two of the interface families it is being used to justify. DEMOTION 2 — STRAW MAN. The finding refutes a "CCU-radio-cost policy, every miss is a wire call on a shared radio" framing. That sentence is not at the cited site: value_cache.go:19-45 says nothing about radio, and '/usr/bin/grep -rn radio internal/model/device/' returns one unrelated hit (definitionexport/export.go:40). The nearest real project text is docs/caching.md:15-17, which is already correctly qualified — "Every value read that actually goes to the radio counts against the CCU's DutyCycle budget" — and docs/caching.md:49 already states MASTER paramsets load from caches with effectively zero radio. Refuting a premise the project does not assert produces a finding that reads as a defect and is not one. WHAT TIER 1 ACTUALLY SETTLES, stated cleanly: (a) there is no MASTER-change event to subscribe to instead of polling, so masterCacheTTL is the only mechanism available; (b) a MASTER re-read on BidCos normally costs no radio, because the CCU's own config cache has no TTL and re-reads only on missing chunks. Neither fact constrains 30 min, 5 min or 0 — those remain policy, and "narrowed" must not be read as tier-1 endorsement of any of the three numbers. The MAX_CACHE_AGE = 10 leg is Tier 3 (I confirmed const.py:308 reads exactly that) and refutes nothing the firmware says. FINALLY, one correction to the composition claim: "composed with a never-expiring daemon cache, the CCU's own 2 s freshness guarantee is unreachable — we never ask again" overstates it. fresh() at :63-69 does return true forever for ttl<=0, but there is an escape the original did not account for — valueCache.invalidate (:143), exposed as Device.InvalidateCache (:390) and used after a write. The staleness window is unbounded only for entries nobody invalidates.

all.title: DeviceDescriptionRegistry.All documents an address ordering it does not produce
all.ourValue: doc comment: "All returns a snapshot of descriptions for iface, ordered by address"; body ranges over a Go map with no sort
all.firmwareValue: the CCU's own listDevices IS address-ordered: src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:382-398 iterates `t_dev_instances` (src/rfd/RFManager.h:591 — `typedef std::map<std::string, RFDevice*>`, i.e. sorted ascending by the string address), appending each device via RFDevice::Describe (src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:230) and then the team instances at the end
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.cpp:382-398; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFManager.h:591; ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFDevice.cpp:230-260
all.finding: The comment is false about our own function — verified by reading it: internal/central/registry/device_description.go:96-104 has no sort call, unlike the sibling registries (internal/central/registry/device.go:83, model_registry.go:53). The CCU source is silent about what OUR snapshot must be ordered by; it only settles the adjacent fact that the wire snapshot the registry is filled from arrives in ascending-address order (std::map iteration), so "ordered by address" is a property that existed upstream and is lost at this seam. The bundle names the callers' order requirement as the missing input; that input is readable in this repo, so I measured it rather than guessing. Of the thirteen call sites, ten are order-independent (448, 657, 678, 771, 1539, 1604, 1752, 1792 build maps or delete/filter over the whole set; configuration.go:266 sorts its own output). Three return the map order to their caller: device.go:717 GetVirtualRemoteAddresses, :732 GetVirtualRemotes, :1839 IdentifyDevicesMissingParamsets. One is genuinely first-match-wins: device.go:756 IdentifyChannel returns the first address containing `text`, so with two substring matches the answer is nondeterministic per process run. `grep -rn '\.IdentifyChannel(' internal/ cmd/ | grep -v _test` shows the only production IdentifyChannel is registry.ModelRegistry's (hub_wiring.go:1337) — the DeviceCoordinator one and all three order-returning functions have test-only callers today. So this is a latent false claim, not a live defect: no production consumer currently depends on the documented order. Fix is either the sort or the comment; adding the sort also restores the property the wire already had.
all.negativeControl: Had the claim been true, the body would carry a sort.Slice on Address (as device.go:83 and model_registry.go:53 do) and the grep for call sites would show at least one production consumer reading position — e.g. `out[0]` or a diff between two passes. Neither is present. Had the CCU emitted devices in an undefined order, RFManager would have iterated an unordered container (std::unordered_map / vector append order) instead of std::map.

all.title: Registry.Released resolves a device address by first-matching central, with no rule for the collision the codebase says exists
all.ourValue: Released(address) walks List() (sorted by central name, central_registry.go:309-312) and returns the release verdict of the FIRST central whose ModelRegistry holds that address — i.e. it treats a bare device address as a key that is unique across centrals
all.firmwareValue: three distinct address spaces are generated per-CCU, not globally: (1) the BidCos central device's serial is the compile-time literal `serial="BidCoS-RF";` — every rfd on every CCU names its own central device that; (2) an HmIP group's legacy device address is `"INT" + <group id, zero-padded to 7, truncated to the last 7 digits if longer>` — a per-CCU group-id counter; (3) the legacy virtual remote's device id is `"HmIP-RCV-" + vrcNr` with `private static Integer vrcNr = 1` incremented per instance, so HmIP-RCV-1 exists on every CCU
all.citation: ../OpenCCU-Base/src/rfd/RFCentral.cpp:37 (`serial="BidCoS-RF";`, alongside `type="HM-RCV-50";` at :36); HMIPServer de.eq3.ccu.groupdevice.service.internal.GroupDeviceAddressHelper#getVirtualDeviceAddressFromGroup and #getGroupIdFromVirtualDeviceAddress; HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.VirtualRemoteControl (DEVICE_ID_BASE = "HmIP-RCV-", the vrcNr counter in the constructor)
all.finding: I read our site first: Released takes only an address, and the loop `return`s inside the first iteration that finds the address — it does not continue to look for a second holder, so on a collision the answer is whichever central sorts first by name, and renaming a central changes the verdict. interface_id.go:19-21's claim that addresses repeat across CCUs is correct and I could ground all three examples it names. The group case is worse than the comment suggests: getVirtualDeviceAddressFromGroup truncates ids longer than 7 digits to their last 7, so INT addresses can collide even within one CCU. The VCU-prefixed HmIP device addresses are the one space that is NOT per-CCU — HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.legacy.bidcos.rpc.internal.DeviceUtil#getDeviceLegacyAddress derives them from the device id by stripping a configured prefix, and the device id is device-borne, so those do not collide. Conclusion for our code: an address-only lookup is not admissible for BidCoS-RF, INT*, or HmIP-RCV-*. Released needs the same scoping every other registry uses — a (central_name, address) or WireInterfaceID key — or, if the caller genuinely has only an address, it must resolve every holder and combine (a device held anywhere is not released).
all.negativeControl: Had device addresses been globally unique, the allocators would derive each address from a device-borne identifier with no per-central counter — as DeviceUtil#getDeviceLegacyAddress does for VCU addresses. Instead RFCentral hard-codes one literal serial into every rfd build, and both the group and virtual-remote address builders start their counters at a per-CCU/per-process origin.
all.challengeNote: UPHELD, and independently reproduced. I read our site first: the loop returns on the first holder, so on a colliding address the verdict is whichever central sorts first by name, and renaming a central silently changes the answer. All three firmware citations are verbatim and on the right surface — RFCentral.cpp is the rfd central device that appears in listDevices, GroupDeviceAddressHelper is the legacy virtual-device address minter, and VirtualRemoteControl's id is fed straight into the legacy DeviceDescription address. Two independent corroborations inside our own tree that the reader did not cite: internal/routingkey/uniqueid.go:40-44 already keeps a `virtualRemoteRoots` set of exactly {"BidCoS-RF", "BidCoS-Wir", "HmIP-RCV-1"} because "the channel address itself repeats across CCUs", and internal/central/adapter/hub_wiring.go:1462-1466 already carries the INT-prefix rule. A recorded live-CCU listAllDetail also shows the BidCoS-RF device present with type HM-RCV-50, matching the two RFCentral.cpp literals. Callers that inherit the defect: internal/central/adapter/devices.go:171 and through it internal/north/rest/handlers/devices.go:640,659,687, snapshot.go:174 and internal/north/mcp/tools.go:339,357. One correction to the reader: the claim that INT addresses can collide WITHIN one CCU is a reading of the truncation branch, not an observed collision — nothing in the source bounds the group-id counter, so whether a CCU ever reaches 8-digit group ids is unestablished. State it as a code path, not as a fact about real installs.

all.title: Display geometry (5 rows, 24 characters) is asserted without a source and is published to Home Assistant as a hard limit
all.ourValue: maxDisplayID = 5 (rows 1..5, enforced at textdisplay.go:527); MaxRowLength = 24 bytes, enforced as `len(r.Text) > MaxRowLength` (textdisplay.go:153) and republished as HA's `"max": 24` (payload.go:122)
all.firmwareValue: row count: DISPLAY_DATA_ID MIN=1 MAX=5 on HmIP-WRCD — matches. Row length: DISPLAY_DATA_STRING's declared MAX is the constraint regex `[0x20-0x7E]{16}` — 16 characters, restricted to printable ASCII 0x20..0x7E, not 24 bytes of anything
all.citation: HMIPServer de.eq3.cbcs.devicedescription.channelspecification.stateparameter.GeneralStateParameterFactory — the DISPLAY_DATA_ID entries register three variants via #createDisplayDataIDParameter, keyed "two" (1,2), "five" (1,5) and "eight" (0,7); DISPLAY_DATA_STRING is registered via #createDisplayDataStringParameter with the max-value regex `[0x20-0x7E]{16}` (default, ASCII converter), `[U+00-U+FF]{16}` ("utf8") and `[U+00-U+FF]{14}[0-9A-F]{0,4}` ("wgd"). Tier 2, the device's own declaration: ../pydevccu/pydevccu/paramset_descriptions/HmIP-WRCD.json, channel VCU4243444:3 VALUES — DISPLAY_DATA_ID {TYPE INTEGER, MIN 1, MAX 5, DEFAULT 1, OPERATIONS 2}; DISPLAY_DATA_STRING {TYPE STRING, MIN "", MAX "[0x20-0x7E]{16}", DEFAULT "", OPERATIONS 2}
all.finding: Our profile is scoped to exactly one device: internal/model/custom/profiles.go:1429-1438 registers IPTextDisplay for DeviceType "hmip-wrcd", channel 3. Within that scope maxDisplayID = 5 is right, and both tiers agree (the WRCD descriptor declares MIN 1 / MAX 5; the firmware's "five" variant is createDisplayDataIDParameter(1, 5)). Note it is right only in that scope — the same parameter is registered with (1,2) and (0,7) for other display channels, so the constant must not be lifted to a fleet-wide rule, and the honest source is the runtime descriptor's MIN/MAX rather than a literal. MaxRowLength = 24 is wrong by 8: firmware and descriptor both cap the row at 16 characters, and additionally restrict the alphabet to 0x20..0x7E (the default variant's converter is the ASCII one). Two consequences, both reaching the device: a 17..24-character row passes our validator and goes out in the put_paramset for the CCU to truncate or reject, and HA is told `max: 24` so operators are invited to type 8 characters that cannot arrive. Our comment cites "the HmIP-SDV* firmware limit" — no HmIP-SDV device appears in the pydevccu descriptor corpus, in ../openccu-data, or in ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/, so that attribution is unsourced as well as numerically wrong. Also worth recording: the descriptor's MAX for a STRING parameter is a constraint regex, not a length, so any code that reads MAX numerically will read nothing usable — the 16 has to be parsed out of the regex or kept as a WRCD-scoped constant with this citation. Separately, the doc comment at textdisplay.go:519 ("Validation: ID must be >= 1") understates the code, which enforces an upper bound too.
all.negativeControl: Had maxDisplayID been wrong, the WRCD descriptor would have declared a different pair — 1/2 or 0/7, the two other variants the firmware registers — and rows 3..5 (or row 0) would have been mis-gated; it declares 1/5. Had MaxRowLength = 24 been right, the declared MAX would read `{24}` or a numeric 24 in at least one of the four DISPLAY_DATA_STRING variants the firmware registers; none contains a 24, and the WRCD's own declaration reads `[0x20-0x7E]{16}`.
all.challengeNote: UPHELD on the contradiction, with the consequence narrowed. Right surface established: internal/model/custom/profiles.go:1429-1438 registers IPTextDisplay for DeviceType "hmip-wrcd" channel 3 only, and the WRCD descriptor's channel :3 is exactly where both DISPLAY_DATA_ID and DISPLAY_DATA_STRING live — so the factory's default (non-utf8, non-bwth, non-wgd) variant is the one this profile writes. maxDisplayID = 5 is right and doubly sourced (firmware "five" variant = (1,5); descriptor MIN 1 / MAX 5); it must stay WRCD-scoped, since the same parameter is also registered (1,2) and (0,7). MaxRowLength = 24 is wrong by 8 in both tiers: 16, not 24. The "HmIP-SDV*" attribution in the comment is unsourced — no HmIP-SDV appears in ../pydevccu, ../openccu-data or ../OpenCCU-Base/src/devicetypes/. THREE CORRECTIONS to the reader. (1) The reader's downstream claim "for the CCU to truncate or reject" is not sourced and I could not source it: the converter bound to this parameter is the no-arg AsciiStringToInteger, whose length field is 0, so #convertLogicalToPhysical allocates `temp.length + 1` bytes and truncates nothing, and I found no length or regex validation of STRING values on the legacy put_paramset path (DeviceUtil#convertParameterValue special-cases only the Unicode/WGD converters and METER_OBIS_SEARCH_STRING). What a 17..24-character row actually does at the device is therefore UNVERIFIED — say that rather than "truncate or reject". (2) The converter's charset is ISO_8859_1, so the 0x20..0x7E alphabet is a DECLARED constraint, not one the conversion enforces. (3) Our validator counts BYTES (`len(r.Text)`) while the declared limit counts characters; inside the declared alphabet these coincide, but a UTF-8 non-ASCII row would be measured wrongly by our check as well. What our code should follow here is the runtime descriptor (MIN/MAX read from the device), not a literal — the firmware's per-variant registration is precisely why a fleet-wide constant is unsafe.

all.title: "<model> <channel address>" is asserted to be the CCU's auto-generated channel name
all.ourValue: autoDefault := strings.TrimSpace(model + " " + channel.Address) — a channel name equal to that is discarded in favour of the synthetic "<device name>:<channel no>"
all.firmwareValue: a never-renamed channel comes back from ReGa as exactly `<TYPE> <channel address>`, single space — e.g. `HmIP-MIO16-PCB VCU9846297:1` for the channel at VCU9846297:1 on a device of type HmIP-MIO16-PCB
all.citation: Recorded live-CCU response: ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic_test_support/data/full_session_randomized_ccu.json, path jsonrpc → Device.listAllDetail → result[] → channels[].name. Across the 124 devices in that capture, 968 channels classify as: 46 exactly `<type> <channel address>` (all on the one device whose channels were never renamed), 494 `<device name>:<no>` (the WebUI rename shape), 428 free operator labels. Zero channels carry any other machine-generated shape. Tier-3 witness for where our rule came from: ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/model/support.py:538 — `default_channel_name = f"{channel.device.model} {channel.address}"`, compared at :541 and replaced at :542 with `f"{channel.device.name}:{channel.no}"`, which is our code line for line.
all.finding: Our site does what the reader summarised, and I confirmed the exact concatenation (model, one space, the FULL channel address including the :no suffix — not the device address). Tier 1 is silent here and I want that on the record: the name is minted by ReGaHss, which ships in the OCCU tree only as a binary (../OpenCCU-Base/bin/{x86_64,aarch64,arm,i686}-*/ReGaHss). I grepped its strings for a naming format and found none that can be attributed to channel creation — the `%s %d` and `%s-%d` literals near the ESP interpreter and CreateServiceMessageDP are other call sites, and claiming either would be exactly the guess this audit exists to catch. Nothing in src/tclrega, src/webui/rega or www/rega constructs a channel name either; they only read chn.Name(). So the grounding is the CCU's own answer over JSON-RPC rather than the CCU's source, which is why I am reporting tier 2 rather than tier 1. Within that limit the evidence is unambiguous and the sample is large. One boundary the rule does not cover: the capture is HmIP (VCU addresses) only — I found no never-renamed BidCos channel in it, so whether a BidCos-RF channel's auto-default uses the same concatenation is untested. If you want that closed, a `Device.listAllDetail` on a CCU with a freshly taught-in BidCos device is the one call that settles it.
all.negativeControl: Had the auto-default been `<model>:<no>`, the bare channel address, or the device serial without the channel suffix, those 46 never-renamed MIO16 channels would carry that shape and zero would match `<type> <channel address>`; they match it exactly, 46 of 46, and no channel anywhere in the capture matches the alternatives. Conversely, had our rule been too greedy, some of the 428 free labels would have collided with the pattern — none does.
all.challengeNote: DEMOTED from confirmed to narrowed — the measurement reproduces exactly, but both its tier and its scope were overstated. I re-ran it independently over the capture: 124 unique devices, 968 channels, 46 matching `<type> <space> <full channel address>`, 494 matching `<device name>:<no>`, 428 free labels — the reader's numbers to the unit (the raw file holds each device twice; de-duplicated it lands on exactly those figures). SCOPE, and this is the demotion: all 46 auto-default channels come from ONE device, HmIP-MIO16-PCB at VCU9846297. n = 1 never-renamed device on one CCU, not a 968-channel sample.
